#### F3_semantic_groups_table
| Group Label | Definition | Representative Expressions | Overlapping / Ambiguous Items | Boundary Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Expressions used in asserting or denying that a statement is true | These expressions appear in contexts where a speaker is affirming or rejecting the factual accuracy of a claim, account, or statement, or making, supporting, or challenging a claim about whether something said or reported corresponds to what actually happened or is the case. They are contrasted with each other directly in usage (e.g., *Òtítọ́ ni ó sọ* vs. *Irọ́ ni ó sọ*) and appear in the same syntactic frames with *sọ* (to say/speak), *ni* (focus/copula), and *kò sí...nínú ọ̀rọ̀ rẹ̀* (there is no...in his/her words). They are used in legal testimony, everyday dispute, and moral instruction. The core contrast is between *sọ òtítọ́* (speak the truth) and *sọ irọ́* (tell a lie), which function as a matched pair across moral, legal, and everyday discourse. | *òtítọ́*; *irọ́*; *sọ òtítọ́*; *sọ irọ́*; *pa irọ́*; *má sọ irọ́*; *òtítọ́ ni*; *Òtítọ́ ni ó sọ*; *Irọ́ ni ó sọ*; *Kò sí òtítọ́ nínú ọ̀rọ̀ rẹ̀*; *Kò sí irọ́ nínú ọ̀rọ̀ rẹ̀*; *fi òtítọ́ sọ̀rọ̀*; *ọ̀rọ̀ òtítọ́*; *ọ̀rọ̀ tọ́*; *ìsọ̀rọ̀ tọ́*; *irọ́ pátápátá*; *òtítọ́ pátápátá*; *irọ́ tótóbi*; *irọ́ funfun*; *olòtítọ́*; *olóirọ́*; *Ó farahàn pé òtítọ́ ni*; *A mọ̀ pé irọ́ ni*; *Òtítọ́ kò ní kú*; *dájúdájú*; *ìjẹ́ òtítọ́*; *ìwádìí òtítọ́* | *ọ̀rọ̀ tọ́* and *ìsọ̀rọ̀ tọ́* shade toward Group 2; *irọ́ funfun* is marginal within this group in that it introduces a gradation not present in the core contrast; *dájúdájú* functions specifically as an intensifier within this group — it does not name truth or falsehood but marks the speaker's certainty about a claim; *ìjẹ́ òtítọ́* and *ìwádìí òtítọ́* appear at the procedural end of truth-assertion contexts rather than in simple first-person assertion | *òtítọ́* and *irọ́* are the most consistently paired terms in the entire dataset. They appear in parallel constructions (*sọ òtítọ́* / *sọ irọ́*), in parallel proverbs (*òtítọ́ kò ní kú* / *irọ́ kò ní dúró*), and in the compound *ẹlẹ́rìí irọ́* (false witness), which is formed by negating the truth-function of the witness role. *ọ̀rọ̀ tọ́* and *ìsọ̀rọ̀ tọ́* also belong here as they evaluate utterances for accuracy, though they shade toward Group 2 as well. *irọ́ funfun* (white lie) is marginal within this group in that it introduces a gradation not present in the core contrast. *dájúdájú* functions specifically as an intensifier within this group — it does not name truth or falsehood but marks the speaker's certainty about a claim. *ìjẹ́ òtítọ́* and *ìwádìí òtítọ́* are compound expressions that presuppose the existence of truth as something that can be admitted or sought; they appear at the procedural end of truth-assertion contexts rather than in simple first-person assertion. |
| Expressions used to evaluate whether something conforms to a standard of correctness or propriety | These expressions appear in contexts where an action, measurement, answer, procedure, or statement is assessed against a criterion of correctness or accuracy, or where the question is not primarily whether a statement is true, but whether an action, decision, procedure, object, or person meets a recognized standard of what is right, proper, or correct. They are not restricted to speech acts and apply broadly to objects, measurements, conduct, and decisions. The predicative construction *ó tọ́* / *kò tọ́* (it is correct / it is not correct) is the most basic instantiation of this group, and the root *tọ́* is the morphological core. The evaluative predicate *ó tọ́* / *kò tọ́* is the anchor of this group, and it appears across factual, moral, procedural, and social domains. | *tọ́*; *òtọ́*; *ó tọ́*; *kò tọ́*; *ó tọ́ pé*; *kò tọ́ pé*; *ìtọ́*; *àìtọ́*; *ìtọ́sí*; *tọ́ sí*; *àtúntọ́* / *ìtúntọ́*; *ìtọ́ni*; *ọ̀nà tọ́*; *ìdáhùn tọ́*; *ìpinnu tọ́*; *àkọsílẹ̀ tọ́*; *ìsọ tọ́*; *ìwà tọ́*; *ìwọ̀n tọ́*; *ìlànà tọ́*; *ìgbésẹ̀ tọ́*; *àṣìṣe*; *Ó tọ́ pé kí a sọ òtítọ́*; *Kò tọ́ pé kí o sọ irọ́*; *Ó tọ́ gẹ́gẹ́ bí ó ti yẹ*; *Ẹ tọ́ ọ sí ọ̀nà tó tọ́* | *ọ̀rọ̀ tọ́* and *ìsọ̀rọ̀ tọ́* shade toward Group 1; *ìwà tọ́* overlaps with Group 4; *àṣìṣe* also appears in Group 4 | This group is the largest and most diffuse. The root *tọ́* appears in factual contexts (Group 1), moral contexts (Group 4), legal contexts (Group 3), and procedural/administrative contexts. The expressions here are those where the evaluative function of *tọ́* is most clearly foregrounded without being reducible to any single domain. *ó tọ́* functions as a discourse marker of affirmation across all these contexts. *ìwà tọ́* overlaps with Group 4 (the character evaluation domain), but in usage it appears specifically in moral evaluation of persons rather than in procedural or factual correctness contexts. |
| Expressions used in legal and formal proceedings to establish what happened | These expressions appear specifically in contexts where the truth of a past event or claim is being formally established through testimony, evidence, questioning, or judgment, or where a party is required to produce, evaluate, or formally accept evidence about events or facts. They are associated with the roles of witness, judge, and party in a proceeding, and they participate in constructions about producing, evaluating, accepting, or rejecting proof. They cluster around the root *ẹ̀rí* (evidence, witness, related to *rí*, to see) and involve distinctions between types of evidence (direct, circumstantial, documentary, hearsay, expert) and between valid and invalid evidence. #### F3_semantic_groups_table
| Group Label | Definition | Representative Expressions | Overlapping / Ambiguous Items | Boundary Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Propositional truth and falsity attribution; asserting or denying that a claim is the case | These expressions are used in Finnish to evaluate whether a proposition, statement, or claim corresponds to how things are. They appear in contexts where a speaker is affirming, denying, or questioning the truth of something said or believed. They are used predicatively (*se on tosi*, *väite on epätosi*), attributively (*väärä väite*, *epätosi väite*), or in constructions that introduce or frame a truth claim (*totuus on se, että...*). They appear in everyday speech, journalism, and formal writing. The core contrast in this group is between expressions that affirm truth and those that deny it. | *tosi*; *totuus*; *epätosi*; *epätotuus*; *pitää paikkansa*; *ei pidä paikkaansa*; *olla totta*; *totta puhuen*; *puhua totta*; *sanoa totta*; *totuusarvo*; *totuudenmukainen*; *totuudenmukaisuus*; *totuudenvastainen*; *totuudenvastaisuus*; *todella*; *todennäköinen*; *todennäköisyys*; *todennäköisesti*; *todenperäinen*; *todenperäisyys*; *tosiseikka*; *tosiasia*; *tosiasiallinen*; *toden totta*; *tosiaan*; *totta kai*; *tosipohjainen*; *todenmukainen*; *todenmukaisuus*; *todenmukaisesti*; *totuudenmukaisesti*; *tosiasia on, että*; *totuus on, että*; *totuus tulee ilmi*; *totuus paljastuu*; *osoittaa epätodeksi*; *todistaa vääräksi*; *osoittautua vääräksi*; *osoittautua oikeaksi*; *väärä* (in propositional use) | *väärä* (see also Ambiguous Items); *totuudenmukaisuus* (bridges this group and Group 4, conformity to standard) | *Todennäköinen* and its derivatives belong here because they are built on the same root and function in the same evaluative space, but they introduce degree rather than binary assertion. *Todenmukainen* and *todenmukaisuus* shade into Group 10 (accuracy evaluation), since their primary context is aesthetic and journalistic evaluation of how faithfully something represents reality. *Tosiaan* and *totta kai* are primarily affirmative particles in spoken Finnish and are only loosely connected to the epistemic core of this group. *Totuudenmukaisuus* bridges this group and Group 4 (conformity to standard): it concerns both truth and conformity to truth as a standard for statements and accounts. |
| Conformity to a standard, norm, or rule; expressions for evaluating whether something meets a standard or norm | These expressions are used when Finnish speakers evaluate whether an answer, action, procedure, or text conforms to what is required, expected, or proper. They are concentrated in administrative, legal, linguistic, and procedural registers. The standard or norm may be explicit (a rule, a qualification requirement, a prescribed procedure) or implicit (common usage, professional expectation). The key distinction from Group 1 is that these expressions do not primarily assert correspondence to reality but rather conformity to a rule or norm: *oikeellisuus* concerns conformity to a linguistic or procedural standard; *totuudenmukaisuus* concerns conformity to the truth as a standard for statements; *oikeakielisyys* concerns conformity to prescriptive language norms. The contrast between *oikeellisuus* (rule-conformity) and *totuus* (correspondence to fact) is explicitly noted in P1. | *oikea*; *oikein*; *olla oikeassa*; *oikeellisuus*; *oikeakielisyys*; *oikeakielinen*; *oikeaoppinen*; *oikeaoppisuus*; *vääräoppinen*; *vääräoppisuus*; *oikaista*; *oikaisu*; *väärä*; *väärin*; *väärinkäsitys*; *väärintulkinta*; *väärintulkita*; *asianmukainen*; *asianmukaisuus*; *asianmukaisesti*; *asianmukainen menettely*; *asianmukainen dokumentaatio*; *poliittinen oikeellisuus*; *tarkistaa oikeellisuus*; *varmistaa tietojen oikeellisuus*; *vastata tietojen oikeellisuudesta*; *perusteeton*; *tarkka*; *tarkkuus*; *tarkasti*; *tarkasti ottaen*; *totuudenmukaisuus*; *totuudenmukainen* | *väärä* (see also Ambiguous Items); *oikea* (highly polysemous — see Ambiguous Items); *perusteeton* (sits between Group 1 and this group — see Ambiguous Items); *totuudenmukaisuus* (see Group 1 and Ambiguous Items); *totuudenmukainen* (see Group 1 and Ambiguous Items) | *Oikeaoppinen* and *vääräoppinen* are specifically about doctrinal conformity and are somewhat peripheral to the core of this group, which is more administrative and procedural. |
| Evaluating genuineness and authenticity versus imitation | These expressions are used when Finnish speakers evaluate whether an object, document, person, or emotion is the real thing as opposed to an imitation, forgery, or performance. They appear in art authentication, consumer protection, legal proceedings, and everyday character evaluation. The central contrast is between *aito* / *alkuperäinen* (genuine/original) and *jäljitelmä* / *väärennös* / *epäaito* (imitation/forgery/inauthentic). The translative constructions *osoittautua aidoksi*, *osoittautua väärennökseksi*, and *todistaa aidoksi* are characteristic of this group. | *aito*; *aitous*; *aidosti*; *aito ja alkuperäinen*; *epäaito*; *epäaitous*; *alkuperäinen*; *alkuperäisyys*; *alkuperäiskappale*; *alkuperäisversio*; *jäljitelmä*; *halpa jäljitelmä*; *pelkkä jäljitelmä*; *jäljitellä*; *jäljittely*; *jäljittelemätön*; *väärennös*; *väärennösepäily*; *epäillä väärennöstä*; *todistaa aidoksi*; *osoittautua aidoksi*; *kyseenalaistaa aitous*; *ei ole aito*; *aito vai väärennös*; *aitoustodistus*; *oikea* (in the sense of genuine) | *väärennös* (also belongs to Group 7, deliberate falsification and fraud); *oikea* (see also Ambiguous Items) | *Aito* and *alkuperäinen* overlap but are not identical: *aito* asserts non-counterfeit status, while *alkuperäinen* asserts temporal priority (being the first version). *Epäaito* and *epäaitous* are used more in philosophical and personal identity contexts than in the object-authentication contexts where *väärennös* and *jäljitelmä* appear. *Jäljitelmä* does not imply fraudulent intent, distinguishing it from *väärennös*. *Kopio* (neutral copy) sits at the edge of this group: it does not inherently imply inauthenticity or fraud, unlike *jäljitelmä* or *väärennös*, and is therefore listed under items without a clear group. |
| Evidence, proof, and their procedural handling in legal and investigative discourse | These expressions cluster in legal, judicial, and investigative contexts where the task is to establish what actually occurred, who is responsible, and what evidence supports a conclusion. They appear in court proceedings, criminal investigations, and formal legal texts. The cluster is organized around the *todistaa* / *todistus* / *todiste* family and the associated procedural vocabulary. The cluster includes both the acts of proving and testifying, the products of those acts, the persons involved, and the procedural concepts governing how evidence is handled. | *todistaa*; *todistaminen*; *todistus*; *todistaja*; *todistajanlausunto*; *todiste*; *todistusaineisto*; *todistustaakka*; *todistusvoima*; *todistuskeino*; *todistuskappale*; *todistusketju*; *todistusharkinta*; *todistusstandardi*; *vapaa todistusharkinta*; *todistusharkinnan vapaus*; *todistettava*; *todistettu*; *todistamaton*; *todistetusti*; *todistettavasti*; *todentaa*; *todentaminen*; *syntymätodistus*; *kuolemantodistus*; *lääkärintodistus*; *koulutodistus*; *työtodistus*; *aitoustodistus*; *tarkistaa*; *tarkistus*; *tarkistaja*; *väärä todistus*; *väärä vala*; *valheellinen*; *valheellisuus*; *valheellisesti todistaa*; *perusteeton*; *perusteltu*; *perusteltu epäilys*; *oikeuden edessä*; *viedä oikeuteen*; *väärennysrikos*; *totuus tulee ilmi* | *tarkistaa* (also Group 5); *todentaa* (also Group 5); *todentaminen* (also Group 5); *valheellinen* (also Group 8 and Group 11); *valheellisuus* (also Group 8 and Group 11) | *Tarkistaa* and *todentaa* appear here because they function in verification roles within legal and administrative proceedings, though they also appear in non-legal contexts (see Group 5). *Valheellinen* belongs here because its primary register is legal and its primary referent is testimony, though it also appears in Group 8 (honesty evaluation of persons). The certificate compounds (*syntymätodistus*, *lääkärintodistus*, etc.) are administrative rather than strictly evidentiary, but they share the same base and the same function of certifying a fact. *Todistaa oikeaksi* and *todistaa aidoksi* also connect to Group 3 (authenticity evaluation). |
| Checking and verification acts; administrative contexts for checking, verifying, and confirming | These expressions describe acts of checking, verifying, inspecting, or monitoring — whether of documents, data, persons, or situations. They appear in administrative, bureaucratic, technical, and scientific contexts where the task is to confirm that data, documents, credentials, or procedures meet required standards. They are used by institutions, officials, and systems rather than primarily in interpersonal or philosophical discourse. The distinction between *tarkistaa* (to check/verify, everyday) and *tarkastaa* (to inspect/audit, formal/official) is register-based and semantically significant: *tarkastaa* implies an authoritative or institutional inspection, while *tarkistaa* is used for routine checking. *Todentaa* (to verify/authenticate) is more technical and is increasingly associated with IT security contexts. | *tarkistaa*; *tarkistus*; *tarkistaja*; *tarkistaminen*; *tarkastaa*; *tarkastus*; *tarkastaja*; *tarkkailla*; *tarkkailu*; *tarkkailija*; *tarkkaavainen*; *tarkkaavaisuus*; *tarkka silmä*; *todentaa*; *todentaminen*; *todennus*; *todentaa henkilöllisyys*; *kaksivaiheinen todennus*; *pätevä*; *pätevyys*; *pätevyysvaatimus*; *pätevyystodistus*; *täyttää pätevyysvaatimukset*; *pätemätön*; *pätemättömyys*; *oikeellisuustarkistus*; *tietojen oikeellisuus*; *asianmukainen*; *asianmukaisesti*; *asianmukainen menettely*; *asianmukainen dokumentaatio*; *luotettavuusarvio*; *tarkkuusvaatimus*; *mittaustarkkuus*; *tarkistaa oikeellisuus* | *tarkistaa* (also Group 4); *todentaa* (also Group 4); *todentaminen* (also Group 4); *pätevä* (also Group 7); *asianmukainen* (also Group 2) | This group overlaps with Group 4 (legal contexts) and Group 2 (norm-conformity) but is distinguished by its specifically administrative and procedural character: the evaluation is performed by an institution or system against formal requirements, and the outcome is typically a binary pass/fail determination. *Tarkkailu* shades into surveillance contexts that are not strictly about truth or accuracy. *Tarkkaavainen* and *tarkkaavaisuus* are more about attentiveness as a personal quality than about verification acts. |
| Evaluating reliability and credibility of sources, persons, and claims | These expressions are used when Finnish speakers evaluate whether a source of information, a witness, an institution, or a claim is such that it can be relied upon or believed. They appear in journalistic, academic, legal, and everyday discourse. The cluster is organized around the contrast between *luotettava* (reliable, dependable) and *uskottava* (credible, believable), which are distinct in Finnish usage: *luotettava lähde* concerns whether a source can be depended upon over time, while *uskottava selitys* concerns whether a specific explanation is believable. | *luotettava*; *luotettavuus*; *luotettavasti*; *epäluotettava*; *epäluotettavuus*; *luotettava lähde*; *luotettava todistaja*; *pitää luotettavana*; *pitää epäluotettavana*; *osoittautua luotettavaksi*; *osoittautua epäluotettavaksi*; *kyseenalaistaa luotettavuus*; *luotettavuusongelma*; *luotettavuuden arviointi*; *heikentää luotettavuutta*; *ei kovin luotettava*; *uskottava*; *uskottavuus*; *uskottavasti*; *epäuskottava*; *epäuskottavuus*; *uskottava selitys*; *uskottava uhka*; *uskottava todistaja*; *tehdä uskottavaksi*; *pitää uskottavana*; *vaikuttaa uskottavalta*; *horjuttaa uskottavuutta*; *menettää uskottavuus*; *uskottavuuden arviointi*; *nauttia uskottavuutta*; *osoittautua luotettavaksi* | (none stated) | The P1 and P2 data explicitly distinguish *luotettava* (reliability/dependability) from *uskottava* (believability/credibility), and Finnish usage maintains this distinction. | Paired truth-assertion and falsity-assertion formulas / Expressions used to assert or deny that a statement is true | These expressions function as the primary predicative formulas for asserting that something is true or false in Basque. They appear in direct parallel syntactic environments (*egia da* / *gezurra da*), are explicitly contrasted with each other, and together constitute the baseline binary for propositional evaluation in everyday, legal, and philosophical discourse. They are used in argumentative discourse, testimony, and everyday factual exchange. The pair is so tightly linked that derivational families, collocations, and discourse functions mirror each other systematically. | *egia*; *egia da*; *egia esan*; *egia hutsa*; *egia osoa eta ezer ez besterik*; *egia esateko*; *egia da, baina...*; *egia da ala ez?*; *egia da ala gezurra?*; *gezurra*; *gezurra da*; *gezurra esan*; *gezurra zabaldu*; *gezurra eta egia nahastu*; *gezurretan ari da*; *gezurra txuri*; *gezurra sinestu*; *oker egon*; *zuzen egon*; *oker nago*; *ziur nago*; *ziur ez egon*; *oker ez banago* | *ziur nago* and *ziur ez egon* also appear in Group 2 (epistemic certainty expressions); *zuzen* and *oker* also appear in Groups 5 and 9 in their other uses | The parallelism is morphological, derivational, and discursive. *Ziur nago* and *ziur ez egon* shade into Group 2 and are listed in both. *Zuzen* and *oker* appear here in their propositional-correctness uses but have additional uses in other contexts. |

| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | உண்மையில் என்ன நடந்தது என்று யாருக்கும் தெரியாது | uṇmaiyil eṉṉa naṭantatu eṉṟu yārukum teriyātu | nobody knows what actually happened, what really happened is unknown to anyone | Extended construction using *uṇmaiyil* as an adverbial frame for an embedded question; illustrates the use of *uṇmaiyil* to introduce a contrast between appearance and reality in complex sentence structures. Common in journalistic and narrative Tamil. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | உண்மை நிலை என்ன? | uṇmai nilai eṉṉa? | What is the actual state of affairs? / What is the true situation? | An interrogative construction using *uṇmai nilai* (true state/condition) as a nominal phrase. Common in journalistic and administrative Tamil when questioning the accuracy of official accounts or reports. The construction presupposes a gap between appearance and reality. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | உண்மை என்னவென்றால்... | uṇmai eṉṉaveṉṟāl... | The truth is that... / What the truth is, is... | A fixed discourse-framing construction used to introduce a clarification or correction of the actual state of affairs. Functions as a topic-introducing frame in spoken and written Tamil. Extremely common across all registers. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | இதில் உண்மை இல்லை | itil uṇmai illai | There is no truth in this / This has no truth to it | A predicative construction using the existential negative *illai* (there is not) to deny the truth of a claim or statement. Common in everyday speech and in formal rebuttals. The locative *itil* (in this) is the standard framing. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | கொஞ்சமாவது உண்மை இருக்கா? | koñcamāvatu uṇmai irukkā? | Is there even a little truth (in this)? | A rhetorical or genuine question construction combining *uṇmai* with the existential *irukku* (there is) and the scalar particle *koñcamāvatu* (at least a little, even a bit). Common in skeptical or accusatory everyday speech. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | உண்மையை நேருக்கு நேர் சொல் | uṇmaiyai nērukku nēr col | Tell the truth face to face / Say it directly to (someone's) face | A construction combining *uṇmai* in the accusative with the fixed adverbial *nērukku nēr* (face to face, directly) and the verb *col* (to say). Emphasizes directness and courage in truth-telling. Common in interpersonal and moral discourse. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | உண்மை என்று நிரூபிக்கணும் | uṇmai eṉṟu nirūpikkāṇum | (It) must be proved to be true / (One) must prove that it is true | A deontic construction combining *uṇmai* with the quotative *eṉṟu* and the verb *nirūpikka* (to prove, to demonstrate). Common in legal and argumentative contexts where the burden of proof is at issue. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | அது உண்மைதான் | atu uṇmaitāṉ | that is indeed true, that is the truth (emphatic) | Predicative construction with *uṇmai* as predicate nominal and *-tāṉ* as emphatic particle; used in spoken Tamil to affirm a statement as true, often in response to a challenge or to emphasize agreement. Extremely common in everyday speech. The particle *tāṉ* adds a sense of acknowledgment or concession. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | உண்மை தான் வெல்லும் | uṇmai tāṉ vellum | Truth alone will prevail / It is truth that will win | A proverbial construction asserting the ultimate triumph of truth. The particle *tāṉ* (alone, only, it is precisely) adds contrastive emphasis. Extremely common in moral and political discourse; appears in speeches, proverbs, and popular culture. Closely related to the Gandhian motto *satyamēva jayatē* in its Tamil cultural function. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | உண்மை எப்போதும் வெல்லும் | uṇmai eppōtum vellum | truth always wins, truth always prevails | Proverbial construction with *vell* (to win, to prevail); a widely attested moral and motivational expression in Tamil, appearing in literature, political speech, and everyday moral discourse. Reflects a culturally salient belief in the ultimate triumph of truth. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | அது உண்மையா? | atu uṇmaiyā? | is that true? is that really so? | Interrogative construction with *uṇmai* as predicate nominal and the question particle *-ā*; the standard way to ask whether a statement is true in spoken Tamil. Extremely common across all registers. The affirmative response *ām, uṇmai* (yes, it is true) is equally frequent. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | உண்மை என்றாலும் சொல்ல வேண்டாம் | uṇmai eṉṟālum colla vēṇṭām | even if it is true, (you) need not say it; even true things need not be said | Concessive conditional construction (*eṉṟālum* = even if it is said/even though); used in pragmatic and moral instruction about the limits of truth-telling, expressing the idea that truth alone does not always justify utterance. Appears in proverb-like and advisory speech. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | உண்மை கசக்கும் | uṇmai kacakkum | the truth is bitter, truth tastes bitter | Idiomatic construction using *kacakku* (to be bitter, to taste bitter); a widely used expression in Tamil to convey that true statements are often unpleasant to hear. Functions as a proverbial observation and appears in everyday speech, literature, and moral discourse. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | உண்மை தெரியும் வரை காத்திரு | uṇmai teriyum varai kāttiru | wait until the truth is known, wait until the truth comes out | Temporal subordinate clause construction (*teriyum varai* = until it becomes known) used in everyday and narrative Tamil to advise patience pending the revelation of facts. Common in spoken Tamil. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | உண்மையை ஒப்புக்கொள் | uṇmaiyai oppukkoḷ | admit the truth, acknowledge the truth | Accusative construction with *oppukkoḷ* (to accept, to admit, to acknowledge); used in legal, interpersonal, and moral contexts for the act of admitting what is true, especially when previously denied. Common in legal discourse and everyday confrontational speech. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | உண்மையை ஒப்புக்கொள்ளணும் | uṇmaiyai oppukkoḷḷāṇum | (One) must acknowledge / admit the truth | A deontic construction combining *uṇmai* in the accusative with the verb *oppukkoḷ* (to accept, to acknowledge, to admit) and the obligative suffix. Common in moral, legal, and interpersonal contexts where admission of facts is at issue. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | உண்மையை ஒத்துக்கொண்டான் | uṇmaiyai ottukkōṇṭāṉ | He admitted the truth / He acknowledged the truth | Construction using *ottukkō* (to admit, acknowledge, concede) with *uṇmai* as accusative object. Common in legal, interpersonal, and narrative contexts to describe the act of admitting a true state of affairs. The construction implies prior concealment or denial. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | உண்மையை திரிக்காதே | uṇmaiyai tirikāte | don't distort the truth, don't twist the truth | Accusative construction with *tiri* (to twist, to distort) in the negative imperative; used in moral and legal condemnation of misrepresentation that falls short of outright lying but involves distortion of facts. Common in journalistic and political discourse. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | உண்மையை முழுவதும் சொல்லவில்லை | uṇmaiyai muḻuvatum collavillai | (he/she) did not tell the whole truth, the full truth was not told | Construction with *muḻuvatum* (completely, fully) as an adverbial modifier; used in legal and moral contexts to characterize partial disclosure as a form of deception. The construction implies that selective truth-telling is itself a form of concealment. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | உண்மையை நம்பவில்லை | uṇmaiyai nampavil̲l̲ai | (He/she/they) did not believe the truth | Construction using *nampu* (to believe/trust) with *uṇmai* as accusative object in the negative. Used in narrative and moral discourse to describe the failure or refusal to accept a true state of affairs. Highlights the distinction between truth and its acceptance. | [CORE] |
| உண்மை / *uṇmai* | உண்மையை எதிர்கொள்ள வேண்டும் | uṇmaiyai etiṟkoḷḷa vēṇṭum | One must face the truth / It is necessary to confront the truth | A deontic construction using *etiṟkoḷ* (to face, confront) + *vēṇṭum*. Used in moral, psychological, and journalistic discourse to express the obligation to acknowledge difficult truths. Less common than *uṇmaiyai aṟiya vēṇṭum* but well-attested in written Tamil. | [CORE] |

#### F3_semantic_groups_table
| Group Label | Definition | Representative Expressions | Overlapping / Ambiguous Items | Boundary Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Asserting and denying factual correspondence / truth-as-correspondence | These expressions are used in contexts where a speaker asserts, affirms, questions, or denies whether a claim, statement, or situation matches what is actually the case. They appear in predicative constructions (*atu uṇmaitāṉ*, *atu uṇmaiyā?*), in adverbial frames that contrast appearance with reality (*uṇmaiyil*, *uṇmaiyilēyē*), and in fixed evaluative phrases used to characterize statements as factually accurate or inaccurate. The core contrast operative in this group is between what is claimed or appears to be the case and what actually is the case. The central contrast is between *uṇmai* and *poy*, which function as direct antonyms across a wide range of registers. | உண்மை / *uṇmai*; பொய் / *poy*; உண்மையான / *uṇmaiyāna*; பொய்யான / *poyyāna*; உண்மையாக / *uṇmaiyāka*; பொய்யாக / *poyyāka*; உண்மையில் / *uṇmaiyil*; உண்மையிலேயே / *uṇmaiyilēyē*; மெய் / *mey*; மெய்ம்மை / *meymmai*; மெய்யான / *meyyāna*; உண்மைத்தன்மை / *uṇmaitaṉmai*; பொய்மை / *poymai*; உண்மையற்ற / *uṇmaiyaṟṟa*; பொய்யில்லாத / *poyyillāta*; உண்மைக்கு மாறான / *uṇmaikkum māṟāna*; சரி / *cari*; தவறு / *tavaṟu* | *uṇmai* and *mey* are near-synonyms in this function but differ in register; *cari* and *tavaṟu* overlap with this group when used to evaluate the accuracy of statements, but they also participate in Group 8; *meyyē vellum* also participates in Group 9 | *uṇmai* is the default across all registers; *mey* is confined to literary, philosophical, and formal contexts; *cari* and *tavaṟu* overlap with Group 8 (correctness and accuracy in practical contexts) |
| Truth coming to light / revelation of concealed facts | These expressions are used in narrative, journalistic, and legal contexts where the focus is on the movement of information between concealment and disclosure — truth coming to light, being suppressed, being sought, or being admitted. They cluster around verbs of motion (*veḷippaṭu*, *teriya va*), concealment (*maṟai*, *mūṭu*), and admission (*ottukkō*), and they presuppose a gap between what is actually the case and what is publicly known or acknowledged. They appear in intransitive constructions where truth is treated as an entity that moves from concealment to visibility, and in constructions describing the acts of hiding or revealing. This group is defined by a specific narrative and processual pattern rather than by a single root, and is distinct from Group 1 in that these expressions are not primarily about evaluating whether something is true, but about the social and epistemic process of truth becoming known or being hidden. | உண்மை வெளியே வந்தது / *uṇmai veḷiyē vantatu*; உண்மை தெரிய வந்தது / *uṇmai teriya vantatu*; உண்மை வெளிப்படுதல் / *uṇmai veḷippaṭutal*; உண்மை வெளிப்பட்டது / *uṇmai veḷippaṭṭatu*; உண்மை தெரிய வருதல் / *uṇmai teriya varutal*; உண்மையை மறைத்தல் / *uṇmaiyai maṟaittal*; உண்மையை மறை / *uṇmaiyai maṟai*; உண்மை மறைக்கப்பட்டது / *uṇmai maṟaikkap-paṭṭatu*; உண்மையை மூடி மறைத்தார்கள் / *uṇmaiyai mūṭi maṟaittārkaḷ*; உண்மை தெரியும் வரை காத்திரு / *uṇmai teriyum varai kāttiru*; பொய் ஒரு நாள் வெளியே வரும் / *poy oru nāḷ veḷiyē varum*; உண்மை என்னவென்று தெரியவில்லை / *uṇmai eṉṉaveṉṟu teriyavillai*; உண்மை தேடுதல் / *uṇmai tēṭutal*; உண்மையை அறிய வேண்டும் / *uṇmaiyai aṟiya vēṇṭum*; உண்மையை எதிர்கொள்ள வேண்டும் / *uṇmaiyai etiṟkoḷḷa vēṇṭum*; உண்மையை ஒத்துக்கொண்டான் / *uṇmaiyai ottukkōṇṭāṉ*; உண்மை நிலை என்ன? / *uṇmai nilai eṉṉa?*; உண்மை விளக்கம் / *uṇmai viḷakkam*; நிரூபணம் / *nirūpaṇam*; நிரூபிக்கப்படாத / *nirūpikkap-paṭāta*; ஆதாரம் இல்லாமல் குற்றம் சாட்டினான் / *ātāram illāmal kuṟṟam cāṭṭiṉāṉ* | *நிரூபணம்* participates in both this group and Group 5; *பொய் ஒரு நாள் வெளியே வரும்* also participates in Group 9 | The same root *uṇmai* is involved as in Group 1, but the usage pattern here is specifically narrative and processual rather than predicative; the intransitive constructions are particularly characteristic; *உண்மையை மறைத்தல்* represents the concealment pole of this pattern |
| Evaluating persons and conduct for honesty and its absence | These expressions are used specifically to evaluate whether a person's character or conduct is straightforward and free of deception, as opposed to evaluating whether a particular statement is factually accurate. They appear most frequently in moral instruction, interpersonal evaluation, and political discourse. The root *nēr* (straight, direct) underlies the central terms in this group. They appear in character evaluations (*avar nērmaiyāna āḷ*, he/she is an honest person), moral instruction (*nērmaiyāka naṭa*, behave honestly), and condemnation of deceptive conduct. The focus is on the person as an agent rather than on a specific statement or object. | நேர்மை / *nērmai*; நேர்மையான / *nērmaiyāna*; நேர்மையாக / *nērmaiyāka*; நேர்மையற்ற / *nērmaiyaṟṟa*; நேர்மையில்லாத / *nērmaiyillāta*; நேர்மையின்மை / *nērmayiṉmai*; நேர்மையுடன் / *nērmaiyuṭaṉ*; நேர்மையாளர் / *nērmayāḷar*; நேர் / *nēr*; நேரடி / *nēraṭi*; நேரடியாக / *nēraṭiyāka*; நேர்தன்மை / *nēr-taṉmai* [MARGINAL]; தூய்மை / *tūymai*; தூய்மையான / *tūymaiyāna*; தூய்மையற்ற / *tūymaiyaṟṟa*; வஞ்சனை / *vañcaṉai*; வஞ்சனையான / *vañcaṉaiyāka*; உண்மையான மனிதன் / *uṇmaiyāna maṉitaṉ* | *நேர்மை* and related terms can appear in contexts where the honesty of a statement (not just a person) is at issue, creating overlap with Group 1; *பொய்* also participates in this group when applied to persons (*poy āḷ*, a lying person), but its primary membership is in Group 1; *வஞ்சனை* also participates in Group 6 and Group 7; *தூய்மை* also appears in religious and aesthetic contexts outside the truth-evaluation domain; *உண்மையான மனிதன்* overlaps with Group 1 | The dominant usage pattern for *நேர்மை* is evaluation of persons and conduct, while *uṇmai/poy* more typically evaluate propositions and states of affairs; *தூய்மை*'s placement in this group reflects only the subset of its usage documented in P1 and P2 |
| Assessing genuineness versus fakeness or copying | These expressions are used in contexts where the question is whether a physical object, document, credential, or person is what it claims to be — an original rather than a copy, a real professional rather than an impostor, a genuine article rather than a counterfeit. The operative contrast is between *acal* (original) and *nakal* (copy) or *pōli* (fake), and the evaluation is applied to things and persons rather than to propositions. This group is especially prominent in commercial, legal, and administrative contexts. | அசல் / *acal*; அசலான / *acalāna*; நகல் / *nakal*; போலி / *pōli*; போலியான / *pōliyāna*; போலித்தனம் / *pōlittaṉam*; உண்மையான / *uṇmaiyāna*; உண்மைத்தன்மை / *uṇmait-taṉmai*; மெய்யான / *meyyāna* | *அசல்* also participates in Group 7; *போலி* also participates in Group 7; *உண்மையான* overlaps with Group 1 when applied to propositions and states of affairs | *nakal* is neutral in connotation (a certified copy of a document is a *nakal* without negative implication), while *pōli* is always negative; *uṇmaiyāna* and *meyyāna* participate in both this group and Group 1, depending on whether they are applied to things/persons (genuineness) or to propositions (truth) |
| Providing and evaluating evidential support / Establishing and evidencing claims | These expressions are used in contexts — primarily legal, journalistic, and formal argumentative — where the question is not merely whether something is true but whether it can be demonstrated, supported, or established on the basis of evidence or proof. They appear in constructions involving the production of evidence, the act of proving, and the evaluation of whether a claim is well-supported. The operative concern is the relationship between a claim and its evidentiary basis. The typical constructions involve demanding evidence (*ātāram illāmal kuṟṟam cāṭṭātē*), asserting its absence (*ātāramaṟṟa vatanti*), or establishing its presence (*cāṉṟu illāmal nirūpikka muṭiyātu*). | ஆதாரம் / *ātāram*; ஆதாரமான / *ātāramāna*; ஆதாரமற்ற / *ātāramaṟṟa*; ஆதாரமில்லாத / *ātāramillāta*; ஆதாரப்படுத்து / *ātārappaṭuttu*; சான்று / *cāṉṟu*; சான்றிதழ் / *cāṉṟitaḻ*; சான்றாளர் / *cāṉṟāḷar*; சான்றுமொழி / *cāṉṟumoḻi*; சான்றற்ற / *cāṉṟaṟṟa*; சாட்சி / *cāṭci*; சாட்சியம் / *cāṭciyam*; மெய்ப்பிக்க / *meyppiкka*; மெய்ப்பித்தல் / *meyppittal*; உண்மையை நிலைநாட்டுதல் / *uṇmaiyai nilaināṭṭutal*; உண்மைச் சான்று / *uṇmaic cāṉṟu*; உண்மைத்தன்மையை நிரூபி / *uṇmait-taṉmaiyai nirūpi*; நம்பகமான / *nampakamāna*; நம்பத்தக்க / *nampattakka*; நம்பத்தகாத / *nampattakāta*; நிரூபணம் / *nirūpaṇam*; நிரூபிக்கு / *nirūpikku* | *நம்பகமான* and *நம்பத்தக்க* overlap with Group 6; *நிரூபணம்* also participates in Group 2; *சான்றாளர்* also participates in Group 7; *சாட்சி* also participates in Group 7; *சாட்சியம்* also participates in Group 7 | *cāṉṟu* is more frequently used in formal legal contexts while *ātāram* is more common in everyday argumentative contexts; both appear in the same constructions and the distinction is one of register and typical context rather than a sharp semantic boundary; *மெய்ப்பிக்க* is the only verbal form in the entire inventory that directly encodes the act of proving |
| Evaluating trustworthiness and credibility of persons and sources | These expressions are used to evaluate whether a person, institution, or source of information can be trusted or relied upon. They appear in journalistic, legal, and everyday contexts, and the typical constructions involve asserting or denying credibility (*nampakamāna takavalu*, *nampakattaṉmai kēḷvikkuṟiyākiviṭṭatu*) or describing the relationship of trust between a person and a source (*nampikkai vai*, *nampikkai iḻa*). The operative question is not whether a specific claim is true but whether the agent making the claim or the source providing information is reliable. This group is anchored in the root *nampu* (to trust). | நம்பிக்கை / *nampikkai*; நம்பகமான / *nampakamāna*; நம்பகம் / *nampakam*; நம்பகத்தன்மை / *nampakattaṉmai*; நம்பகமற்ற / *nampakamāṟṟa*; நம்பிக்கையான / *nampikkaiāna*; நம்பிக்கையற்ற / *nampikkaiāṟṟa*; நம்பத்தக்க / *nampattakka*; நம்பத்தகாத / *nampattakāta*; நம்பமுடியாத / *nampamuṭiyāta*; நம்பிக்கையின்மை / *nampikkaiinmai* | *நம்பகமான* and *நம்பத்தக்க* also participate in Group 5; *வஞ்சனை* also participates in this group (noted in Group 3 as participating in Group 6 and Group 7) | This group is anchored in the root *nampu* (to trust); the operative question is not whether a specific claim is true but whether the agent making the claim or the source providing information is reliable |

#### F3_semantic_groups_table
| Group Label | Definition | Representative Expressions | Overlapping / Ambiguous Items | Boundary Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Factual correctness evaluation | These terms are used to assess whether a proposition, report, or claim corresponds to what is actually the case. They appear in contexts of verification, denial, correction, and acknowledgment — in journalism, legal proceedings, everyday conversation, and formal discourse. The central contrast in this group is between terms that affirm correspondence with reality and terms that deny it. | *benar*, *tidak benar*, *salah*, *keliru*, *bohong*, *dusta*, *kebenaran*, *kebohongan*, *kekeliruan*, *sebenarnya*, *sebenar-benarnya*, *memang benar bahwa*, *ada benarnya*, *benar, tapi*, *tidak terbukti*, *informasi yang keliru*, *berita palsu*, *benar adanya*, *kebenaran ilmiah*, *kebenaran formal*, *kebenaran materiil*, *akurat*, *tepat*, *nyata*, *kenyataan*, *diakui kebenarannya* | *bohong* and *dusta* (also Group 3); *keliru* and *salah* (also Group 2); *nyata* (shades into Group 3 when emphasizing perceptibility); *kebenaran* in philosophical/religious collocations (*kebenaran hakiki*, *kebenaran sejati*, *kebenaran mutlak*) shades into Group 7; *akurat* and *tepat* overlap substantially | Within this group, *bohong* and *dusta* specifically imply deliberate deception, while *keliru* and *salah* do not necessarily carry this implication. *Benar* and *tidak benar* are the most neutral and widely distributed; *dusta* is restricted to formal, literary, and religious registers where *bohong* would be used in everyday speech. *benar* and *keliru* are frequently contrasted in educational and analytical contexts. *akurat* and *tepat* overlap substantially but *akurat* is more restricted to formal and technical registers. *nyata* shades into Group 3 (genuineness) when it emphasizes perceptibility rather than factual correctness. |
| Characterizing error and mistaken belief | These terms are used to indicate that a belief, judgment, statement, or action is incorrect — typically without implying deliberate deception. They appear in contexts of correction, diagnosis of misunderstanding, and acknowledgment of fault. They contrast with Group 3 (deliberate falsehood) and Group 1 (factual correctness). | *salah*, *keliru*, *kesalahan*, *salah paham*, *salah kaprah*, *salah tafsir*, *salah sangka*, *kekeliruan*, *tidak benar*, *salah baca*, *salah dengar*, *salah tulis*, *salah ucap*, *salah cetak* | *salah* and *keliru* (also Group 1); *tidak benar* (also Group 1) | The distinction between *salah* and *keliru* in practice is one of register and implied agency: *keliru* more often describes innocent error or misunderstanding, while *salah* covers a wider range including moral fault. *salah kaprah* is distinctive in that it describes error that has become socially normalized. The *salah* + [verb/noun] compounding pattern is highly productive and generates new forms as needed. |
| Characterizing deliberate falsehood and lying | These terms are used to describe statements or persons where the untruth is understood to be intentional — where the speaker knows the statement is false and makes it anyway. They appear in moral, interpersonal, legal, and journalistic contexts. They contrast with Group 2 (innocent error) and are often paired with terms from Group 6 (deception and manipulation). | *bohong*, *dusta*, *kebohongan*, *tidak benar*, *bohong demi kebaikan*, *sekali bohong, selamanya tidak dipercaya*, *ketahuan bohong*, *sengaja menyesatkan*, *berbohong*, *pembohong*, *membohongi*, *berdusta*, *pendusta*, *kedustaan* | *bohong* and *dusta* (also Group 1); *sengaja menyesatkan* bridges this group and Group 6; *palsu* (Group 4) can describe false statements but is more typically applied to objects and documents | *bohong* and *dusta* are near-synonyms distinguished primarily by register; *bohong* is the everyday term, *dusta* is formal and literary. #### F3_semantic_groups_table
| Group Label | Definition | Representative Expressions | Overlapping / Ambiguous Items | Boundary Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Evaluating statements as correct or incorrect | These terms are applied to propositions, claims, statements, and representations to judge whether they correspond to fact or to an accepted standard. They appear in contexts where the question is whether something said or asserted is accurate. They contrast with each other primarily along dimensions of register and degree of moral charge, not along a simple true/false binary. | *doğru*; *yanlış*; *doğruluk*; *doğruluk değeri*; *doğruluk koşulu*; *doğruluk tablosu*; *yanlışlık*; *doğrulanabilir* / *doğrulanabilirlik*; *yanlışlanabilir* / *yanlışlanabilirlik*; *doğrulamak* / *doğrulama*; *yanlışlamak* / *yanlışlama*; *doğru mu yanlış mı?*; *doğruyu yanlıştan ayırt etmek*; *doğru bilgi*; *doğru haber*; *doğruyu söylemek*; *gerçeğe aykırı beyan*; *gerçeğe uygun beyan*; *gerçeği söylemek*; *hakikati söylemek*; *doğru yanlış sorusu*; *doğruluk payı var*; *doğruluk payı olmak*; *asılsız*; *asılsız iddia*; *asılsızlık*; *aslında*; *doğru çıkmak*; *yalan çıkmak*; *yalan yanlış* | *gerçek* (overlaps when used predicatively of statements but more typically asserts ontological status); *hakikat* and *hakikaten* (belong primarily here but carry a more elevated register; see also Group 5); *yalan* (overlaps but carries an additional implication of intentionality; see Group 3) | *doğru* and *gerçek* overlap when used predicatively of statements (e.g., *bu doğru* and *bu gerçek* can both mean "this is true/correct"), but *gerçek* more typically asserts that something is real rather than that a statement is accurate. *Yalan* overlaps with this group but carries an additional implication of intentionality (see Group 3). |

| Factual correspondence markers | These terms are used primarily to evaluate whether a specific claim, report, or statement matches what actually happened or is the case. ABSTRACT NOMINALIZATION** — Native Korean -(으)ㅁ nominalization | 올바름의 기준 | olbareum ui gijun | "The standard of rightness/correctness." | Less common in everyday use; these forms (올바름, 옳음, 그름) tend toward philosophical or literary registers. AGENTIVE NOMINALIZATION** — [거짓말] + 쟁이/꾼 | 위조범 | wijobom | "Forger / Counterfeiter (legal register)" | Restricted to formal, legal, and journalistic registers; the Sino-Korean -범 suffix marks criminal agency. ## Narrative Analysis

### Recurring Partition Patterns

**The propositional truth / personal honesty split is universal.** Every language in the dataset maintains a lexical distinction between evaluating whether a statement is true and evaluating whether a person is honest. The terms used for these two functions are never identical, though they may share a root. Georgian uses *simartle/č̣ešmariteba* for propositional truth and *gulc̣rpeli* for sincerity; Yoruba uses *òtítọ́* for propositional truth and *ìwà rere* for moral character; Finnish uses *tosi/totuus* for propositional truth and *rehellinen* for honesty; Basque uses *egia* for propositional truth and *benetako* for genuine sincerity; Tamil uses *uṇmai* for propositional truth and *nērmai* for honesty/integrity; Indonesian uses *benar* for correctness and *jujur* for honesty; Turkish uses *doğru* for correctness and *dürüst* for uprightness; Korean uses *사실* for factual accuracy and *정직* for honesty. The split is consistent, though the degree of lexical elaboration on each side varies.

**The source-trustworthiness / content-credibility distinction is present in all eight languages.** Georgian explicitly distinguishes *sarc̣muno* (inherent trustworthiness of a source) from *damajerebeliˈ* (persuasive effect on a hearer). Yoruba distinguishes *fidagarri* (trustworthy source) from *sinesgarri* (believable content). Finnish distinguishes *luotettava* (reliable/dependable over time) from *uskottava* (believable for a specific claim). Basque distinguishes *fidagarria* (trustworthy source) from *sinesgarria* (believable content). Tamil distinguishes *nampakamāna* (reliable) from *nampattakka* (worth trusting for a specific claim). Indonesian distinguishes *terpercaya* (trusted/reliable) from *kredibel* (credible). Turkish distinguishes *güvenilir* (reliable) from *inanılır* (believable). Korean distinguishes *신뢰성* (reliability of a source) from *신빙성* (credibility of a specific claim). The distinction is lexically encoded in all eight languages, though the degree of elaboration varies.

**The neutral-copy / fraudulent-fake distinction is present in at least six languages.** Finnish distinguishes *jäljitelmä* (imitation, without necessarily implying fraud) from *väärennös* (forgery, implying fraudulent intent). Basque distinguishes *kopiakoa* (copy) from *faltsua* (fake) from *faltsifikatu* (to forge). Tamil distinguishes *nakal* (copy, neutral) from *pōli* (fake, negative). Indonesian distinguishes *tiruan* (imitation, neutral) from *palsu* (fake, fraudulent). Turkish distinguishes *taklit* (imitation) from *sahte* (counterfeit). Korean distinguishes *모조품* (imitation goods) from *위조품* (forged item). Georgian and Yoruba show less elaboration of this three-way contrast, though Georgian has *namdvili* vs. *q̇albi* as a binary and Yoruba lacks a dedicated forgery vocabulary.

**The legal/procedural validity vs. moral/substantive legitimacy distinction is present in all eight languages.** Georgian distinguishes *kanonieri* (lawful, tied to positive law) from *legitimuri* (legitimate, with possible normative dimension). Finnish distinguishes *pätevä* (valid/competent) from *oikeudenmukainen* (just/fair). Basque distinguishes *baliozko* (valid) from *zilegi* (lawful/permissible) from *zuzen* (correct/just). Tamil distinguishes *caṭṭappaṭi* (according to law) from *niyāyam* (justice/rightness). Indonesian distinguishes *sah* (legally valid) from *adil* (fair/just). Turkish distinguishes *yasal* (legal) from *meşru* (legitimate, extending beyond legality). Korean distinguishes *합법* (lawful) from *정당* (legitimate/justified). The distinction is present in all eight languages, though the degree of lexical elaboration and the specific terms used vary considerably.

**The intransitive/passive framing of truth-revelation is cross-linguistically consistent.** All eight languages show constructions in which truth is the grammatical subject of an intransitive or passive verb expressing emergence or disclosure: Georgian *simartle gamovida* (the truth came out), Yoruba *ó farahàn pé òtítọ́ ni* (it became clear that it is the truth), Finnish *totuus tulee ilmi* (the truth comes to light), Basque *egia argitara atera* (truth brought to light), Tamil *uṇmai veḷippaṭṭatu* (the truth came to light), Indonesian *kebenaran akan terungkap* (the truth will come out), Turkish *gerçek ortaya çıkmak* (the truth comes out), Korean *진실이 드러나다* (the truth emerges). This framing — treating truth as an entity that moves from concealment to visibility — is consistent across all eight languages.

**The proverbial assertion that truth ultimately prevails is present in all eight languages.** Georgian *simartle gamarjvebs* (truth prevails), Yoruba *òtítọ́ kò ní kú* (truth will not die), Finnish *totuus tulee ilmi* (used in this sense), Basque *egia beti ateratzen da azalera* (the truth always comes to the surface), Tamil *uṇmai tāṉ vellum* (truth alone will prevail), Indonesian *kebenaran akan terungkap pada akhirnya* (the truth will come out in the end), Turkish *gerçek ortaya çıkar* (the truth comes out), Korean *진실은 하나다* (there is only one truth) and related expressions. This proverbial pattern is present in all eight languages, though the specific formulation varies.

**No language has a lexicalized single-word agentive for "truth-teller."** All eight languages have lexicalized agentives for habitual liars (Georgian *mt'q̇uari*, Yoruba *aṣírọ́*, Finnish *valehtelija*, Basque *gezurti*, Tamil *poyyaṉ*, Indonesian *pembohong*, Turkish *yalancı*, Korean *거짓말쟁이*), but none has a parallel single-word agentive for "truth-teller." The concept is expressed periphrastically in all languages. This asymmetry is consistent across all eight languages and across unrelated language families.

**No language has a dedicated lexical item for "half-truth" as a distinct category.** All eight languages can express the concept of a partially true statement, but none has a single lexicalized term for it. The concept is expressed through compositional phrases: Georgian *naxevari č̣ešmariteba*, Yoruba *ìdajú kan nínú òtítọ́*, Finnish *puoli totuus*, Basque *egia erdi*, Tamil *uṇmai zati bat*, Indonesian (no fixed phrase documented), Turkish (no fixed phrase documented), Korean (no fixed phrase documented). This gap is consistent across all eight languages.

---

### Where Languages Split Distinctions More Finely

**Korean splits the truth domain most finely**, maintaining distinct Sino-Korean roots for factual accuracy (*사실*), truthfulness/sincerity (*진실*), precision/exactness (*정확*), honesty in conduct (*정직*), trustworthiness (*신뢰*), and authenticity of inner state (*진정성*). These are not merely register variants of a single concept but distinct evaluative categories with different collocational patterns, different semantic groups, and different constructional behaviors. No other language in the dataset shows this degree of internal differentiation within the truth domain.

**Basque splits the verifiability domain most finely**, distinguishing *egiaztagarria* (verifiable, capable of being verified), *egiaztagaitza* (difficult to verify), and *egiaztaezina* (impossible to verify) as three distinct forms within the same derivational paradigm. The *-garri*/*-gaitz*/*-ezin* three-way distinction — potential/difficult/impossible — is not paralleled in any other language in the dataset, which typically show only a binary verifiable/unverifiable opposition.

**Turkish splits the verification/falsification domain most finely**, maintaining a productive morphological opposition between *doğrulamak* (to verify) and *yanlışlamak* (to falsify) with parallel derivational stacking generating *doğrulanabilirlik* (verifiability) and *yanlışlanabilirlik* (falsifiability) as technical philosophical terms. While other languages have vocabulary for verification and for showing something to be false, only Turkish shows this as a productive morphological pair built on contrasting truth-domain bases.

**Finnish splits the checking/verification domain most finely**, explicitly distinguishing *tarkistaa* (to check, everyday) from *tarkastaa* (to inspect, formal/official) as register-differentiated near-synonyms where the distinction is semantic (institutional authority) rather than merely stylistic. No other language in the dataset shows this register distinction documented at the same level of explicitness.

**Georgian splits the register dimension of propositional truth most finely**, maintaining *č̣ešmariteba* (philosophical/theological register) and *simartle* (everyday/legal register) as distinct nominals for truth, with different collocational patterns, different discourse functions, and different derivational families. Finnish has a similar distinction (*totuus* vs. *tosi*) but the Georgian distinction is more elaborated in the data.

---

### Where Languages Merge Distinctions

**Yoruba merges propositional correctness and procedural correctness** under the single *tọ́* root, which covers both "this statement is correct" and "this procedure is proper." The same predicative construction *ó tọ́* (it is correct/right/proper) applies across factual, moral, and procedural evaluation without lexical differentiation. Other languages (Finnish, Korean, Georgian) maintain distinct vocabulary for these functions.

**Indonesian merges the innocent-error and deliberate-falsehood distinction less sharply than some other languages**, though it does distinguish *keliru* (innocent error) from *bohong* (deliberate lie). The *salah* root covers both error and fault/blame without a dedicated term for the innocent-error pole, relying on context and the *keliru*/*salah* distinction to convey the difference. Georgian, Finnish, and Korean show more explicit lexical differentiation between error-without-intent and deliberate deception.

**Tamil merges the classical/literary and everyday registers of truth** under *uṇmai* more completely than Georgian merges *simartle* and *č̣ešmariteba*. While *mey* (classical truth) exists as a literary near-synonym, it is documented as marginal in everyday use, and the *uṇmai* root covers both philosophical and everyday truth without the sharp register split seen in Georgian.

**Turkish merges epistemic truth and legal entitlement** under the *hak* root (from Arabic *ḥaqq*), which simultaneously generates *haklı* (justified/in the right), *haksız* (unjust), *hakkaniyet* (equity), *hak etmek* (to deserve), and *insan hakları* (human rights). While other languages show some overlap between truth and justice vocabulary (Georgian *martal-* covers both correctness and justice; Yoruba *òdodo* covers both righteousness and justice), the Turkish *hak* root shows the most complete merger of epistemic and entitlement senses within a single productive root.

**Basque merges the sincerity and genuineness dimensions** under the *benetako* cluster more completely than other languages. *Benetako* covers both "genuine (not fake)" and "sincere (not performed)," and *benetan* functions as both an authenticity marker and a sincerity marker. Other languages (Korean, Finnish, Indonesian) maintain more distinct vocabulary for these two functions.

---

### Cases Where a Language Appears to Lack a Clear Lexical Contrast Found Elsewhere

**Yoruba lacks a dedicated vocabulary for documentary forgery and counterfeiting** as a distinct legal category. While Yoruba has vocabulary for lying (*irọ́*), false testimony (*ẹlẹ́rìí irọ́*), and deception (*ìtànjẹ́*), the data does not document a dedicated term for the act of producing a forged document or counterfeit currency parallel to Georgian *gaq̇albeba*, Finnish *väärentää*, Basque *faltsifikatu*, Tamil *pōli āvaṇam*, Indonesian *pemalsuan*, Turkish *sahte belge*, or Korean *위조*. The concept would presumably be expressed through general deception vocabulary applied to documents.

**Yoruba lacks a dedicated vocabulary for legal/procedural validity** as a distinct category. While Yoruba has *ẹ̀tọ́* (right/entitlement) and *òdodo* (righteousness/justice), the data does not document a dedicated term for the validity or invalidity of legal instruments parallel to Georgian *kanonieri/legitimuri*, Finnish *pätevä/pätemätön*, Basque *baliozkoa/baliogabea*, Tamil *caṭṭappaṭi*, Indonesian *sah/tidak sah*, Turkish *geçerli/geçersiz*, or Korean *유효/무효*.

**Tamil lacks a dedicated vocabulary for the philosophical/technical truth domain** (truth values, truth conditions, truth tables) that is documented in Finnish (*totuusarvo*, *totuusehdot*, *totuustaulu*), Turkish (*doğruluk değeri*, *doğruluk koşulu*, *doğruluk tablosu*), and Korean (*진리값*). While Tamil has *uṇmai* in philosophical contexts, the data does not document technical logical vocabulary built on the *uṇmai* root.

**Indonesian lacks a dedicated vocabulary for the appearance-vs.-reality distinction** as elaborated as Basque *itxura* (appearance/semblance) or Georgian *moč̣venebiti* (apparent/seeming/ostensible). While Indonesian has *nyata* (real/manifest) and *sebenarnya* (actually/in truth), the data does not document a dedicated adjectival term for "merely apparent" or "ostensible" parallel to these.

**Georgian lacks a dedicated vocabulary for the inner-state authenticity dimension** as elaborated as Korean *진정성* (authenticity of inner state) or Finnish *aito tunne* (genuine feeling). While Georgian has *gulc̣rpeli* (sincere/straight-hearted) and *tvaltmaqcoba* (hypocrisy/eye-deceiving), the data does not document a term specifically for the authenticity of expressed feelings or political commitments as a public evaluative category.

### Distinguishing Cross-Language Patterns from Single-Language Observations

**Well-attested cross-language patterns** (present in five or more languages with explicit documentation):
- The propositional truth / personal honesty split (all eight languages)
- The source-trustworthiness / content-credibility distinction (all eight languages)
- The neutral-copy / fraudulent-fake distinction (at least six languages)
- The legal/procedural validity vs. moral/substantive legitimacy distinction (all eight languages)
- The intransitive/passive framing of truth-revelation (all eight languages)
- The proverbial assertion that truth ultimately prevails (all eight languages)
- The absence of a lexicalized single-word agentive for "truth-teller" (all eight languages)
- The absence of a dedicated lexical item for "half-truth" (all eight languages)
- The spatial metaphor of straightness underlying truth/correctness vocabulary (at least six languages: Georgian, Yoruba, Finnish, Basque, Tamil, Turkish, Korean)

**Patterns present in a minority of languages** (two to four languages):
- The register-differentiated split between philosophical/theological and everyday truth nominals (Georgian *č̣ešmariteba*/*simartle*, Finnish *totuus*/*tosi*, Korean *진리*/*진실*/*사실* — three languages)
- The explicit *doğrulamak*/*yanlışlamak* morphological opposition for verification/falsification (Turkish only, with partial parallels in Finnish *todistaa*/*osoittaa epätodeksi* and Korean *사실확인*/*허위*)
- The *있다/없다* existential frame as the primary predication strategy for abstract quality nominals (Korean only)
- The *-garri*/*-gaitz*/*-ezin* three-way verifiability distinction (Basque only)
- The bifurcation of a single form into "credibility" (secular) and "faith/religion" (theological) meanings (Georgian *sarwmunoeba* only, with a partial parallel in Yoruba *ìgbàgbọ́* covering both belief and faith)

**Single-language observations** (documented in only one language):
- The *ìwà* (character/manner of being) as the organizing concept of moral evaluation with the specific proverbial elaboration *ìwà ló ń ṣe ènìyàn* (Yoruba only)
- The *martal-* root extending into orthography (*martlc̣era*) and Orthodox Christianity (*martlmadidebeli*) (Georgian only)
- The *진정성* (authenticity of inner state) as a highly elaborated public evaluative category with a rich collocation network (Korean only, though the concept exists in other languages)
- The *ziurrenik* semantic shift from "certainly" to "probably/most likely" (Basque only)
- The *ikhlas* (selflessly sincere, from Arabic *ikhlāṣ*) as a distinct sincerity term with specifically religious connotations of selfless acceptance (Indonesian only, though Arabic-derived terms appear in Turkish and Georgian as well)
- The *salah* + verb compounding pattern generating a large family of misaction compounds (*salah paham*, *salah kaprah*, *salah sasaran*) (Indonesian only, though Turkish *yanlış anlamak* is a partial parallel)

- **ko (Korean)** — A language isolate (or Koreanic) with agglutinative morphology and a large Sino-Korean vocabulary layer; the data shows a core opposition between *jinsil* (truth) and *geojit* (falsehood), a genuineness pair *jinjja* (real) vs. *gajja* (fake), and a character-evaluation cluster around *jeongjik* (honesty) and *jinjeongseong* (authenticity/genuineness of inner state).

## 2. Per-Language Semantic Sketch

### 2.1 Georgian (ka)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):**
The data documents two primary truth nominals: *simarṭle* (truth, more colloquial and concrete, also covering moral rightness and justice) and *č̣ešmariteba* (truth, more philosophical and theological). These are not interchangeable: *simarṭle* dominates everyday speech and legal fact-finding, while *č̣ešmariteba* appears in religious, philosophical, and elevated literary registers. A third cluster around *namdvili* (genuine, real) handles authenticity of objects and persons, contrasting with *q̇albi* (false, counterfeit, forged). The *q̇alb-* root is borrowed (from Persian/Arabic via Turkish) and is concentrated in legal and commercial forgery contexts, while *namdvili* covers the positive authenticity pole. A separate cluster around *sarcmuno/sando* (credible/reliable) handles source evaluation. The *marṭl-* root is exceptionally productive, generating terms for orthography (*marṭlc̣era*), Orthodox Christianity (*marṭlmadidebeli*), the justice system (*marṭlmsajuleba*), proportionality (*marṭlzomiereba*), and justification/acquittal (*gamarṭleba*).

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries:**
The *marṭl-* root is the most morphologically productive in the dataset for this language, generating compounds across legal, religious, linguistic, and moral domains that have no parallel in the other languages. The *si-...-e* circumfix nominalization pattern produces the primary abstract truth nominals (*simarṭle*, *siq̇albe*, *sicrue*, *sizuste*). The *-eba* suffix produces a second set of nominals with slightly more elevated register (*č̣ešmariteba*). The *-oba* suffix produces a third set naming properties of specific entities (*namdviloba*, *avtentiuroba*). These three patterns are documented as non-interchangeable.

**Constructional patterns (F4):**
The enclitic copula *-a* is the default for affirmative predication; negation requires the full copula *aris* (*ar aris*). The *osoittautua*-equivalent is *gamodga* (turned out to be) and *aġmočnda* (was found to be), both used in inchoative truth-evaluation contexts. The discourse-framing construction *simarṭle rom vtq̇vat* (to tell the truth, frankly) is specific to *simarṭle* and has no parallel with *č̣ešmariteba*. The concessive *martalia, magram* (it is true, but) is highly lexicalized and specific to *martali*.

**Oppositional structures (F5):**
The primary lexical oppositions are *simarṭle/siq̇albe*, *simarṭle/sicrue*, *namdvili/q̇albi*, *sc̣ori/mcdari*, and *zusti/uzusto*. A notable distinction is drawn between *q̇albi* (implying deliberate deception) and *mcdari* (implying honest error), and between *piqtiuri* (fictitious, sham — for transactions and entities) and *q̇albi* (forged — for physical documents and objects). The *sarcmuno/sando* near-synonym pair is distinguished by register and by whether epistemic credibility or practical reliability is foregrounded.

### 2.2 Yoruba (yo)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):**
The core opposition is *òtítọ́* (truth) vs. *irọ́* (lie/falsehood), which are the most consistently paired terms in the dataset and appear in parallel constructions, parallel proverbs, and parallel agentive nominals. The root *tọ́* (straight/correct) underlies both *òtítọ́* and a large cluster of correctness-evaluation terms (*ó tọ́*, *kò tọ́*, *àtúntọ́*, *ẹ̀tọ́*). A separate cluster around *ìwà* (character/nature) handles moral character evaluation, with the central opposition *ìwà rere* (good character) vs. *ìwà burúkú/búburú* (bad character). Evidence and testimony evaluation is handled by a cluster around *ẹ̀rí* (evidence, related to *rí*, to see) and *ìjẹ́rìísí* (attestation/certification). The term *gidi* (genuine/real) handles colloquial authenticity evaluation, contrasting with *kì í ṣe nǹkan gidi* (it is not the real thing).

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries:**
The *ì-* nominalizing prefix is the most productive in the truth domain, generating *ìmọ̀* (knowledge), *ìgbàgbọ́* (belief/faith), *ìgbẹ́kẹ̀lé* (trust/reliance), *ìjẹ́rìísí* (attestation), *ìtànjẹ́* (deception), *ìdánwò* (testing), *ìdájọ́* (judgment), and others. The *a-* prefix generates morally evaluative agent nouns (*aṣírọ́*, liar; *adájọ́*, judge), while *olù-* generates functional role agents (*olùgbàgbọ́*, believer; *olùdánwò*, examiner). No single-word agentive for "truth-teller" is attested; the concept requires periphrastic expression. The *àì-* negation prefix is productive for nominals (*àìmọ̀*, ignorance; *àìgbàgbọ́*, unbelief).

**Constructional patterns (F4):**
The focus construction with *ni* (predicate focus) and *ló* (subject focus, fused *ni* + *ó*) is highly productive in truth-domain assertions and proverbs. The existential negative *kò sí* (there is not) is the standard construction for denying the presence of truth, evidence, or justice. The *pé* complementizer is the standard frame for propositional complements after epistemic and evidential verbs. The *di* + nominal/adjectival inchoative is the general change-of-state construction. No dedicated inchoative morpheme exists; change-of-state is expressed periphrastically.

**Oppositional structures (F5):**
The primary lexical opposition is *òtítọ́/irọ́*, with parallel verbal constructions (*sọ òtítọ́/sọ irọ́*) and parallel proverbs (*òtítọ́ kò ní kú/irọ́ kò ní dúró*). The *ìwà rere/ìwà burúkú* opposition is the central character-evaluation pair. The *ẹlẹ́rìí ojú* (eyewitness) vs. *ẹlẹ́rìí irọ́* (false witness) compound pair is notable for combining a term from the evidence domain with a term from the truth/falsehood domain.

### 2.3 Finnish (fi)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):**
The *tosi/tode-* root generates the largest documented derivational family in Finnish, covering truth (*totuus*), reality (*todellisuus*, *todellinen*), verification (*todentaa*, *todistaa*), probability (*todennäköinen*), and realization (*toteutua*, *toteuttaa*). A separate cluster around *aito* (genuine/authentic) handles object and personal authenticity, contrasting with *väärennös* (forgery) and *jäljitelmä* (imitation). The distinction between *luotettava* (reliable/dependable) and *uskottava* (credible/believable) is explicitly documented: *luotettava* evaluates a source's intrinsic dependability, while *uskottava* evaluates the believability of a specific claim or account. The *oikea/väärä* pair handles correctness/incorrectness across factual, normative, and identity-evaluation contexts. The compound adjective pattern using *mukainen* (conforming to) and *vastainen* (contrary to) on a genitive base is highly productive: *totuudenmukainen* (truthful), *totuudenvastainen* (contrary to truth), *oikeaoppinen* (orthodox), *vääräoppinen* (heterodox).

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries:**
The *-uus/-yys* suffix is the primary abstract nominalizer for truth-domain adjectives (*totuus*, *luotettavuus*, *uskottavuus*, *aitous*, *rehellisyys*). The *epä-* prefix is the productive negation prefix for adjectives (*epäluotettava*, *epäaito*, *epärehellinen*). The *väärentää* (to forge) vs. *vääristää* (to distort) distinction is morphologically encoded: both derive from *väärä* but differ in whether they produce a fraudulent object or distort existing content. The *tarkistaa* (to check, everyday) vs. *tarkastaa* (to inspect, formal/official) distinction is register-based and semantically significant.

**Constructional patterns (F4):**
The *osoittautua* + translative construction is the primary inchoative for truth-domain adjectives (*väite osoittautui epätodeksi*, the claim turned out to be false). The *pitää* + essive construction (*pidän selitystä uskottavana*) expresses ongoing evaluative stance. The *todistaa* + NP + translative construction (*asiantuntija todisti maalauksen aidoksi*) is the standard certification construction. The *ei pidä paikkaansa* (it does not hold) is the most colloquial construction for propositional falsity, preferred over *ei ole tosi* in spoken Finnish. The *vastata* + partitive correspondence construction (*kuvaus vastaa totuutta*) explicitly encodes a two-place correspondence relation.

**Oppositional structures (F5):**
The *totuudenmukainen/totuudenvastainen* pair is a productive morphological opposition using contrasting postpositional elements on the same genitive base. The *aito/epäaito* pair is morphological; the *aito/väärennös* pair is lexical. The *kopio* (neutral copy) vs. *jäljitelmä* (imitation with lesser status) vs. *väärennös* (fraudulent forgery) three-way distinction is explicitly documented. The *tarkistaa/tarkastaa* register distinction is noted as semantically significant rather than purely stylistic.

### 2.4 Basque (eu)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):**
The core opposition is *egia* (truth) vs. *gezurra* (lie/falsehood), with parallel derivational families (*egiazkoa/gezurrezkoa*, *egia esan/gezurra esan*, *egia da/gezurra da*). A verification cluster built on *egiazta-* generates *egiaztatu* (to verify), *egiaztapen* (attestation), *egiaztagarria* (verifiable), *egiaztaezina* (unverifiable), and *egiaztagaitza* (difficult to verify). A validity cluster around *balio* (value/validity) generates *baliozkoa* (valid), *baliogabea* (invalid), *baliozkotu* (to validate), and *baliogabetu* (to invalidate). A separate cluster around *benetakoa* (genuine/real) handles authenticity with an emphasis on sincerity and non-artificiality, while *egiazkoa* handles factual correspondence. The *ziur* (certain) cluster generates *ziurtatu* (to certify), *ziurtasun* (certainty), and *ziurtagiri* (certificate). The *itxura* (appearance/semblance) cluster handles the appearance-versus-reality contrast.

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries:**
The *-tasun* suffix is the primary abstract nominalizer (*egiazkotasuna*, *benetakotasuna*, *fidagarritasuna*, *zuzentasuna*). The *-garri* suffix generates potential/worthy-of adjectives (*fidagarria*, *sinesgarria*, *egiaztagarria*, *frogagarria*), with *-gaitz* as the preferred negative counterpart (*fidagaitza*, *sineskaitza*) rather than *-gabe* (which expresses absence rather than impossibility). The *-gabe* privative suffix expresses absence (*baliogabea*, *egiaztatu gabe*), while *ezin* expresses impossibility (*egiaztaezina*, *frogaezina*); these are documented as non-interchangeable. The *-keria* pejorative suffix generates *gezurkeria* (habitual lying), *itxurakeria* (pretense/hypocrisy), *ustelkeria* (corruption).

**Constructional patterns (F4):**
The *bihurtu* periphrastic inchoative is the most productive change-of-state construction for truth-domain nominals and adjectives (*egia bihurtu da*, it has become true; *baliogabea bihurtu da*, it has become invalid). Morphological *-tu* inchoatives are attested for some bases (*okertu*, *zintzotu*, *usteldu*) but not for *egia* or *gezurra* directly. The *-tzat jo/hartu/onartu* translative construction (*egiazkotzat jo*, to consider as genuine) is characteristic of legal and administrative registers. The *egia da ala gezurra?* disjunctive interrogative is a fixed binary framing construction.

**Oppositional structures (F5):**
The *egiaztagarria/egiaztaezina* and *egiaztagarria/egiaztagaitza* pairs are morphological oppositions on the same verbal stem using contrasting suffixes (*-garri* vs. *-ezin* vs. *-gaitz*). The *baliozkoa/baliogabea* pair is morphological (*-zko* vs. *-gabe* on the same root). The *baliozkotu/baliogabetu* causative pair is documented as the only attested causative pair in the domain built on the same base with contrasting morphology. The *egiaztatu/egiaztatu gabeko* opposition is morphological (participial vs. participial + privative *gabe*).

### 2.5 Tamil (ta)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):**
The core term *uṇmai* (truth/reality) is the most semantically broad in the dataset, covering propositional truth, factual reality, genuineness of objects, and sincerity of persons. It contrasts with *poy* (lie/falsehood) as its primary antonym. A separate cluster around *nērmai* (honesty/integrity, from *nēr*, straight/direct) handles character evaluation, contrasting with *vañcaṉai* (deceit) and *kaḷḷam* (guile). The genuineness-versus-counterfeit domain is handled by *acal* (original/genuine) vs. *nakal* (copy) vs. *pōli* (fake/counterfeit), with *nakal* documented as neutral (a certified copy is a *nakal* without negative implication) and *pōli* as always negative. The *cari* (correct/right) vs. *tavaṟu* (mistake/error/wrong) pair handles factual and moral correctness in everyday speech. The *niyāyam* (justice/fairness/reasonableness) cluster handles normative evaluation.

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries:**
The *-āna* adjectival copular suffix is the primary attributive derivation strategy (*uṇmaiyāna*, *poyyāna*, *cariyāna*, *tavaṟāna*, *nērmaiyāna*). The *-āka* adverbial copular suffix generates manner adverbials (*uṇmaiyāka*, *nērmaiyāka*, *cariyāka*). The *-il* locative suffix generates the discourse-framing adverbial *uṇmaiyil* (in truth/actually). The *-aṟṟa* privative participial suffix generates negative attributive adjectives (*uṇmaiyaṟṟa*, *nērmaiyaṟṟa*, *ātāramaṟṟa*), while *illāta* (lacking/without) generates a parallel set (*nērmaiyillāta*, *ātāramillāta*); both are productive but *illāta* is slightly more common in spoken registers. No single-word agentive for "truth-teller" is attested; the concept requires periphrastic expression. Agentive forms for negative roles (*poyyaṉ*, liar; *vañcakaṉ*, deceiver) are more lexicalized than positive counterparts.

**Constructional patterns (F4):**
The zero-copula predication with *uṇmai* (*atu uṇmaitāṉ*, that is indeed true) is the default. The *veḷippaṭu* (to come to light) intransitive construction treats truth as an entity moving from concealment to visibility. The *-āki viṭu* completive inchoative (*uṇmaiyākiviṭṭatu*, it has become true) marks completed change of state. The *uṇmaiyil* sentence-initial adverbial is a grammaticalized correction/contrast marker. The *tāṉ vellum* proverbial pattern (*uṇmai tāṉ vellum*, truth alone will prevail) is lexically restricted to a small set of moral-domain nominals.

**Oppositional structures (F5):**
The *uṇmaiyāna/poyyāna* pair is morphological (parallel *-āna* derivations on contrasting bases). The *acal/nakal/pōli* three-way distinction is explicitly documented, with *nakal* occupying a neutral intermediate position. The *nampattakka/nampattakāta* pair is a morphological minimal pair (same base, contrasting participial suffixes *takka* vs. *takāta*). The *niyāyam/aniyāyam* and *niyāyam/anyāyam* pairs are lexical oppositions with Sanskrit-origin privative prefixation.

### 2.6 Indonesian (id)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):**
The root *benar* (correct/true) generates the most productive derivational family in Indonesian, covering truth (*kebenaran*), confirmation (*membenarkan*), justification (*pembenaran*), and the discourse adverb *sebenarnya* (actually/in truth). The *sah/absah* cluster handles legal validity, with *sah* as the general-purpose term and *absah* as a more formal variant; the primary abstract nominal *keabsahan* is built on *absah* rather than *sah*, creating a morphological asymmetry. The *asli* (genuine/original) vs. *palsu* (fake/counterfeit) pair handles object authenticity, with *tiruan* (imitation) occupying a neutral intermediate position (parallel to Tamil *nakal*). The *jujur* (honest) cluster handles character evaluation. The *sahih* cluster is restricted to Islamic scholarly discourse. The *benar/salah* pair covers both propositional truth/falsity and moral right/wrong.

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries:**
The *ke-...-an* circumfix is the primary abstract nominalizer (*kebenaran*, *kesalahan*, *keaslian*, *kejujuran*, *keabsahan*). The *meN-...-kan* active transitive and *di-...-kan* passive are the primary verbal derivation strategies. The *pe(N)-* agentive suffix generates agent nouns for negative roles (*pembohong*, liar; *pemalsu*, forger; *peniru*, imitator) but no parallel lexicalized agent noun for "truth-teller" is attested. The *-itas* suffix applies only to loanword bases (*validitas*, *kredibilitas*, *otentisitas*) and does not extend to native roots. The *salah* root generates a large set of misaction compounds (*salah paham*, misunderstanding; *salah kaprah*, widespread misconception; *salah sasaran*, off-target; *salah tafsir*, misinterpretation) that have no parallel in other languages.

**Constructional patterns (F4):**
The zero-copula predication (*kabar itu benar*, that news is true) is the default. The *menjadi kenyataan* (to become reality) is a fixed inchoative collocation. The *terungkap* (to be revealed) and *terbukti* (to be proven) stative passives are the primary inchoative constructions for truth-revelation. The *sebenarnya* sentence-initial discourse marker is a grammaticalized correction/disclosure frame. The *ada benarnya* (there is some truth to it) partial-concession construction is highly conventionalized. The *benar atau tidak* (true or not) suspension-of-judgment construction is documented as a fixed pragmatic frame.

**Oppositional structures (F5):**
The *benar/salah* pair is the primary lexical opposition. The *asli/palsu* pair is the primary authenticity opposition, with *tiruan* as a neutral intermediate. The *sah/tidak sah* pair is morphosyntactic (negation with *tidak*). The *sah/absah* near-synonym pair is distinguished by register rather than meaning. The *kebenaran formal/kebenaran materiil* pair is a legal-technical opposition between procedural and substantive truth.
