### 2.7 Turkish (tr)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):**
The root *doğru* (straight/correct/true) generates the largest documented derivational family in the dataset, covering truth (*doğruluk*), verification (*doğrulamak*, *doğrulama*), direction (*doğrultu*, *doğrudan*), linearity (*doğrusal*), and numerous compounds (*doğru yol*, *doğru bilgi*, *doğruluk değeri*, *doğruluk tablosu*). The parallel *yanlış* (wrong/false) root generates a matching falsification cluster (*yanlışlamak*, *yanlışlama*, *yanlışlanabilir*, *yanlışlanabilirlik*). The *gerçek* (real/genuine) cluster handles ontological genuineness, contrasting with *sahte* (fake/counterfeit). The *haklı/haksız* pair handles justification and rightfulness. The *meşru* (legitimate) vs. *yasal* (legal) distinction is explicitly documented: *yasal* evaluates conformity to written law, while *meşru* can extend to moral or political legitimacy beyond strict legality. The *sah* root (from Arabic, shared with Indonesian and Basque *sahih*) appears in Turkish as *sahih* (restricted to Islamic scholarly discourse) and in the compound *sahte* (fake).

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries:**
The *-lık/-lik* suffix is the primary abstract nominalizer (*doğruluk*, *yanlışlık*, *güvenilirlik*, *özgünlük*, *dürüstlük*). The *-la-* factitive verbalizer is the primary verbalization strategy (*doğrulamak*, *yanlışlamak*). The *doğrulamak/yanlışlamak* parallel pair is the most explicitly documented morphological opposition in the dataset, encoding the logical positivist/Popperian distinction in Turkish academic discourse. The *-laş-* inchoative and *-laştır-* causative-inchoative chain is productive for some bases (*meşrulaşmak*, *meşrulaştırmak*) but not others. The *gayri meşru* (illegitimate) uses an Arabic-pattern negation rather than the Turkish privative *-sız*, creating a morphological asymmetry. The *doğrusal* (linear) technical term uses the *-sal* suffix restricted to scientific/technical vocabulary.

**Constructional patterns (F4):**
The null-copula predication (*bu haber doğru*, this news is correct) is the default; the *-dır* variant is restricted to formal, assertive, or written registers. The *değil* negation particle is the sole negation strategy for adjectival predicates. The *osoittautua*-equivalent is *çıkmak* (to come out/turn out: *tahmini doğru çıktı*, his prediction turned out to be correct). The *sebenarnya*-equivalent is *aslında* (actually/in fact), a grammaticalized correction marker. The *doğrusu* possessive form functions as a sincerity hedge (*doğrusu, bilmiyorum*, honestly, I don't know). The *gerçeğe aykırı/gerçeğe uygun* postpositional pair is a productive legal construction.

**Oppositional structures (F5):**
The *doğru/yanlış* pair is the primary lexical opposition. The *doğrulamak/yanlışlamak* and *doğrulanabilirlik/yanlışlanabilirlik* pairs are the most explicitly parallel morphological oppositions in the dataset. The *gerçeğe uygun/gerçeğe aykırı* pair is a constructional opposition using contrasting postpositional elements on the same dative base. The *meşru/gayri meşru* pair uses Arabic-pattern negation. The *yasal/meşru* distinction is a documented lexical contrast between legality and legitimacy.

### 2.8 Korean (ko)

**Main lexical distinctions and overlaps (F1–F3):**
The data documents a large Sino-Korean vocabulary layer alongside native Korean roots. The core opposition is *jinsil* (眞實, truth/truthfulness) vs. *geojit* (falsehood), with *geojitmal* (lie, literally "false word") as the everyday spoken form. The *jinjja/gajja* pair handles colloquial genuineness-versus-counterfeit evaluation. The *jinjeongseong* (眞正性, authenticity/genuineness of inner state) cluster is prominent in contemporary public discourse about sincerity of apologies, political commitments, and artistic works. The *jeongjik* (正直, honesty/integrity) cluster handles character evaluation. The *sasil* (事實, fact/actuality) cluster handles factual correspondence. The *jinwi* (眞僞, truth or falsity) compound frames the binary question of authenticity. The *jinsang* (眞相, true state of affairs) cluster handles investigative truth-finding. The *tadasng* (妥當, valid/reasonable) cluster handles logical and normative soundness.

**Derivational/morphological asymmetries:**
The *-seong* (性) suffix is the primary abstract nominalizer for Sino-Korean bases (*jinsilseong*, *jinjeongseong*, *sinloeseong*, *sinbyeongseong*, *jeonghwakseong*, *tadangseong*). The *-hada* suffix is the primary predicative verbalization strategy for Sino-Korean bases (*jinsil-hada*, *jeongjik-hada*, *wijo-hada*). The *-doeda* suffix generates stative or resultant predicates (*jinsil-doeda*, *mosun-doeda*); the *-hada/-doeda* distinction is documented as semantically conditioned rather than freely variable. No single-word agentive for "truth-teller" is attested; the concept requires periphrastic expression. Agentive forms for negative roles (*geojitmal-jaengi*, liar; *wijobom*, forger) are more lexicalized than positive counterparts. The *-화하다* causative is productive for Sino-Korean bases (*muhyohwa-hada*, to invalidate; *hapbeophwa-hada*, to legalize) but not for native Korean bases.

**Constructional patterns (F4):**
The *[noun] + ida/i anida* copular predication is the default. The *있다/없다* existential frame is the primary predication strategy for abstract quality nouns (*jinjeongseong-i itda/eopda*, *sinbyeongseong-i itda/eopda*); these nouns do not take *-hada* as a predicative suffix. The *[noun]-(으)로 밝혀지다/드러나다/판명되다* inchoative constructions are the primary truth-revelation constructions. The *높다/낮다* scalar frame is used for degree-of-quality assessment (*jeonghwakdo-ga nopda*, accuracy is high). The *옳고 그름* (right and wrong) fixed coordinate pair is documented as a lexicalized collocation.

**Oppositional structures (F5):**
The *jinjja/gajja* pair is the primary colloquial genuineness opposition. The *jinsil/geojit* pair is the primary truth/falsehood opposition. The *matda/teullida* pair handles everyday factual correctness. The *olta/geureuda* pair handles moral and philosophical rightness/wrongness, with *teullida* having largely displaced *geureuda* in everyday factual contexts. The *유효/무효* (valid/invalid) pair is a Sino-Korean morphological opposition. The *합법/불법* (legal/illegal) pair handles lawfulness evaluation.

## 3. Cross-Language Summary

### Recurring Convergences (patterns observed across many languages)

- **A spatial/directional metaphor underlies truth and correctness terms in multiple languages.** Georgian *marṭl-* (straight/right), Yoruba *tọ́* (straight/correct), Finnish *oikea* (right, also directional), Basque *zuzen* (straight/correct), Tamil *nēr* (straight/direct), Indonesian *benar* (correct, possibly related to straightness), Turkish *doğru* (straight/correct/true), and Korean *olbareuda* (upright/correct) all show a root or base that combines spatial straightness with epistemic or moral correctness. This convergence is present in all eight languages.

- **All eight languages distinguish between propositional truth/falsity (is this claim accurate?) and object/identity genuineness (is this thing the real article?).** The two domains are handled by different lexical items in every language: Georgian *simarṭle/č̣ešmariteba* (propositional truth) vs. *namdvili/q̇albi* (genuine/fake); Yoruba *òtítọ́/irọ́* vs. *gidi/kì í ṣe gidi*; Finnish *totuus/epätotuus* vs. *aito/väärennös*; Basque *egia/gezurra* vs. *benetakoa/faltsua*; Tamil *uṇmai/poy* vs. *acal/pōli*; Indonesian *kebenaran/kebohongan* vs. *asli/palsu*; Turkish *doğru/yanlış* vs. *gerçek/sahte*; Korean *jinsil/geojit* vs. *jinjja/gajja*. In all cases the genuineness pair is more colloquial and object-oriented than the propositional truth pair.

- **All eight languages distinguish between deliberate deception and honest error.** Georgian *q̇albi* (deliberate forgery) vs. *mcdari* (honest mistake); Yoruba *irọ́* (deliberate lie) vs. *àṣìṣe* (error/mistake); Finnish *valhe/bohong* (deliberate lie) vs. *virhe* (error); Basque *gezurra* (lie) vs. *okerra* (mistake/error); Tamil *poy* (deliberate lie) vs. *tavaṟu* (mistake/error); Indonesian *bohong/dusta* (deliberate lie) vs. *keliru* (honest error); Turkish *yalan* (deliberate lie) vs. *yanlış* (error/mistake); Korean *geojitmal* (deliberate lie) vs. *olyyu* (error/fallacy). The distinction is lexically encoded in all eight languages, though the degree of morphological marking varies.

- **All eight languages have a cluster of terms for source/testimony credibility that is distinct from the cluster for propositional truth.** Georgian *sarcmuno/sando* (credible/reliable); Yoruba *fidagarri/sinesgarri* (trustworthy/believable); Finnish *luotettava/uskottava* (reliable/credible); Basque *fidagarria/sinesgarria* (trustworthy/believable); Tamil *nampakamāna/nampattakka* (reliable/credible); Indonesian *terpercaya/kredibel* (trusted/credible); Turkish *güvenilir/inanılır* (reliable/believable); Korean *sinloeseong/sinbyeongseong* (reliability/credibility). In all cases the credibility cluster is distinct from the truth-value cluster, and in several languages (Finnish, Basque, Yoruba) a further distinction is drawn between source reliability and content believability.

- **All eight languages show a three-way distinction in the genuineness-versus-counterfeit domain: original/genuine, neutral copy/imitation, and fraudulent fake.** Georgian *namdvili* (genuine) / *asli* (original) / *q̇albi* (forged); Finnish *aito/alkuperäinen* (genuine/original) / *kopio* (neutral copy) / *jäljitelmä* (imitation) / *väärennös* (forgery); Basque *jatorrizkoa* (original) / *kopiakoa* (copy) / *faltsua* (fake); Tamil *acal* (original) / *nakal* (neutral copy) / *pōli* (fake); Indonesian *asli* (genuine/original) / *tiruan* (imitation) / *palsu* (fake); Turkish *orijinal/özgün* (original/authentic) / *taklit* (imitation) / *sahte* (fake); Korean *jinpum* (genuine article) / *mojopum* (imitation goods) / *wijopum* (forged item). The neutral intermediate position (copy/imitation without fraudulent intent) is explicitly documented in at least six of the eight languages.

- **All eight languages show an asymmetry in agentive nominalization: lexicalized agent nouns for liars and forgers are more common than lexicalized agent nouns for truth-tellers.** Georgian has *mt'q̇uari* (liar) and *gamaq̇albebeli* (forger) but no single-word truth-teller agentive. Yoruba has *aṣírọ́* (liar) but no single-word truth-teller. Finnish has *valehtelija* (liar) and *väärentäjä* (forger) but no single-word truth-teller. Basque has *gezurti* (liar) but no single-word truth-teller. Tamil has *poyyaṉ* (liar) and *vañcakaṉ* (deceiver) but no single-word truth-teller. Indonesian has *pembohong* (liar) and *pemalsu* (forger) but no single-word truth-teller. Turkish has *yalancı* (liar) and *sahteci* (forger) but no single-word truth-teller. Korean has *geojitmal-jaengi* (liar) and *wijobom* (forger) but no single-word truth-teller. In all eight languages the concept of "truth-teller" requires periphrastic expression.

- **All eight languages show a proverbial or formulaic construction asserting the ultimate triumph or indestructibility of truth.** Georgian *simarṭle gamarjvebs* (truth prevails); Yoruba *òtítọ́ kò ní kú* (truth will not die); Finnish *totuus tulee ilmi* (the truth comes out); Basque *egia beti ateratzen da azalera* (the truth always comes to the surface); Tamil *uṇmai tāṉ vellum* (truth alone will prevail); Indonesian *kebenaran akan terungkap pada akhirnya* (the truth will come out in the end); Turkish *doğruluk her zaman ödüllendirilmez* (truthfulness is not always rewarded — a more pessimistic variant, but the proverbial frame is present); Korean *jinsil-eun hanada* (there is only one truth). The specific framing varies (triumph, indestructibility, singularity), but the proverbial register is present in all eight languages.

---

### Major Divergences (patterns observed in only a few languages or showing strong cross-language differences)

- **The degree of morphological productivity of the primary truth root varies enormously across languages.** Turkish *doğru* and Georgian *marṭl-* generate the largest derivational families, extending into technical domains (Turkish: *doğrusal*, linear; *doğrultu*, direction; *doğrulanabilirlik*, verifiability), religious domains (Georgian: *marṭlmadidebeli*, Orthodox Christian; *marṭlsaidumlo*, true sacrament), and institutional domains (Georgian: *marṭlmsajuleba*, justice system; *marṭlc̣era*, orthography). By contrast, Yoruba *tọ́* and Tamil *uṇmai* generate smaller derivational families, with the Tamil family concentrated in adjectival, adverbial, and verbal noun forms rather than compound institutional terms.

- **The legality/legitimacy distinction is explicitly documented in Turkish, Georgian, and Korean but is less prominent in the other languages.** Turkish explicitly contrasts *yasal* (conforming to written law) with *meşru* (legitimate, potentially beyond strict legality). Georgian explicitly contrasts *kanonieri* (lawful, tied to positive law) with *legitimuri* (legitimate, with possible normative dimension beyond legality). Korean explicitly contrasts *hapbeop* (lawful) with *jeongdang* (legitimate/justified). In Basque, *zilegi* (lawful/permissible) and *baliozko* (valid) are documented but the legality/legitimacy distinction is less explicitly drawn. In Finnish, Indonesian, and Yoruba, the distinction is present but less prominently documented.

- **The appearance-versus-reality contrast is lexically encoded with dedicated terms in Georgian, Basque, and Finnish, but is handled more periphrastically in other languages.** Georgian *močvenebiti* (apparent/seeming/ostensible) and *piqtiuri* (fictitious/sham) are dedicated terms for the appearance-without-reality contrast. Basque *itxurazko* (apparent/seeming) and *itxurakeria* (pretense/hypocrisy) form a dedicated cluster. Finnish *näennäinen* (apparent/seeming/ostensible) is a dedicated term. In Yoruba, Tamil, Indonesian, Turkish, and Korean, the contrast is expressed through constructions (*itxuraz*, *sebenarnya*, *aslında*, *uṇmaiyil*) rather than dedicated adjectives.

- **The inner-state authenticity concept (sincerity/genuineness of feeling or intention, as opposed to performance) is most prominently developed in Korean and Georgian.** Korean *jinjeongseong* (authenticity/genuineness of inner state) is documented as a prominent contemporary public discourse term with its own evaluative construction (*jinjeongseong itda/eopda*). Georgian *gulc̣rpeli* (sincere/straight-hearted) and *tvaltmaqcoba* (eye-deceiving/hypocrisy) form a dedicated sincerity/hypocrisy pair. In other languages, sincerity is covered by more general terms: Yoruba *ìwà rere* (good character), Finnish *rehellinen* (honest), Basque *benetakoa* (genuine/sincere), Tamil *nērmai* (honesty/integrity), Indonesian *tulus/ikhlas* (sincere/selfless), Turkish *sahici* (genuine/real in an affective sense).

- **The philosophical/theological register for truth is most prominently developed in Georgian, Turkish, and Indonesian.** Georgian *č̣ešmariteba* is the dedicated philosophical and theological truth term, contrasting with the more everyday *simarṭle*. Turkish *hakikat* (from Arabic *ḥaqīqa*) is the elevated philosophical/religious truth term, contrasting with the more everyday *gerçek* and *doğru*. Indonesian *hakikat/hakiki* (from the same Arabic root) occupies a similar elevated register. In Yoruba, Finnish, Basque, Tamil, and Korean, the philosophical register is handled by the same terms as everyday truth discourse, without a dedicated elevated register term.

- **The verification/authentication cluster is most elaborately developed in Basque and Finnish.** Basque has a dedicated verbal stem *egiazta-* generating *egiaztatu* (to verify), *egiaztapen* (attestation), *egiaztagarria* (verifiable), *egiaztaezina* (unverifiable), *egiaztagaitza* (difficult to verify), and *egiaztatze-agiri* (verification document). Finnish has *todentaa* (to verify/authenticate), *todistaa* (to prove/testify), *tarkistaa* (to check), and *tarkastaa* (to inspect/audit), with explicit register distinctions between them. In other languages, verification is handled by more general terms or light-verb constructions without a dedicated verification stem.

- **The Islamic scholarly register for authenticity (*sahih*, from Arabic *ṣaḥīḥ*) appears in Turkish, Indonesian, and Basque but not in the other languages.** Turkish *sahih* (sound/authentic, restricted to Islamic hadith scholarship), Indonesian *sahih* (sound/correct, primarily in Islamic and academic methodology contexts), and Basque *sahih* (not documented — but the Arabic root appears in *sah/absah* in Indonesian and Turkish) share an Arabic-origin authenticity term that is absent from Georgian, Yoruba, Finnish, Tamil, and Korean. This reflects the historical influence of Islamic scholarship on these languages.

---

### Asymmetries, Gaps, and Irregularities

- **The *-hada/-doeda* distinction in Korean (active/agentive vs. stative/resultant predication) has no direct parallel in the other languages.** Korean documents a systematic semantic distinction between *jinsil-hada* (to be truthful, active/performed quality) and *jinsil-doeda* (to be truthful, inherent/resultant quality), and between *wijo-hada* (to forge, agentive) and *wijo-doeda* (to be forged, passive/resultant). This morphological distinction between performed and inherent quality is not documented in the other seven languages.

- **The *doğrulamak/yanlışlamak* parallel morphological pair in Turkish, encoding the logical positivist/Popperian verification/falsification distinction, is unique in the dataset.** No other language documents a morphologically parallel pair of verbs specifically encoding the philosophical distinction between verifying and falsifying a hypothesis. Finnish has *todistaa* (to prove) and *osoittaa epätodeksi* (to show to be false), but these are not morphologically parallel. Basque has *frogatu* (to prove) and *gezurtatu* (to give the lie to), but these are not a parallel pair encoding the same philosophical distinction.

- **The *salah* + [verb/noun] misaction compound pattern in Indonesian is unique in the dataset.** Indonesian documents a highly productive pattern in which *salah* (wrong/mistaken) combines with verbs and nouns to generate misaction compounds: *salah paham* (misunderstanding), *salah kaprah* (widespread misconception), *salah sasaran* (off-target), *salah tafsir* (misinterpretation), *salah langkah* (misstep), *salah alamat* (wrong address/barking up the wrong tree). No other language in the dataset shows this degree of productivity in misaction compounding from a single error root.

- **The *sarwmunoeba* (credibility/faith) semantic bifurcation in Georgian — where the same form means "credibility" in secular contexts and "faith/religion" in theological contexts — is unique in the dataset.** No other language documents a single form that covers both epistemic credibility and religious faith as its primary meanings in different registers.

- **The *ìwà* (character/nature) cluster in Yoruba, which treats character evaluation as a distinct semantic domain organized around the concept of "the manner of being," has no direct structural parallel in the other languages.** While all languages have terms for honesty and dishonesty, Yoruba uniquely organizes character evaluation around a single abstract nominal (*ìwà*) that generates a large cluster of compounds and collocations (*ìwà rere*, *ìwà burúkú*, *ìwà pẹ̀lẹ́*, *ìwà ìdúróṣinṣin*, *ìwà ló ń ṣe ènìyàn*). The proverb *ìwà ló ń ṣe ènìyàn* (character is what makes a person) is the clearest statement of this organizing principle.

- **The *kebenaran formal/kebenaran materiil* (formal truth/material truth) legal distinction in Indonesian is unique in the dataset.** This distinction between truth established through proper legal procedure and truth as the actual facts of a case is documented as a technical term in Indonesian criminal procedure. No other language in the dataset documents an equivalent formal/material truth distinction as a technical legal term, though the underlying conceptual distinction (procedural correctness vs. substantive accuracy) is present in the legal vocabulary of several languages.

- **The *ziurrenik* (probably/most likely) semantic shift in Basque — where a form derived from *ziur* (certain) functions in practice as a probability hedge rather than an assertion of full certainty — is unique in the dataset.** No other language documents a comparable semantic shift from certainty to probability within the same derivational family. The data notes this as a fully established shift rather than a marginal usage.

# G3 — Emergent Cross-Language Semantic Dimensions

## Methodology Note

The dimensions below are derived inductively from the F3 semantic grouping tables, the F1 vocabulary inventories, the F2 derivational and constructional data, and the G2 comparative analysis. Each dimension is defined by co-occurrence patterns, grouping decisions, and explicit contrasts documented in the source data. No dimension is asserted unless it is supported by evidence from at least two languages; single-language observations are flagged as such.

---

## Proposed Semantic Dimensions

### Dimension 1: Propositional Correspondence

**Definition.** This dimension concerns whether a specific statement, claim, or report matches what is actually the case in the world. It is the dimension along which terms like "true," "false," "accurate," and "incorrect" are evaluated. The evaluative target is a proposition or utterance, not a person or object.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: *simartle* (truth, everyday), *č̣ešmariteba* (truth, philosophical), *mcdari* (erroneous), *poy* (falsehood)
- Yoruba: *òtítọ́* (truth), *irọ́* (lie/falsehood), *ó tọ́* (it is correct)
- Finnish: *tosi* (true), *totuus* (truth), *epätosi* (untrue), *pitää paikkansa* (to hold/be true)
- Basque: *egia* (truth), *gezurra* (lie/falsehood), *egia da* (it is true)
- Tamil: *uṇmai* (truth), *poy* (falsehood), *cari* (correct), *tavaṟu* (wrong/error)
- Indonesian: *benar* (correct/true), *salah* (wrong), *kebenaran* (truth)
- Turkish: *doğru* (correct/true), *yanlış* (wrong/false), *doğruluk* (truthfulness/accuracy)
- Korean: *사실* (fact/truth), *허위* (falsehood), *맞다* (to be correct), *틀리다* (to be wrong)

**Distribution:** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. This is the most consistently attested dimension in the dataset. Every language maintains at least one dedicated nominal for truth and one for falsehood in this propositional sense, and these are the most productive bases for further derivation.

**Internal variation:** Several languages split this dimension by register. Georgian maintains *č̣ešmariteba* (philosophical/theological) vs. *simartle* (everyday/legal). Finnish maintains *totuus* (nominal, formal) vs. *tosi* (predicative, colloquial). Korean maintains *진리* (philosophical/universal) vs. *진실* (everyday truthfulness) vs. *사실* (factual accuracy). Yoruba and Tamil show less register differentiation within this dimension.

---

### Dimension 2: Personal Honesty and Integrity in Conduct

**Definition.** This dimension concerns whether a person's habitual conduct, character, or disposition is free from deception and consistent with truthful expression. The evaluative target is a person or their pattern of behavior, not a specific proposition. Terms in this dimension evaluate character rather than the truth-value of a claim.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: *gulc̣rpeli* (sincere/straight-hearted), *nērmai*-equivalent absent as single term; *tvaltmaqcoba* (hypocrisy)
- Yoruba: *ìwà rere* (good character), *ìwà burúkú* (bad character), *olòtítọ́* (truthful person)
- Finnish: *rehellinen* (honest), *rehellisyys* (honesty), *vilpitön* (sincere/in good faith), *vilpillinen* (fraudulent/deceitful)
- Basque: *benetakoa* (genuine/sincere), *benetan* (truly/in earnest), *itxurakeria* (pretense/hypocrisy)
- Tamil: *nērmai* (honesty/integrity), *kaḷḷam* (deceit/guile), *vañcaṉai* (deception)
- Indonesian: *jujur* (honest), *kejujuran* (honesty), *tulus* (sincere), *ikhlas* (selflessly sincere)
- Turkish: *dürüst* (upright/honest), *dürüstlük* (honesty/integrity), *özü sözü bir* (one whose word matches their character)
- Korean: *정직* (honesty/integrity), *정직하다* (to be honest), *거짓말* (lie), *거짓말하다* (to lie)

**Distribution:** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. The dimension is universally present but the specific terms used are not cognate across languages. The evaluative target (person/character vs. proposition) is the defining criterion.

**Internal variation:** Yoruba elaborates this dimension most extensively through the *ìwà* (character/manner of being) concept, which organizes a large cluster of moral evaluation vocabulary. Indonesian distinguishes *tulus* (sincere inner motivation) from *ikhlas* (selflessly sincere, with specifically religious connotations of acceptance without expectation of reward) — a sub-distinction not documented in other languages. The absence of a lexicalized single-word agentive for "truth-teller" is consistent across all eight languages, while agentives for "liar" are lexicalized in all eight.

---

### Dimension 3: Source Trustworthiness vs. Content Credibility

**Definition.** This dimension concerns whether a person, institution, or source of information can be depended upon to provide accurate information (source trustworthiness), and whether a specific claim or account is such that it merits belief (content credibility). These two evaluative targets — the source and the content — are distinguished in all eight languages, though the degree of lexical differentiation varies.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: *sarc̣muno* (credible/trustworthy, inherent property of source) vs. *damajerebeliˈ* (convincing/persuasive, effect on hearer); *sando* (reliable/dependable, interpersonal)
- Yoruba: *fidagarri* (trustworthy source) vs. *sinesgarri* (believable content); *ìgbẹ́kẹ̀lé* (reliance/dependability)
- Finnish: *luotettava* (reliable/dependable over time) vs. *uskottava* (believable for a specific claim); *luotettavuus* vs. *uskottavuus*
- Basque: *fidagarria* (trustworthy source) vs. *sinesgarria* (believable content); *fidagarritasuna* vs. *sinesgarritasuna*
- Tamil: *nampakamāna* (reliable) vs. *nampattakka* (worth trusting for a specific claim); *nampikkai* (trust/faith)
- Indonesian: *terpercaya* (trusted/reliable) vs. *kredibel* (credible); *kepercayaan* (trust)
- Turkish: *güvenilir* (reliable/trustworthy) vs. *inanılır* (believable); *güvenilirlik* vs. *inanılırlık*
- Korean: *신뢰성* (reliability of a source) vs. *신빙성* (credibility of a specific claim); *신뢰도* (degree of reliability)

**Distribution:** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. The distinction between source trustworthiness and content credibility is explicitly documented in the F3 grouping tables for Georgian, Yoruba, Finnish, Basque, Tamil, Indonesian, Turkish, and Korean. In several languages (Georgian, Yoruba, Finnish, Basque), the distinction is explicitly noted in the boundary notes of the relevant semantic groups.

**Internal variation:** The degree of lexical differentiation varies. Georgian, Yoruba, Finnish, and Basque show the most explicit lexical separation. Korean shows the most internal differentiation within the trustworthiness dimension, maintaining distinct terms for *신뢰* (trust as a relationship), *신뢰성* (reliability as a property), *신뢰도* (degree of reliability), and *신빙성* (credibility of a specific claim).

---

### Dimension 4: Genuineness of Objects vs. Fraudulent Imitation

**Definition.** This dimension concerns whether a physical object, document, artwork, currency, or credential is what it purports to be (genuine/original) or is a fraudulent substitute (counterfeit/forged). The evaluative target is a physical item or document, not a proposition or person. Terms in this dimension appear in legal, commercial, and art-authentication contexts.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: *namdvili* (genuine/real), *q̇albi* (fake/counterfeit), *gaq̇albeba* (forgery/falsification), *avtentiuri* (authentic, formal)
- Yoruba: *gidi* (genuine/real), *ìjẹ́rìísí* (attestation/certification); less elaborated than other languages
- Finnish: *aito* (genuine/authentic), *alkuperäinen* (original), *väärennös* (forgery), *jäljitelmä* (imitation, neutral)
- Basque: *benetakoa* (genuine/real), *jatorrizkoa* (original), *faltsua* (fake), *faltsifikatu* (to forge)
- Tamil: *acal* (original/genuine), *nakal* (copy, neutral), *pōli* (fake/counterfeit)
- Indonesian: *asli* (genuine/original), *tiruan* (imitation, neutral), *palsu* (fake/fraudulent), *pemalsuan* (forgery)
- Turkish: *orijinal* (original), *özgün* (authentic/original, creative), *sahte* (counterfeit/fake), *taklit* (imitation)
- Korean: *진짜* (genuine/real), *가짜* (fake/counterfeit), *진품* (genuine article), *위조* (forgery), *모조품* (imitation goods)

**Distribution:** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages, though the degree of elaboration varies. At least six languages (Finnish, Basque, Tamil, Indonesian, Turkish, Korean) explicitly distinguish a neutral-copy pole (imitation without fraudulent intent) from a fraudulent-fake pole (counterfeit with intent to deceive). Georgian and Yoruba show less elaboration of this three-way contrast.

**Internal variation:** The neutral-copy / fraudulent-fake distinction is the most consistently documented sub-distinction within this dimension. Finnish *jäljitelmä* (imitation, neutral) vs. *väärennös* (forgery, fraudulent); Tamil *nakal* (copy, neutral) vs. *pōli* (fake, negative); Indonesian *tiruan* (imitation, neutral) vs. *palsu* (fake, fraudulent); Turkish *taklit* (imitation) vs. *sahte* (counterfeit); Korean *모조품* (imitation goods) vs. *위조품* (forged item). Yoruba shows the least elaboration of this dimension.

### Dimension 5: Legal/Procedural Validity vs. Moral/Substantive Legitimacy

**Definition.** This dimension concerns whether an action, document, contract, or authority meets the formal conditions required for legal recognition (procedural validity) and whether it is rightful or justified in a broader normative sense that may extend beyond strict legality (legitimacy). All eight languages maintain some distinction between these two evaluative targets, though the degree of lexical differentiation varies.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: *kanonieri* (lawful, tied to positive law) vs. *legitimuri* (legitimate, with possible normative dimension); *sasamartlo* (court), *martlmsajuleba* (justice/administration of justice)
- Yoruba: *ẹ̀tọ́* (right/entitlement/correctness), *ìdájọ́* (judgment/adjudication), *òdodo* (righteousness/justice); less lexically differentiated
- Finnish: *pätevä* (valid/competent) vs. *oikeudenmukainen* (just/fair); *geçerli*-equivalent: *voimassa oleva* (in force)
- Basque: *baliozkoa* (valid) vs. *zilegi* (lawful/permissible) vs. *zuzen* (correct/just); *baliogabea* (invalid)
- Tamil: *caṭṭappaṭi* (according to law) vs. *niyāyam* (justice/rightness); *takuti* (qualification/eligibility)
- Indonesian: *sah* (legally valid) vs. *adil* (fair/just); *meşru*-equivalent: *meşru* (legitimate, from Arabic); *geçerli*-equivalent: *berlaku* (in force)
- Turkish: *yasal* (legal, conforming to written law) vs. *meşru* (legitimate, extending beyond legality); *geçerli* (valid/in force) vs. *geçersiz* (invalid/void)
- Korean: *합법* (lawful) vs. *정당* (legitimate/justified); *유효* (valid/in force) vs. *무효* (invalid/void)

**Distribution:** Present in all eight languages. The distinction between strict legality and broader legitimacy is explicitly documented in the F3 grouping tables for Georgian, Finnish, Basque, Indonesian, Turkish, and Korean. The distinction between operative validity (in force) and invalidity (void) is documented in all eight languages.

**Internal variation:** Turkish shows the most explicit lexical differentiation, with *yasal* (legal), *meşru* (legitimate), and *geçerli* (valid/in force) as three distinct terms. Korean similarly distinguishes *합법* (lawful), *정당* (legitimate/justified), and *유효* (valid/in force). Yoruba shows the least elaboration of this dimension, with the relevant concepts expressed through more general vocabulary.

---

### Dimension 6: Precision and Exactness of Correspondence

**Definition.** This dimension concerns the degree to which a measurement, description, translation, or representation corresponds closely and exactly to its referent or standard. Unlike Dimension 1 (propositional correspondence, which is binary), this dimension is scalar and concerns the closeness of fit between a representation and what it represents. Terms in this dimension appear in scientific, technical, journalistic, and administrative contexts.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: *zusti* (exact/precise), *sizuste* (accuracy/precision), *tarkka*-equivalent: *zusti targmani* (accurate translation)
- Yoruba: *tọ́ pátápátá* (completely correct), *zehaztasun*-equivalent: less elaborated as a distinct dimension
- Finnish: *tarkka* (precise/accurate), *tarkkuus* (accuracy/precision), *akurat*-equivalent: *tarkka mittaus* (accurate measurement)
- Basque: *zehatza* (precise/exact/accurate), *zehaztasuna* (precision/accuracy)
- Tamil: *uṇmaiyāna* (true/genuine/accurate), *caripārtttal* (verification/checking); *jeonghwak*-equivalent: less elaborated
- Indonesian: *tepat* (precise/exact/fitting), *akurat* (accurate), *cermat* (careful/meticulous/precise)
- Turkish: *doğru* (correct/accurate), *doğruluk* (accuracy/truthfulness); *kesinlik* (precision) — less elaborated as distinct from correctness
- Korean: *정확* (accuracy/precision), *정확성* (accuracy as a property), *정확히* (accurately/exactly), *정확도* (degree of accuracy)

**Distribution:** Clearly lexicalized in at least six languages (Georgian, Finnish, Basque, Indonesian, Korean, and partially Turkish). In Yoruba and Tamil, the dimension is less elaborated as a distinct lexical category; the concept is expressed through the general correctness vocabulary rather than through dedicated precision terms.

**Internal variation:** Korean shows the most elaboration of this dimension, with *정확* generating a productive derivational family including *정확성* (accuracy as a property), *정확도* (degree of accuracy), *정확히* (accurately), and *부정확* (inaccuracy). Finnish similarly shows elaboration through *tarkka*, *tarkkuus*, *tarkistaa* (to check/verify), and *tarkastaa* (to inspect/audit). The *tarkistaa*/*tarkastaa* register distinction (everyday checking vs. formal inspection) is documented only in Finnish.

### Dimension 7: Authenticity of Inner States and Expressed Feelings

**Definition.** This dimension concerns whether a person's expressed feelings, intentions, apologies, or commitments reflect genuine inner conviction rather than performance, calculation, or pretense. The evaluative target is the relationship between inner state and outward expression, not the truth-value of a proposition or the genuineness of a physical object. Terms in this dimension appear in interpersonal, political, and artistic evaluation contexts.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: *gulc̣rpeli* (sincere/straight-hearted, literally "straight-hearted"), *tvaltmaqcoba* (hypocrisy/eye-deceiving)
- Yoruba: *ìwà rere* (good character), *àgàbàgebè* (pretense/hypocrisy/sham behavior)
- Finnish: *aito tunne* (genuine feeling), *epäaito* (inauthentic), *vilpitön* (sincere/in good faith)
- Basque: *benetakoa* (genuine/sincere), *benetan* (truly/in earnest), *itxurakeria* (pretense/hypocrisy)
- Tamil: *uṇmai aṉpu* (true love/genuine affection), *nērmai* (honesty/integrity); less elaborated as a distinct dimension
- Indonesian: *tulus* (sincere), *ikhlas* (selflessly sincere), *sungguh-sungguh* (in earnest/genuinely)
- Turkish: *sahici* (genuine/authentic, colloquial), *özü sözü bir* (one whose word matches their character)
- Korean: *진정성* (authenticity of inner state), *진심* (sincere heart/genuine feeling), *진심으로* (sincerely/from the heart)

**Distribution:** Present in all eight languages, but the degree of lexical elaboration varies considerably. Korean shows the most elaboration, with *진정성* functioning as a highly developed public evaluative category with a rich collocation network (*진정성 있다/없다*, *진정성 논란*, *진정성을 의심받다*). Basque and Finnish show moderate elaboration. Tamil and Turkish show less elaboration of this as a distinct dimension.

**Internal variation:** Korean's *진정성* is documented as a specifically contemporary public evaluative category applied to political apologies, artistic works, and public figures — a use that is more elaborated than in any other language in the dataset. The Yoruba *ìwà* (character/manner of being) concept organizes this dimension differently, treating it as a matter of fundamental character rather than the authenticity of specific expressions.

### Dimension 8: Appearance vs. Underlying Reality

**Definition.** This dimension concerns the contrast between how something appears on the surface and what it actually is. Terms in this dimension are used to signal that a surface appearance may be misleading, that something presents itself as other than it is, or that the true nature of something differs from its apparent nature. This dimension is distinct from Dimension 4 (genuineness of objects) in that it applies to situations, arguments, and qualities rather than primarily to physical items.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: *moč̣venebiti* (apparent/seeming/ostensible), *garegnuli* (external/outward/superficial), *šinaˈarsi* (content/substance/inner meaning)
- Yoruba: *ìfarahàn* (appearance/manifestation), *àgàbàgebè* (pretense/sham); less elaborated as a distinct dimension
- Finnish: *näennäinen* (apparent/seeming/ostensible), *todellinen* (real/actual), *todellisuus* (reality)
- Basque: *itxura* (appearance/semblance), *itxurazko* (apparent/seeming/superficial), *itxurakeria* (pretense/hypocrisy), *itxuraz* (apparently/seemingly)
- Tamil: *uṇmai nilavaram* (true state of affairs), *uṇmai nilai* (the actual situation); less elaborated as a distinct dimension
- Indonesian: *sebenarnya* (actually/in truth), *pada kenyataannya* (in reality), *nyata* (real/manifest)
- Turkish: *gerçek dışı* (unreal/contrary to fact), *gerçeğe aykırı* (contrary to reality), *aslında* (actually/in fact)
- Korean: *실체* (true nature/underlying reality), *실제* (actuality/reality), *실제로* (actually/in reality)

**Distribution:** Present in all eight languages, but the degree of lexical elaboration varies. Basque shows the most elaboration, with *itxura* generating a productive derivational family (*itxurazko*, *itxurakeria*, *itxuragilea*, *itxuraz*). Georgian shows elaboration through *moč̣venebiti* (ostensible) and the *šinaˈarsi*/*garegnuli* (inner content/outer appearance) contrast. Finnish shows elaboration through *näennäinen* (apparent/seeming). Yoruba and Tamil show less elaboration of this as a distinct lexical dimension.

**Internal variation:** The Basque *itxura* cluster is the most productive single-root elaboration of this dimension in the dataset. The Georgian *moč̣venebiti* is explicitly distinguished from *q̇albi* (fake, implying deliberate deception) and from *namdvili* (genuine) in the F5 opposition tables — a three-way distinction that is not paralleled in other languages.

### Dimension 9: Evidential Grounding and Proof

**Definition.** This dimension concerns whether a claim is supported by adequate evidence or grounds, and the processes by which evidence is produced, evaluated, and used to establish the truth of a claim. Terms in this dimension appear in legal, scientific, journalistic, and argumentative contexts. The evaluative question is not merely whether a claim is true but whether it can be demonstrated to be true.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: *mt'k'icebuleba* (proof/evidence), *mt'k'iceba* (assertion/act of proving), *dadastureba* (confirmation/verification), *utyuari* (irrefutable/beyond doubt)
- Yoruba: *ẹ̀rí* (evidence/proof/witness), *ìjẹ́rìísí* (testimony/attestation/certification), *ìdánwò* (test/trial/verification)
- Finnish: *todiste* (piece of evidence), *todistus* (proof/testimony/certificate), *todistustaakka* (burden of proof), *todistusvoima* (probative force)
- Basque: *froga* (proof/evidence), *frogatu* (to prove/demonstrate), *egiaztagarria* (verifiable), *egiaztaezina* (unverifiable)
- Tamil: *ātāram* (evidence/basis/grounds), *cāṉṟu* (evidence/proof/attestation), *nirūpaṇam* (proof/demonstration)
- Indonesian: *bukti* (evidence/proof), *pembuktian* (proof/verification), *tidak berdasar* (unfounded/baseless)
- Turkish: *kanıt* (evidence/proof), *kanıtlamak* (to prove), *ispat* (proof, formal), *asılsız* (unfounded/baseless)
- Korean: *근거* (basis/grounds/evidence), *신빙성* (credibility of a claim), *타당성* (validity/soundness), *위증* (perjury/false testimony)

**Distribution:** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. This dimension is particularly elaborated in legal contexts across all languages. The distinction between the act of proving (*mt'k'iceba*, *frogatu*, *todistaa*, *kanıtlamak*) and the product of proof (*mt'k'icebuleba*, *froga*, *todiste*, *kanıt*) is documented in at least five languages.

**Internal variation:** Basque shows the most elaboration of the verifiability sub-dimension, with the three-way *egiaztagarria* (verifiable) / *egiaztagaitza* (difficult to verify) / *egiaztaezina* (impossible to verify) distinction. Finnish shows elaboration through the *todistaa* derivational family (*todistus*, *todiste*, *todistaja*, *todistustaakka*, *todistusvoima*). Turkish shows the unique *doğrulanabilirlik*/*yanlışlanabilirlik* (verifiability/falsifiability) morphological opposition.

### Dimension 10: Truth Revelation and Concealment as Processes

**Definition.** This dimension concerns the processes by which truth is brought to light, concealed, sought, or suppressed. Terms in this dimension treat truth as an entity that can be revealed, hidden, distorted, or discovered, and they appear in investigative, journalistic, narrative, and legal contexts. This dimension is distinct from Dimension 1 (propositional correspondence) in that it concerns the dynamics of truth-disclosure rather than the static evaluation of a proposition.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: *simartle gamovida* (the truth came out), *simartle damalva* (concealment of truth), *simartle gamovlena* (revelation of truth)
- Yoruba: *ó farahàn pé òtítọ́ ni* (it became clear that it is the truth), *ó ń pa òtítọ́ mọ́* (he/she is concealing the truth)
- Finnish: *totuus tulee ilmi* (the truth comes to light), *totuus paljastuu* (the truth is revealed), *menyembunyikan kebenaran*-equivalent: *totuutta salataan* (the truth is being hidden)
- Basque: *egia argitara atera* (to bring truth to light), *egia ezkutatu* (to hide the truth), *egiaren bila ibili* (to go about seeking the truth)
- Tamil: *uṇmai veḷippaṭṭatu* (the truth came to light), *uṇmai maṟaittal* (concealment of truth), *uṇmai tēṭutal* (seeking the truth)
- Indonesian: *mengungkap kebenaran* (to reveal the truth), *menyembunyikan kebenaran* (to conceal the truth), *kebenaran akan terungkap* (the truth will come out)
- Turkish: *gerçeği ortaya çıkarmak* (to bring the truth to light), *gerçeği gizlemek* (to hide the truth), *hakikati aramak* (to seek the truth)
- Korean: *진실이 드러나다* (the truth emerges), *진실을 밝히다* (to reveal the truth), *진실을 숨기다* (to conceal the truth), *진상 규명* (clarification of the true facts)

**Distribution:** Present in all eight languages. The intransitive/passive framing of truth-revelation (truth as grammatical subject of an emergence verb) is documented in all eight languages. The transitive framing (agent reveals/conceals truth) is also documented in all eight languages. The proverbial assertion that truth ultimately prevails is documented in all eight languages.

**Internal variation:** Korean shows the most elaboration of the investigative sub-dimension, with *진상 규명* (clarification of the true facts) and *진실화해위원회* (Truth and Reconciliation Commission) as institutionalized expressions. Georgian shows elaboration through the *simartle* derivational family (*simartle gamovida*, *simartle damalva*, *simartle gamovlena*, *simartle madziebeliˈ*). The spatial metaphor of truth "coming to light" or "coming to the surface" is consistent across all eight languages.

### Dimension 11: Correctness of Reasoning, Judgment, and Understanding

**Definition.** This dimension concerns whether a judgment, inference, interpretation, or understanding is correct — whether it follows properly from evidence or reasoning. It is distinct from Dimension 1 (propositional correspondence) in that the evaluative target is a cognitive process or its output rather than a simple factual claim. Terms in this dimension appear in educational, philosophical, and argumentative contexts.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: *martebuli* (correct/appropriate/well-founded), *martebuloba* (correctness/soundness), *gamarṭleba* (justification/vindication)
- Yoruba: *ó tọ́ pé* (it is right that), *àṣìṣe* (error/mistake/wrongdoing), *ẹ̀ṣẹ̀* (sin/fault/offense)
- Finnish: *perusteltu* (justified/well-founded), *perusteeton* (unfounded/groundless), *pätevä* (valid/sound)
- Basque: *zuzena* (correct/right/just), *okerra* (wrong/incorrect/crooked), *tadunga*-equivalent: *zuzentasun* (correctness/justice)
- Tamil: *niyāyamāna* (just/fair/reasonable), *cariyāna* (correct/proper), *tavaṟāna* (wrong/erroneous)
- Indonesian: *tepat* (precise/fitting/appropriate), *wajar* (reasonable/natural/proper), *pantas* (fitting/appropriate/deserved)
- Turkish: *haklı* (justified/in the right), *haksız* (unjust/wrongful), *tarafsız* (impartial/neutral)
- Korean: *타당* (valid/reasonable/sound), *타당성* (validity/soundness), *올바르다* (to be correct/right/proper), *옳다* (to be right/correct)

**Distribution:** Present in all eight languages, but the degree of lexical differentiation from Dimension 1 (propositional correspondence) varies. In some languages (Yoruba, Tamil), the same root covers both propositional correctness and correctness of reasoning. In others (Georgian, Finnish, Korean), distinct vocabulary is used for these two functions.

**Internal variation:** Georgian shows the most elaboration of the justification sub-dimension, with *gamarṭleba* (justification/vindication/acquittal) generating a productive derivational family. Turkish shows elaboration through the *haklı*/*haksız* pair (justified/unjustified), which covers both epistemic and moral justification. Korean shows elaboration through the *타당성* (validity/soundness) cluster, which is specifically associated with argumentative and policy contexts.

### Dimension 12: Deliberate Deception vs. Innocent Error

**Definition.** This dimension concerns the distinction between statements or representations that are false because of deliberate intent to deceive and those that are false because of honest mistake or misunderstanding. Terms in this dimension appear in moral, legal, and everyday evaluative contexts where the agent's intent is relevant to the evaluation. This dimension is a sub-distinction within the broader domain of falsehood.

**Representative terms:**
- Georgian: *sicrue*/*ẗq̇uili* (deliberate lie) vs. *mcdari* (erroneous/mistaken, without implying intent); *q̇albi* (fake, implying deliberate deception) vs. *mcdari* (erroneous)
- Yoruba: *irọ́* (deliberate lie) vs. *àṣìṣe* (error/mistake, without strong implication of intent); *ìtànjẹ́* (deliberate deception/fraud)
- Finnish: *valhe* (lie, deliberate) vs. *virhe* (error, neutral); *väärentää* (to forge, implying intent) vs. *vääristymä* (distortion, possibly unintentional)
- Basque: *gezurra* (lie, deliberate) vs. *oker* (wrong/mistaken, without implying intent); *faltsifikatu* (to forge, implying intent)
- Tamil: *poy* (lie, deliberate) vs. *tavaṟu* (mistake/error, without implying intent); *vañcaṉai* (deliberate deception)
- Indonesian: *bohong* (deliberate lie) vs. *keliru* (innocent error/misunderstanding); *salah* (wrong, neutral to intent)
- Turkish: *yalan* (deliberate lie) vs. *yanlış* (wrong/incorrect, neutral to intent); *aldatıcı* (deceptive, implying intent) vs. *yanıltıcı* (misleading, possibly unintentional)
- Korean: *거짓말* (deliberate lie) vs. *실수* (mistake, innocent); *허위* (falsehood, formal) vs. *오류* (error/fallacy, neutral)

**Distribution:** Present in all eight languages. The distinction between deliberate deception and innocent error is explicitly documented in the F3 grouping tables for Georgian, Finnish, Basque, Indonesian, Turkish, and Korean. In Yoruba and Tamil, the distinction is present but less elaborated as a distinct lexical category.

**Internal variation:** Indonesian shows the most explicit lexical differentiation, with *bohong* (deliberate lie) vs. *keliru* (innocent error) explicitly distinguished in the F3 grouping tables. Turkish shows elaboration through the *aldatıcı* (deceptive, implying intent) vs. *yanıltıcı* (misleading, possibly unintentional) distinction. Finnish shows elaboration through the *väärentää* (to forge, implying intent) vs. *vääristymä* (distortion, possibly unintentional) distinction.

## Evaluation of Cross-Linguistic Support

### Strongly Supported Dimensions (present and clearly lexicalized in all 8 languages)

- **D1: Propositional Correspondence** — The most consistently attested dimension. Every language has dedicated nominals for truth and falsehood in the propositional sense, and these are the most productive derivational bases.
- **D2: Personal Honesty and Integrity** — Universally present. The evaluative target (person/character) consistently distinguishes this from D1 across all languages.
- **D3: Source Trustworthiness vs. Content Credibility** — Explicitly documented in all 8 languages, with the source/content distinction noted in F3 boundary notes for multiple languages.
- **D5: Legal/Procedural Validity vs. Moral/Substantive Legitimacy** — Present in all 8 languages. The operative validity vs. invalidity sub-distinction is documented in all 8 languages.
- **D9: Evidential Grounding and Proof** — Clearly lexicalized in all 8 languages. The act-of-proving vs. product-of-proof distinction is documented in at least 5 languages.
- **D10: Truth Revelation and Concealment as Processes** — Present in all 8 languages. The intransitive/passive framing of truth-revelation and the proverbial assertion that truth ultimately prevails are both documented in all 8 languages.
- **D12: Deliberate Deception vs. Innocent Error** — Present in all 8 languages. Explicitly documented in F3 grouping tables for at least 6 languages.

### Moderately Supported Dimensions (present in most languages, but degree of elaboration varies)

- **D4: Genuineness of Objects vs. Fraudulent Imitation** — Clearly lexicalized in all 8 languages, but the neutral-copy vs. fraudulent-fake sub-distinction is documented in only 6 languages. Yoruba shows the least elaboration.
- **D6: Precision and Exactness of Correspondence** — Clearly lexicalized in at least 6 languages. Less elaborated in Yoruba and Tamil as a distinct dimension separate from D1.
- **D7: Authenticity of Inner States and Expressed Feelings** — Present in all 8 languages, but degree of elaboration varies considerably. Korean shows the most elaboration; Tamil and Turkish show less.
- **D8: Appearance vs. Underlying Reality** — Present in at least 6 languages with explicit documentation. Basque shows the most elaboration. Yoruba and Tamil show less elaboration as a distinct lexical dimension.
- **D11: Correctness of Reasoning, Judgment, and Understanding** — Present in all 8 languages, but degree of differentiation from D1 varies. Some languages use the same root for both propositional correctness and correctness of reasoning.

### Dimensions That Split, Merge, or Vary Across Specific Languages

**D1 and D11 merge in Yoruba and Tamil:** The *tọ́* root in Yoruba covers both propositional correctness (*ó tọ́*, "it is correct") and procedural/moral correctness (*ó tọ́ pé*, "it is right that") without lexical differentiation. Similarly, Tamil *cari* covers both factual correctness and procedural correctness. Georgian, Finnish, and Korean maintain more distinct vocabulary for these two functions.

**D2 and D7 merge in Basque and Indonesian:** Basque *benetakoa* covers both "genuine (not fake)" and "sincere (not performed)," merging D4 and D7 partially. Indonesian *tulus* and *ikhlas* cover both personal honesty (D2) and authenticity of inner states (D7) without a sharp lexical boundary.

**D4 and D7 partially merge in Basque:** *Benetakoa* applies to both genuine objects (D4) and genuine feelings/intentions (D7), while other languages (Finnish, Korean) maintain more distinct vocabulary for these two functions.

**D5 splits into three sub-dimensions in Turkish and Korean:** Turkish distinguishes *yasal* (legal), *meşru* (legitimate), and *geçerli* (valid/in force) as three distinct terms. Korean similarly distinguishes *합법* (lawful), *정당* (legitimate/justified), and *유효* (valid/in force). Other languages show less lexical differentiation within D5.

**D6 is weakly attested in Yoruba and Tamil:** The precision/exactness dimension is not elaborated as a distinct lexical category in these languages; the concept is expressed through the general correctness vocabulary of D1.

**D8 is weakly attested in Yoruba and Tamil:** The appearance-vs.-reality dimension is not elaborated as a distinct lexical category in these languages; the concept is expressed through more general vocabulary.

**D9 shows unique elaboration in Basque:** The three-way *egiaztagarria* (verifiable) / *egiaztagaitza* (difficult to verify) / *egiaztaezina* (impossible to verify) distinction within the verifiability sub-dimension has no parallel in any other language in the dataset.

**D10 shows unique institutionalization in Korean:** The *진상 규명* (clarification of the true facts) and *진실화해위원회* (Truth and Reconciliation Commission) expressions represent an institutionalized elaboration of this dimension not paralleled in other languages.

## Narrative Analysis

### Recurring Partition Patterns

**The propositional truth / personal honesty split is present in all eight languages.** Every language maintains a lexical distinction between evaluating whether a statement is true and evaluating whether a person is honest. The terms used for these two functions are never identical, though they may share a root. Georgian uses *simarṭle/č̣ešmariteba* for propositional truth and *gulc̣rpeli* for sincerity; Yoruba uses *òtítọ́* for propositional truth and *ìwà rere* for moral character; Finnish uses *tosi/totuus* for propositional truth and *rehellinen* for honesty; Basque uses *egia* for propositional truth and *benetakoa* for genuine sincerity; Tamil uses *uṇmai* for propositional truth and *nērmai* for honesty/integrity; Indonesian uses *benar* for correctness and *jujur* for honesty; Turkish uses *doğru* for correctness and *dürüst* for uprightness; Korean uses *사실* for factual accuracy and *정직* for honesty. The split is consistent across all eight languages, though the degree of lexical elaboration on each side varies considerably.

**The source-trustworthiness / content-credibility distinction is present in all eight languages.** Georgian explicitly distinguishes *sarc̣muno* (inherent trustworthiness of a source) from *damajerebeliˈ* (persuasive effect on a hearer). Yoruba distinguishes *fidagarri* (trustworthy source) from *sinesgarri* (believable content). Finnish distinguishes *luotettava* (reliable/dependable over time) from *uskottava* (believable for a specific claim). Basque distinguishes *fidagarria* (trustworthy source) from *sinesgarria* (believable content). Tamil distinguishes *nampakamāna* (reliable) from *nampattakka* (worth trusting for a specific claim). Indonesian distinguishes *terpercaya* (trusted/reliable) from *kredibel* (credible). Turkish distinguishes *güvenilir* (reliable) from *inanılır* (believable). Korean distinguishes *신뢰성* (reliability of a source) from *신빙성* (credibility of a specific claim). The distinction is lexically encoded in all eight languages, though the degree of elaboration varies.

**The neutral-copy / fraudulent-fake distinction is present in at least six languages.** Finnish distinguishes *jäljitelmä* (imitation, without necessarily implying fraud) from *väärennös* (forgery, implying fraudulent intent). Basque distinguishes *kopiakoa* (copy) from *faltsua* (fake). Tamil distinguishes *nakal* (copy, neutral) from *pōli* (fake, negative). Indonesian distinguishes *tiruan* (imitation, neutral) from *palsu* (fake, fraudulent). Turkish distinguishes *taklit* (imitation) from *sahte* (counterfeit). Korean distinguishes *모조품* (imitation goods) from *위조품* (forged item). Georgian and Yoruba show less elaboration of this three-way contrast: Georgian has *namdvili* vs. *q̇albi* as a binary, and Yoruba lacks a dedicated forgery vocabulary.

**The legal/procedural validity vs. moral/substantive legitimacy distinction is present in all eight languages.** Georgian distinguishes *kanonieri* (lawful, tied to positive law) from *legitimuri* (legitimate, with possible normative dimension). Finnish distinguishes *pätevä* (valid/competent) from *oikeudenmukainen* (just/fair). Basque distinguishes *baliozko* (valid) from *zilegi* (lawful/permissible) from *zuzen* (correct/just). Tamil distinguishes *caṭṭappaṭi* (according to law) from *niyāyam* (justice/rightness). Indonesian distinguishes *sah* (legally valid) from *adil* (fair/just). Turkish distinguishes *yasal* (legal) from *meşru* (legitimate, extending beyond legality). Korean distinguishes *합법* (lawful) from *정당* (legitimate/justified). The distinction is present in all eight languages, though the degree of lexical elaboration and the specific terms used vary considerably.

**The intransitive/passive framing of truth-revelation is cross-linguistically consistent.** All eight languages show constructions in which truth is the grammatical subject of an intransitive or passive verb expressing emergence or disclosure: Georgian *simarṭle gamovida* (the truth came out), Yoruba *ó farahàn pé òtítọ́ ni* (it became clear that it is the truth), Finnish *totuus tulee ilmi* (the truth comes to light), Basque *egia argitara atera* (truth brought to light), Tamil *uṇmai veḷippaṭṭatu* (the truth came to light), Indonesian *kebenaran akan terungkap* (the truth will come out), Turkish *gerçek ortaya çıkmak* (the truth comes out), Korean *진실이 드러나다* (the truth emerges). This framing — treating truth as an entity that moves from concealment to visibility — is consistent across all eight languages.

**The proverbial assertion that truth ultimately prevails is present in all eight languages.** Georgian *simarṭle gamarjvebs* (truth prevails), Yoruba *òtítọ́ kò ní kú* (truth will not die), Finnish *totuus tulee ilmi* (used in this sense), Basque *egia beti ateratzen da azalera* (the truth always comes to the surface), Tamil *uṇmai tāṉ vellum* (truth alone will prevail), Indonesian *kebenaran akan terungkap pada akhirnya* (the truth will come out in the end), Turkish *doğruluk her zaman ödüllendirilmez* (a more pessimistic variant, but the proverbial frame is present), Korean *진실은 하나다* (there is only one truth) and related expressions. The specific framing varies, but the proverbial register is present in all eight languages.

**No language has a lexicalized single-word agentive for "truth-teller."** All eight languages have lexicalized agentives for habitual liars (Georgian *mt'q̇uari*, Yoruba *aṣírọ́*, Finnish *valehtelija*, Basque *gezurti*, Tamil *poyyaṉ*, Indonesian *pembohong*, Turkish *yalancı*, Korean *거짓말쟁이*), but none has a parallel single-word agentive for "truth-teller." The concept is expressed periphrastically in all languages. This asymmetry is consistent across all eight languages and across unrelated language families.

**No language has a dedicated lexical item for "half-truth" as a distinct category.** All eight languages can express the concept of a partially true statement, but none has a single lexicalized term for it. The concept is expressed through compositional phrases: Georgian *naxevari č̣ešmariteba*, Yoruba (no fixed phrase documented), Finnish *puoli totuus*, Basque *egia erdi*, Tamil *uṇmai zati bat*, Indonesian (no fixed phrase documented), Turkish (no fixed phrase documented), Korean (no fixed phrase documented). This gap is consistent across all eight languages.

### Where Languages Split Distinctions More Finely

**Korean splits the truth domain most finely**, maintaining distinct Sino-Korean roots for factual accuracy (*사실*), truthfulness/sincerity (*진실*), precision/exactness (*정확*), honesty in conduct (*정직*), trustworthiness (*신뢰*), and authenticity of inner state (*진정성*). These are not merely register variants of a single concept but distinct evaluative categories with different collocational patterns, different semantic groups, and different constructional behaviors. No other language in the dataset shows this degree of internal differentiation within the truth domain.

**Basque splits the verifiability domain most finely**, distinguishing *egiaztagarria* (verifiable, capable of being verified), *egiaztagaitza* (difficult to verify), and *egiaztaezina* (impossible to verify) as three distinct forms within the same derivational paradigm. The *-garri*/*-gaitz*/*-ezin* three-way distinction — potential/difficult/impossible — is not paralleled in any other language in the dataset, which typically show only a binary verifiable/unverifiable opposition.

**Turkish splits the verification/falsification domain most finely**, maintaining a productive morphological opposition between *doğrulamak* (to verify) and *yanlışlamak* (to falsify) with parallel derivational stacking generating *doğrulanabilirlik* (verifiability) and *yanlışlanabilirlik* (falsifiability) as technical philosophical terms. While other languages have vocabulary for verification and for showing something to be false, only Turkish shows this as a productive morphological pair built on contrasting truth-domain bases.

**Finnish splits the checking/verification domain most finely**, explicitly distinguishing *tarkistaa* (to check, everyday) from *tarkastaa* (to inspect, formal/official) as register-differentiated near-synonyms where the distinction is semantic (institutional authority) rather than merely stylistic. No other language in the dataset documents this register distinction at the same level of explicitness.

**Georgian splits the register dimension of propositional truth most finely**, maintaining *č̣ešmariteba* (philosophical/theological register) and *simarṭle* (everyday/legal register) as distinct nominals for truth, with different collocational patterns, different discourse functions, and different derivational families. Finnish has a similar distinction (*totuus* vs. *tosi*) but the Georgian distinction is more elaborated in the data.

**Georgian and Basque split the appearance-versus-reality contrast most finely.** Georgian has *moč̣venebiti* (apparent/seeming/ostensible) as a dedicated adjective, and Basque has *itxurazko* (apparent/seeming) and *itxurakeria* (pretense/hypocrisy) as a dedicated cluster. Finnish has *näennäinen* (apparent/seeming). In Yoruba, Tamil, Indonesian, Turkish, and Korean, the contrast is expressed through constructions and discourse markers rather than dedicated adjectives.

---

### Where Languages Merge Distinctions

**Yoruba merges propositional correctness and procedural correctness** under the single *tọ́* root, which covers both "this statement is correct" and "this procedure is proper." The same predicative construction *ó tọ́* (it is correct/right/proper) applies across factual, moral, and procedural evaluation without lexical differentiation. Other languages (Finnish, Korean, Georgian) maintain distinct vocabulary for these functions.

**Indonesian merges the innocent-error and deliberate-falsehood distinction less sharply than some other languages**, though it does distinguish *keliru* (innocent error) from *bohong* (deliberate lie). The *salah* root covers both error and fault/blame without a dedicated term for the innocent-error pole, relying on context and the *keliru*/*salah* distinction to convey the difference. Georgian, Finnish, and Korean show more explicit lexical differentiation between error-without-intent and deliberate deception.

**Tamil merges the classical/literary and everyday registers of truth** under *uṇmai* more completely than Georgian merges *simarṭle* and *č̣ešmariteba*. While *mey* (classical truth) exists as a literary near-synonym, it is documented as marginal in everyday use, and the *uṇmai* root covers both philosophical and everyday truth without the sharp register split seen in Georgian.

**Turkish merges epistemic truth and legal entitlement** under the *hak* root (from Arabic *ḥaqq*), which simultaneously generates *haklı* (justified/in the right), *haksız* (unjust), *hakkaniyet* (equity), *hak etmek* (to deserve), and *insan hakları* (human rights). While other languages show some overlap between truth and justice vocabulary (Georgian *marṭal-* covers both correctness and justice; Yoruba *òdodo* covers both righteousness and justice), the Turkish *hak* root shows the most complete merger of epistemic and entitlement senses within a single productive root.

**Basque merges the sincerity and genuineness dimensions** under the *benetako* cluster more completely than other languages. *Benetako* covers both "genuine (not fake)" and "sincere (not performed)," and *benetan* functions as both an authenticity marker and a sincerity marker. Other languages (Korean, Finnish, Indonesian) maintain more distinct vocabulary for these two functions.

---

### Cases Where a Language Appears to Lack a Clear Lexical Contrast Found Elsewhere

**Yoruba lacks a dedicated vocabulary for documentary forgery and counterfeiting** as a distinct legal category. While Yoruba has vocabulary for lying (*irọ́*), false testimony (*ẹlẹ́rìí irọ́*), and deception (*ìtànjẹ́*), the data does not document a dedicated term for the act of producing a forged document or counterfeit currency parallel to Georgian *gaq̇albeba*, Finnish *väärentää*, Basque *faltsifikatu*, Tamil *pōli āvaṇam*, Indonesian *pemalsuan*, Turkish *sahte belge*, or Korean *위조*. **Yoruba lacks a dedicated vocabulary for legal/procedural validity** as a distinct category. While Yoruba has *ẹ̀tọ́* (right/entitlement) and *òdodo* (righteousness/justice), the data does not document a dedicated term for the validity or invalidity of legal instruments parallel to Georgian *kanonieri/legitimuri*, Finnish *pätevä/pätemätön*, Basque *baliozkoa/baliogabea*, Tamil *caṭṭappaṭi*, Indonesian *sah/tidak sah*, Turkish *geçerli/geçersiz*, or Korean *유효/무효*.
