| **Spatial metaphor underlying truth/correctness base** | The primary truth or correctness root has a spatial meaning of "straight" or "direct" that underlies its epistemic and moral uses | ka, yo, fi, eu, ta, id, tr, ko | ka: *marṭl-* (straight/right); yo: *tọ́* (straight/correct); fi: *oikea* (right, also directional); eu: *zuzen* (straight/correct); ta: *nēr* (straight/direct); id: *benar* (correct, possibly related to straightness); tr: *doğru* (straight/correct/true); ko: *olbareuda* (upright/correct) | **Widely attested** (all 8 languages). The spatial metaphor of straightness underlying correctness and truth is the most consistently attested morphological/semantic pattern in the dataset. The antonym in several languages is also spatial: ka *eğri* (crooked), eu *oker* (crooked/wrong), tr *eğri* (crooked/dishonest). |

---

## 2. Narrative Analysis

### Patterns Recurring Across Unrelated Language Families

**The abstract property nominalization strategy is universal in the dataset.** Every language produces abstract nouns naming truth-domain qualities (truthfulness, accuracy, reliability, authenticity) through a suffix or circumfix on an adjectival or verbal base. The specific morphological mechanism varies — Turkish *-luk*, Finnish *-uus*, Basque *-tasun*, Tamil *-mai*, Indonesian *ke-...-an* circumfix, Korean *-seong*, Georgian *-eba* — but the functional outcome is the same: a nominal that names the property as an abstract entity and participates in evaluative constructions. This pattern is productive in all eight languages and shows no signs of being lexicalized or fossilized; new forms can be created as needed.

**The agentive asymmetry (liar lexicalized, truth-teller not) is consistent across all eight languages and all language families represented.** Georgian (South Caucasian), Yoruba (Niger-Congo), Finnish (Finno-Ugric), Basque (isolate), Tamil (Dravidian), Indonesian (Austronesian), Turkish (Turkic), and Korean (Koreanic) all have lexicalized single-word agentives for habitual liars and forgers, but none has a parallel lexicalized agentive for habitual truth-tellers. This is a one-way blocked pathway: the derivational process that generates *yalancı* (liar), *aṣírọ́* (liar), *valehtelija* (liar), *gezurti* (liar), *poyyaṉ* (liar), *pembohong* (liar), *거짓말쟁이* (liar) does not generate a corresponding positive-role agentive. The concept of "truth-teller" is expressed periphrastically in all eight languages. This asymmetry is not a gap in the data; it is consistently documented across the F4 construction tables and F7 agentive nominalization sections for all eight languages.

**The spatial metaphor of straightness underlying truth and correctness is attested in all eight languages.** Georgian *marṭl-* (straight/right), Yoruba *tọ́* (straight/correct), Finnish *oikea* (right, also directional), Basque *zuzen* (straight/correct), Tamil *nēr* (straight/direct), Indonesian *benar* (correct), Turkish *doğru* (straight/correct/true), and Korean *olbareuda* (upright/correct) all show a root or base that combines spatial straightness with epistemic or moral correctness. The antonym in several languages is also spatial: Turkish *eğri* (crooked/dishonest), Basque *oker* (crooked/wrong), Georgian *eğri* (crooked). This convergence across unrelated language families suggests that the spatial metaphor is a robust cross-linguistic pattern in this domain, though the data does not permit claims about its origin or directionality.

**The intransitive/passive framing of truth-revelation is documented in all eight languages.** In every language, truth can be the grammatical subject of an intransitive or passive verb expressing emergence or disclosure: Georgian *simartle gamovida* (the truth came out), Yoruba *ó farahàn pé òtítọ́ ni* (it became clear that it is the truth), Finnish *totuus tulee ilmi* (the truth comes to light), Basque *egia argitara atera* (truth brought to light), Tamil *uṇmai veḷippaṭṭatu* (the truth came to light), Indonesian *kebenaran akan terungkap* (the truth will come out), Turkish *gerçek ortaya çıkmak* (the truth comes out), Korean *진실이 드러나다* (the truth emerges). This constructional pattern — treating truth as an entity that moves from concealment to visibility — is consistent across all eight languages and all language families.

**The discourse-framing adverbial derived from a truth base is attested in seven of eight languages.** Georgian *marṭla* (really/truly), Finnish *totta puhuen* (to tell the truth), Basque *egia esan behar* (truth be told), Tamil *uṇmaiyil* (in truth/actually), Indonesian *sebenarnya* (actually/in truth), Turkish *aslında* (actually/in fact), and Korean *사실을 말하자면* (to tell the truth) all function as sentence-level discourse markers introducing corrections, frank statements, or contrasts with appearance. The degree of grammaticalization varies — Indonesian *sebenarnya* and Turkish *aslında* are fully grammaticalized, while others are more compositional — but the functional pattern is consistent. Yoruba uses a hortative construction (*jẹ́ kí a sọ òtítọ́*, let us speak the truth) for the same discourse function rather than a grammaticalized adverbial.

---

### Striking Asymmetries

**The most striking asymmetry in the dataset is the one-way blocked pathway for truth-teller agentives.** As noted above, all eight languages have lexicalized agentives for liars and forgers but none for truth-tellers. This is not a gap in documentation; the F4 construction tables for all eight languages explicitly note the absence and describe the periphrastic alternatives. The asymmetry is consistent across unrelated language families and appears to reflect a cross-linguistic pattern in how the truth domain is lexicalized.

**The degree of morphological productivity of the primary truth root varies enormously across languages.** Turkish *doğru* and Georgian *marṭl-* generate the largest documented derivational families, extending into technical domains (Turkish: *doğrusal*, linear; *doğrultu*, direction; *doğrulanabilirlik*, verifiability), religious domains (Georgian: *marṭlmadidebeli*, Orthodox Christian; *marṭlsaidumlo*, true sacrament), and institutional domains (Georgian: *marṭlmsajuleba*, justice system; *marṭlc̣era*, orthography). By contrast, Yoruba *tọ́* and Tamil *uṇmai* generate smaller derivational families, with the Tamil family concentrated in adjectival, adverbial, and verbal noun forms rather than compound institutional terms. This asymmetry is not explained by language family or morphological type alone; it reflects the specific historical and cultural elaboration of the truth domain in each language.

**The negative agentive derivation is more productive than the positive agentive derivation in all eight languages.** Not only is the truth-teller agentive absent, but the forger/deceiver agentive is more elaborated than any positive-role agentive in the truth domain. Finnish has *väärentäjä* (forger), *valehtelija* (liar), and *pettäjä* (deceiver) but no parallel positive-role agentives. Korean has *위조범* (forger), *거짓말쟁이* (liar), and *위선자* (hypocrite) but no parallel positive-role agentives. This asymmetry is consistent across all eight languages.

**The *-hada/-doeda* stative/agentive distinction in Korean is unique in the dataset.** Korean documents a systematic semantic distinction between *jinsil-hada* (to be truthful, active/performed quality) and *jinsil-doeda* (to be truthful, inherent/resultant quality). This morphological distinction between performed and inherent quality is not documented in any other language in the dataset. It is a productive pattern in Korean that applies across the truth domain (*jinsil-hada/-doeda*, *wijo-hada/-doeda*, *mosun-doeda* — where only the *-doeda* form is attested).

---

### One-Way or Blocked Derivational Pathways

**The truth-teller agentive pathway is blocked in all eight languages.** As documented above, the agentive derivation that produces liars and forgers does not produce truth-tellers. This is the most consistently documented blocked pathway in the dataset.

**The *-hada* predicative suffix is blocked for *-seong* quality nominals in Korean.** Korean *-seong* nominals (*jinjeongseong*, *sinbyeongseong*, *tadangseong*) cannot take *-hada* as a predicative suffix; they require the existential *있다/없다* frame instead. This is a morphological restriction documented in the F4 construction tables for Korean and has no parallel in other languages.

**The *-garri* potential suffix in Basque does not extend to all truth-domain bases.** While *egiaztagarria* (verifiable), *fidagarria* (trustworthy), *sinesgarria* (believable), and *frogagarria* (provable) are all attested, the suffix does not apply freely to all truth-domain bases. The data documents this as a restricted rather than fully productive pattern.

**The *-itas* suffix in Indonesian applies only to loanword bases.** Indonesian *validitas*, *kredibilitas*, and *otentisitas* use the *-itas* suffix, but this suffix does not extend to native Indonesian roots (*\*benarittas*, *\*asliitas* are not attested). This is a morphological restriction documented in the F2a derivation table for Indonesian.

**The *ke-...-an* circumfix in Indonesian does not apply to all truth-domain bases.** While *kebenaran* (truth), *kesalahan* (error), *keaslian* (authenticity), and *kejujuran* (honesty) are all attested, the circumfix does not apply freely to all bases. Loanword bases (*\*kevaliditasan*, *\*kekredibilitasan*) use the *-itas* suffix instead.

**The morphological causative-inchoative chain (*-laş-/-leş-*) in Turkish is restricted to bases that have already undergone *-laş-* derivation.** *Meşrulaştırmak* (to legitimize) is attested because *meşrulaşmak* (to become legitimate) is attested, but the chain does not apply to all truth-domain adjectives. *\*Doğrulaştırmak* (to make more correct) is not documented as a standard form; *doğrulamak* (to verify) uses a different derivational path.

---

### Productivity, Restriction, Lexicalization, and Unclear Attestation

**Productive patterns** (can generate new forms as needed, not restricted to a closed set):
- Abstract property nominalization via suffix (all 8 languages)
- Adverbial derivation from truth base (all 8 languages)
- Verbal noun / process nominalization (all 8 languages)
- Negative agentive nominalization for liars and forgers (all 8 languages)
- Privative/negative nominal (all 8 languages)
- Indonesian *salah* + [noun/verb] misaction compounding
- Turkish *doğru-* and *yanlış-* derivational families
- Basque *-garri/-gaitz/-ezin* potential/difficult/impossible adjectival series
- Korean *-seong* abstract quality nominalization

**Restricted patterns** (attested but not freely productive across all bases):
- Compound adjective with *mukainen/vastainen* (Finnish, restricted to genitive nominal bases)
- Causative-inchoative chain *-laş-/-leş-tir-* (Turkish, restricted to bases that have undergone *-laş-* derivation)
- *-garri* potential suffix (Basque, restricted to verbal stems; not all truth-domain bases accept it)
- *-itas* suffix (Indonesian, restricted to loanword bases)
- Pejorative *-keria* suffix (Basque, restricted to a closed or near-closed set of bases)
- Korean *-화하다* causative (restricted to Sino-Korean bases; not available for native Korean bases)

**Lexicalized / fossilized patterns** (forms that were once productive but are now fixed):
- Georgian *sarwmunoeba* (credibility/faith) — the bifurcation into secular and theological meanings is a lexicalized semantic split, not a productive derivational pattern
- Indonesian *sebenarnya* (actually/in truth) — fully grammaticalized as a discourse marker; the compositional meaning (*se-benar-nya*, "in its truth") is no longer active
- Turkish *aslında* (actually/in fact) — fully grammaticalized as a discourse marker; the compositional meaning (*asl-ında*, "in its origin") is no longer synchronically active
- Basque *ziurrenik* (probably/most likely) — the semantic shift from "certainly" to "probably" is a lexicalized change; the form is no longer compositionally interpreted as expressing certainty
- Korean *틀림없다* (certainly, without error) — lexicalized as a fixed expression of certainty; the compositional meaning (without deviation) is backgrounded

**Unclear or weakly attested patterns:**
- Georgian *uč̣ešmarito* (untrue, privative form) — documented as [UNCERTAIN] in the F2a table; the form exists but its productivity and register distribution are unclear
- Basque *egiazkeria* (false pretense of truth) — documented as [MARGINAL] in the F2a table; attested in literary and critical registers but not clearly productive
- Finnish *aitoutua* (to become authentic) — documented as [MARGINAL] in the F4 construction table; attested but not productively available across the truth-domain adjective class
- Indonesian *mengasli* (to authenticate/to revert to original state) — documented as [UNCERTAIN] in the F2a table; the form is encountered but its usage is not fully stable across registers
- Tamil *uṇmaippaṭuttutal* (authentication/verification) — documented as [MARGINAL] in the F1 and F2a tables; attested in official Tamil but not common in everyday speech
- Yoruba *tọ̀nà* (right path/correct way) — documented as [UNCERTAIN] in the F1 table; the morphological analysis is not fully settled and the form is less common in younger urban registers

# G3 — Emergent Cross-Language Semantic Dimensions

## Methodology Note

The dimensions below are derived from the F3 semantic grouping tables, F1 vocabulary inventories, F2 derivational and constructional data, and the G1–G2 comparative analyses already in context. Each dimension is defined by co-occurrence patterns, grouping decisions, and explicit contrasts documented in the source data. No dimension is asserted unless it is supported by evidence from at least two languages. Single-language observations are flagged as such. Where prior G-phase steps have already identified a pattern, that identification is confirmed or refined here rather than repeated in full.

---

## Proposed Semantic Dimensions

### Dimension 1: Propositional Correspondence

**Definition.** This dimension concerns whether a specific statement, claim, or report matches what is actually the case in the world. The evaluative target is a proposition or utterance, not a person or object. Terms in this dimension appear in contexts of assertion, denial, correction, and verification of factual claims.

**Representative terms:**
- ka: *simarṭle* (truth, everyday), *č̣ešmariteba* (truth, philosophical), *mcdari* (erroneous), *sicrue* (falsehood)
- yo: *òtítọ́* (truth), *irọ́* (lie/falsehood), *ó tọ́* (it is correct)
- fi: *tosi* (true), *totuus* (truth), *epätosi* (untrue), *pitää paikkansa* (to hold/be true)
- eu: *egia* (truth), *gezurra* (lie/falsehood), *egia da* (it is true)
- ta: *uṇmai* (truth), *poy* (falsehood), *cari* (correct), *tavaṟu* (wrong/error)
- id: *benar* (correct/true), *salah* (wrong), *kebenaran* (truth)
- tr: *doğru* (correct/true), *yanlış* (wrong/false), *doğruluk* (truthfulness/accuracy)
- ko: *사실* (fact/truth), *허위* (falsehood), *맞다* (to be correct), *틀리다* (to be wrong)

**Distribution:** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. This is the most consistently attested dimension in the dataset. Every language maintains at least one dedicated nominal for truth and one for falsehood in the propositional sense, and these are the most productive bases for further derivation. Several languages split this dimension by register: ka maintains *č̣ešmariteba* (philosophical/theological) vs. *simarṭle* (everyday/legal); fi maintains *totuus* (nominal, formal) vs. *tosi* (predicative, colloquial); ko maintains *진리* (philosophical/universal) vs. *진실* (everyday truthfulness) vs. *사실* (factual accuracy). yo and ta show less register differentiation within this dimension.

---

### Dimension 2: Personal Honesty and Integrity in Conduct

**Definition.** This dimension concerns whether a person's habitual conduct, character, or disposition is free from deception and consistent with truthful expression. The evaluative target is a person or their pattern of behavior, not a specific proposition. Terms in this dimension evaluate character rather than the truth-value of a claim.

**Representative terms:**
- ka: *gulc̣rpeli* (sincere/straight-hearted), *tvaltmaqcoba* (hypocrisy/eye-deceiving)
- yo: *ìwà rere* (good character), *ìwà burúkú* (bad character), *olòtítọ́* (truthful person)
- fi: *rehellinen* (honest), *rehellisyys* (honesty), *vilpitön* (sincere/in good faith), *vilpillinen* (fraudulent/deceitful)
- eu: *benetakoa* (genuine/sincere), *benetan* (truly/in earnest), *itxurakeria* (pretense/hypocrisy)
- ta: *nērmai* (honesty/integrity), *kaḷḷam* (deceit/guile), *vañcaṉai* (deception)
- id: *jujur* (honest), *kejujuran* (honesty), *tulus* (sincere), *ikhlas* (selflessly sincere)
- tr: *dürüst* (upright/honest), *dürüstlük* (honesty/integrity), *özü sözü bir* (one whose word matches their character)
- ko: *정직* (honesty/integrity), *정직하다* (to be honest), *거짓말* (lie), *거짓말하다* (to lie)

**Distribution:** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. The evaluative target (person/character vs. proposition) is the defining criterion distinguishing this from D1. The absence of a lexicalized single-word agentive for "truth-teller" is consistent across all eight languages, while agentives for "liar" are lexicalized in all eight. yo elaborates this dimension most extensively through the *ìwà* (character/manner of being) concept, which organizes a large cluster of moral evaluation vocabulary with no close structural parallel in other languages. id distinguishes *tulus* (sincere inner motivation) from *ikhlas* (selflessly sincere, with specifically religious connotations of acceptance without expectation of reward) — a sub-distinction not documented in other languages.

---

### Dimension 3: Source Trustworthiness vs. Content Credibility

**Definition.** This dimension concerns whether a person, institution, or source of information can be depended upon to provide accurate information (source trustworthiness), and whether a specific claim or account is such that it merits belief (content credibility). These two evaluative targets — the source and the content — are distinguished in all eight languages, though the degree of lexical differentiation varies.

**Representative terms:**
- ka: *sarc̣muno* (credible/trustworthy, inherent property of source) vs. *damajerebeliˈ* (convincing/persuasive, effect on hearer); *sando* (reliable/dependable, interpersonal)
- yo: *fidagarri* (trustworthy source) vs. *sinesgarri* (believable content); *ìgbẹ́kẹ̀lé* (reliance/dependability)
- fi: *luotettava* (reliable/dependable over time) vs. *uskottava* (believable for a specific claim)
- eu: *fidagarria* (trustworthy source) vs. *sinesgarria* (believable content)
- ta: *nampakamāna* (reliable) vs. *nampattakka* (worth trusting for a specific claim); *nampikkai* (trust/faith)
- id: *terpercaya* (trusted/reliable) vs. *kredibel* (credible); *kepercayaan* (trust)
- tr: *güvenilir* (reliable/trustworthy) vs. *inanılır* (believable)
- ko: *신뢰성* (reliability of a source) vs. *신빙성* (credibility of a specific claim); *신뢰도* (degree of reliability)

**Distribution:** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. The source/content distinction is explicitly noted in F3 boundary notes for ka, yo, fi, and eu. ko shows the most internal differentiation within the trustworthiness dimension, maintaining distinct terms for *신뢰* (trust as a relationship), *신뢰성* (reliability as a property), *신뢰도* (degree of reliability), and *신빙성* (credibility of a specific claim).

---

### Dimension 4: Genuineness of Objects vs. Fraudulent Imitation

**Definition.** This dimension concerns whether a physical object, document, artwork, currency, or credential is what it purports to be (genuine/original) or is a fraudulent substitute (counterfeit/forged). The evaluative target is a physical item or document, not a proposition or person. Terms in this dimension appear in legal, commercial, and art-authentication contexts.

**Representative terms:**
- ka: *namdvili* (genuine/real), *q̇albi* (fake/counterfeit), *gaq̇albeba* (forgery/falsification), *avtentiuri* (authentic, formal)
- yo: *gidi* (genuine/real); less elaborated than other languages
- fi: *aito* (genuine/authentic), *alkuperäinen* (original), *väärennös* (forgery), *jäljitelmä* (imitation, neutral)
- eu: *benetakoa* (genuine/real), *jatorrizkoa* (original), *faltsua* (fake), *faltsifikatu* (to forge)
- ta: *acal* (original/genuine), *nakal* (copy, neutral), *pōli* (fake/counterfeit)
- id: *asli* (genuine/original), *tiruan* (imitation, neutral), *palsu* (fake/fraudulent), *pemalsuan* (forgery)
- tr: *orijinal* (original), *özgün* (authentic/original, creative), *sahte* (counterfeit/fake), *taklit* (imitation)
- ko: *진짜* (genuine/real), *가짜* (fake/counterfeit), *진품* (genuine article), *위조* (forgery), *모조품* (imitation goods)

**Distribution:** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages, though the degree of elaboration varies. At least six languages (fi, eu, ta, id, tr, ko) explicitly distinguish a neutral-copy pole (imitation without fraudulent intent) from a fraudulent-fake pole (counterfeit with intent to deceive). ka and yo show less elaboration of this three-way contrast: ka has *namdvili* vs. *q̇albi* as a binary, and yo lacks a dedicated forgery vocabulary.

---

### Dimension 5: Legal/Procedural Validity vs. Moral/Substantive Legitimacy

**Definition.** This dimension concerns whether an action, document, contract, or authority meets the formal conditions required for legal recognition (procedural validity) and whether it is rightful or justified in a broader normative sense that may extend beyond strict legality (legitimacy). All eight languages maintain some distinction between these two evaluative targets, though the degree of lexical differentiation varies.

**Representative terms:**
- ka: *kanonieri* (lawful, tied to positive law) vs. *legitimuri* (legitimate, with possible normative dimension); *sasamartlo* (court), *marṭlmsajuleba* (justice/administration of justice)
- yo: *ẹ̀tọ́* (right/entitlement/correctness), *ìdájọ́* (judgment/adjudication), *òdodo* (righteousness/justice); less lexically differentiated
- fi: *pätevä* (valid/competent) vs. *oikeudenmukainen* (just/fair)
- eu: *baliozkoa* (valid) vs. *zilegi* (lawful/permissible) vs. *zuzen* (correct/just); *baliogabea* (invalid)
- ta: *caṭṭappaṭi* (according to law) vs. *niyāyam* (justice/rightness); *takuti* (qualification/eligibility)
- id: *sah* (legally valid) vs. *adil* (fair/just)
- tr: *yasal* (legal, conforming to written law) vs. *meşru* (legitimate, extending beyond legality); *geçerli* (valid/in force) vs. *geçersiz* (invalid/void)
- ko: *합법* (lawful) vs. *정당* (legitimate/justified); *유효* (valid/in force) vs. *무효* (invalid/void)

**Distribution:** Present in all eight languages. The distinction between strict legality and broader legitimacy is explicitly documented in F3 grouping tables for ka, fi, eu, id, tr, and ko. The distinction between operative validity (in force) and invalidity (void) is documented in all eight languages. tr shows the most explicit lexical differentiation, with *yasal* (legal), *meşru* (legitimate), and *geçerli* (valid/in force) as three distinct terms. ko similarly distinguishes *합법* (lawful), *정당* (legitimate/justified), and *유효* (valid/in force). yo shows the least elaboration of this dimension.

---

### Dimension 6: Precision and Exactness of Correspondence

**Definition.** This dimension concerns the degree to which a measurement, description, translation, or representation corresponds closely and exactly to its referent or standard. Unlike D1 (propositional correspondence, which is binary), this dimension is scalar and concerns the closeness of fit between a representation and what it represents. Terms in this dimension appear in scientific, technical, journalistic, and administrative contexts.

**Representative terms:**
- ka: *zusti* (exact/precise), *sizuste* (accuracy/precision), *zusti targmani* (accurate translation)
- yo: *tọ́ pátápátá* (completely correct); less elaborated as a distinct dimension
- fi: *tarkka* (precise/accurate), *tarkkuus* (accuracy/precision), *tarkka mittaus* (accurate measurement)
- eu: *zehatza* (precise/exact/accurate), *zehaztasuna* (precision/accuracy)
- ta: *uṇmaiyāna* (true/genuine/accurate), *caripārtttal* (verification/checking); less elaborated as a distinct dimension
- id: *tepat* (precise/exact/fitting), *akurat* (accurate), *cermat* (careful/meticulous/precise)
- tr: *doğru* (correct/accurate), *doğruluk* (accuracy/truthfulness); less elaborated as distinct from correctness
- ko: *정확* (accuracy/precision), *정확성* (accuracy as a property), *정확히* (accurately/exactly), *정확도* (degree of accuracy)

**Distribution:** Clearly lexicalized in at least six languages (ka, fi, eu, id, ko, and partially tr). In yo and ta, the dimension is less elaborated as a distinct lexical category; the concept is expressed through the general correctness vocabulary rather than through dedicated precision terms. ko shows the most elaboration, with *정확* generating a productive derivational family including *정확성*, *정확도*, *정확히*, and *부정확*. fi shows elaboration through *tarkka*, *tarkkuus*, *tarkistaa* (to check/verify), and *tarkastaa* (to inspect/audit), with the *tarkistaa*/*tarkastaa* register distinction documented only in fi.

---

### Dimension 7: Authenticity of Inner States and Expressed Feelings

**Definition.** This dimension concerns whether a person's expressed feelings, intentions, apologies, or commitments reflect genuine inner conviction rather than performance, calculation, or pretense. The evaluative target is the relationship between inner state and outward expression, not the truth-value of a proposition or the genuineness of a physical object. Terms in this dimension appear in interpersonal, political, and artistic evaluation contexts.

**Representative terms:**
- ka: *gulc̣rpeli* (sincere/straight-hearted, literally "straight-hearted"), *tvaltmaqcoba* (hypocrisy/eye-deceiving)
- yo: *ìwà rere* (good character), *àgàbàgebè* (pretense/hypocrisy/sham behavior)
- fi: *aito tunne* (genuine feeling), *epäaito* (inauthentic), *vilpitön* (sincere/in good faith)
- eu: *benetakoa* (genuine/sincere), *benetan* (truly/in earnest), *itxurakeria* (pretense/hypocrisy)
- ta: *uṇmai aṉpu* (true love/genuine affection), *nērmai* (honesty/integrity); less elaborated as a distinct dimension
- id: *tulus* (sincere), *ikhlas* (selflessly sincere), *sungguh-sungguh* (in earnest/genuinely)
- tr: *sahici* (genuine/authentic, colloquial), *özü sözü bir* (one whose word matches their character)
- ko: *진정성* (authenticity of inner state), *진심* (sincere heart/genuine feeling), *진심으로* (sincerely/from the heart)

**Distribution:** Present in all eight languages, but the degree of lexical elaboration varies considerably. ko shows the most elaboration, with *진정성* functioning as a highly developed public evaluative category with a rich collocation network (*진정성 있다/없다*, *진정성 논란*, *진정성을 의심받다*). eu and fi show moderate elaboration. ta and tr show less elaboration of this as a distinct dimension. yo's *ìwà* (character/manner of being) concept organizes this dimension differently, treating it as a matter of fundamental character rather than the authenticity of specific expressions.

### Dimension 8: Appearance vs. Underlying Reality

**Definition.** This dimension concerns the contrast between how something appears on the surface and what it actually is. Terms in this dimension are used to signal that a surface appearance may be misleading, that something presents itself as other than it is, or that the true nature of something differs from its apparent nature. This dimension is distinct from D4 (genuineness of objects) in that it applies to situations, arguments, and qualities rather than primarily to physical items.

**Representative terms:**
- ka: *moč̣venebiti* (apparent/seeming/ostensible), *garegnuli* (external/outward/superficial), *šinaˈarsi* (content/substance/inner meaning)
- yo: *ìfarahàn* (appearance/manifestation), *àgàbàgebè* (pretense/sham); less elaborated as a distinct dimension
- fi: *näennäinen* (apparent/seeming/ostensible), *todellinen* (real/actual), *todellisuus* (reality)
- eu: *itxura* (appearance/semblance), *itxurazko* (apparent/seeming/superficial), *itxurakeria* (pretense/hypocrisy), *itxuraz* (apparently/seemingly)
- ta: *uṇmai nilavaram* (true state of affairs), *uṇmai nilai* (the actual situation); less elaborated as a distinct dimension
- id: *sebenarnya* (actually/in truth), *pada kenyataannya* (in reality), *nyata* (real/manifest)
- tr: *gerçek dışı* (unreal/contrary to fact), *gerçeğe aykırı* (contrary to reality), *aslında* (actually/in fact)
- ko: *실체* (true nature/underlying reality), *실제* (actuality/reality), *실제로* (actually/in reality)

**Distribution:** Present in all eight languages, but the degree of lexical elaboration varies. eu shows the most elaboration, with *itxura* generating a productive derivational family (*itxurazko*, *itxurakeria*, *itxuragilea*, *itxuraz*). ka shows elaboration through *moč̣venebiti* (ostensible) and the *šinaˈarsi*/*garegnuli* (inner content/outer appearance) contrast. fi shows elaboration through *näennäinen* (apparent/seeming). yo and ta show less elaboration of this as a distinct lexical dimension; the contrast is expressed through constructions and discourse markers rather than dedicated adjectives. The ka *moč̣venebiti* is explicitly distinguished from *q̇albi* (fake, implying deliberate deception) and from *namdvili* (genuine) in the F5 opposition tables — a three-way distinction not paralleled in other languages.

---

### Dimension 9: Evidential Grounding and Proof

**Definition.** This dimension concerns whether a claim is supported by adequate evidence or grounds, and the processes by which evidence is produced, evaluated, and used to establish the truth of a claim. Terms in this dimension appear in legal, scientific, journalistic, and argumentative contexts. The evaluative question is not merely whether a claim is true but whether it can be demonstrated to be true.

**Representative terms:**
- ka: *mt'k'icebuleba* (proof/evidence), *mt'k'iceba* (assertion/act of proving), *dadastureba* (confirmation/verification), *utyuari* (irrefutable/beyond doubt)
- yo: *ẹ̀rí* (evidence/proof/witness), *ìjẹ́rìísí* (testimony/attestation/certification), *ìdánwò* (test/trial/verification)
- fi: *todiste* (piece of evidence), *todistus* (proof/testimony/certificate), *todistustaakka* (burden of proof), *todistusvoima* (probative force)
- eu: *froga* (proof/evidence), *frogatu* (to prove/demonstrate), *egiaztagarria* (verifiable), *egiaztaezina* (unverifiable)
- ta: *ātāram* (evidence/basis/grounds), *cāṉṟu* (evidence/proof/attestation), *nirūpaṇam* (proof/demonstration)
- id: *bukti* (evidence/proof), *pembuktian* (proof/verification), *tidak berdasar* (unfounded/baseless)
- tr: *kanıt* (evidence/proof), *kanıtlamak* (to prove), *ispat* (proof, formal), *asılsız* (unfounded/baseless)
- ko: *근거* (basis/grounds/evidence), *신빙성* (credibility of a claim), *타당성* (validity/soundness), *위증* (perjury/false testimony)

**Distribution:** Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. The distinction between the act of proving and the product of proof is documented in at least five languages (ka *mt'k'iceba* vs. *mt'k'icebuleba*; fi *todistaa* vs. *todiste*; eu *frogatu* vs. *froga*; id *membuktikan* vs. *bukti*; tr *kanıtlamak* vs. *kanıt*). eu shows the most elaboration of the verifiability sub-dimension, with the three-way *egiaztagarria* (verifiable) / *egiaztagaitza* (difficult to verify) / *egiaztaezina* (impossible to verify) distinction unique in the dataset. tr shows the unique *doğrulanabilirlik*/*yanlışlanabilirlik* (verifiability/falsifiability) morphological opposition.

### Dimension 10: Truth Revelation and Concealment as Processes

**Definition.** This dimension concerns the processes by which truth is brought to light, concealed, sought, or suppressed. Terms in this dimension treat truth as an entity that can be revealed, hidden, distorted, or discovered, and they appear in investigative, journalistic, narrative, and legal contexts. This dimension is distinct from D1 (propositional correspondence) in that it concerns the dynamics of truth-disclosure rather than the static evaluation of a proposition.

**Representative terms:**
- ka: *simarṭle gamovida* (the truth came out), *simarṭle damalva* (concealment of truth), *simarṭle gamovlena* (revelation of truth)
- yo: *ó farahàn pé òtítọ́ ni* (it became clear that it is the truth), *ó ń pa òtítọ́ mọ́* (he/she is concealing the truth)
- fi: *totuus tulee ilmi* (the truth comes to light), *totuus paljastuu* (the truth is revealed)
- eu: *egia argitara atera* (to bring truth to light), *egia ezkutatu* (to hide the truth), *egiaren bila ibili* (to go about seeking the truth)
- ta: *uṇmai veḷippaṭṭatu* (the truth came to light), *uṇmai maṟaittal* (concealment of truth), *uṇmai tēṭutal* (seeking the truth)
- id: *mengungkap kebenaran* (to reveal the truth), *menyembunyikan kebenaran* (to conceal the truth), *kebenaran akan terungkap* (the truth will come out)
- tr: *gerçeği ortaya çıkarmak* (to bring the truth to light), *gerçeği gizlemek* (to hide the truth), *hakikati aramak* (to seek the truth)
- ko: *진실이 드러나다* (the truth emerges), *진실을 밝히다* (to reveal the truth), *진실을 숨기다* (to conceal the truth), *진상 규명* (clarification of the true facts)

**Distribution:** Present in all eight languages. The intransitive/passive framing of truth-revelation (truth as grammatical subject of an emergence verb) is documented in all eight languages. The transitive framing (agent reveals/conceals truth) is also documented in all eight languages. The proverbial assertion that truth ultimately prevails is documented in all eight languages. ko shows the most elaboration of the investigative sub-dimension, with *진상 규명* (clarification of the true facts) and *진실화해위원회* (Truth and Reconciliation Commission) as institutionalized expressions. The spatial metaphor of truth "coming to light" or "coming to the surface" is consistent across all eight languages.

### Dimension 11: Correctness of Reasoning, Judgment, and Understanding

**Definition.** This dimension concerns whether a judgment, inference, interpretation, or understanding is correct — whether it follows properly from evidence or reasoning. It is distinct from D1 (propositional correspondence) in that the evaluative target is a cognitive process or its output rather than a simple factual claim. Terms in this dimension appear in educational, philosophical, and argumentative contexts.

**Representative terms:**
- ka: *martebuli* (correct/appropriate/well-founded), *martebuloba* (correctness/soundness), *gamarṭleba* (justification/vindication)
- yo: *ó tọ́ pé* (it is right that), *àṣìṣe* (error/mistake/wrongdoing)
- fi: *perusteltu* (justified/well-founded), *perusteeton* (unfounded/groundless), *pätevä* (valid/sound)
- eu: *zuzena* (correct/right/just), *okerra* (wrong/incorrect/crooked), *zuzentasun* (correctness/justice)
- ta: *niyāyamāna* (just/fair/reasonable), *cariyāna* (correct/proper), *tavaṟāna* (wrong/erroneous)
- id: *tepat* (precise/fitting/appropriate), *wajar* (reasonable/natural/proper), *pantas* (fitting/appropriate/deserved)
- tr: *haklı* (justified/in the right), *haksız* (unjust/wrongful), *tarafsız* (impartial/neutral)
- ko: *타당* (valid/reasonable/sound), *타당성* (validity/soundness), *올바르다* (to be correct/right/proper), *옳다* (to be right/correct)

**Distribution:** Present in all eight languages, but the degree of differentiation from D1 (propositional correspondence) varies. In some languages (yo, ta), the same root covers both propositional correctness and correctness of reasoning. In others (ka, fi, ko), distinct vocabulary is used for these two functions. ka shows the most elaboration of the justification sub-dimension, with *gamarṭleba* (justification/vindication/acquittal) generating a productive derivational family. tr shows elaboration through the *haklı*/*haksız* pair (justified/unjustified), which covers both epistemic and moral justification. ko shows elaboration through the *타당성* (validity/soundness) cluster, specifically associated with argumentative and policy contexts.

### Dimension 12: Deliberate Deception vs. Innocent Error

**Definition.** This dimension concerns the distinction between statements or representations that are false because of deliberate intent to deceive and those that are false because of honest mistake or misunderstanding. Terms in this dimension appear in moral, legal, and everyday evaluative contexts where the agent's intent is relevant to the evaluation. This dimension is a sub-distinction within the broader domain of falsehood.

**Representative terms:**
- ka: *sicrue*/*ẗq̇uili* (deliberate lie) vs. *mcdari* (erroneous/mistaken, without implying intent); *q̇albi* (fake, implying deliberate deception) vs. *mcdari* (erroneous)
- yo: *irọ́* (deliberate lie) vs. *àṣìṣe* (error/mistake, without strong implication of intent); *ìtànjẹ́* (deliberate deception/fraud)
- fi: *valhe* (lie, deliberate) vs. *virhe* (error, neutral); *väärentää* (to forge, implying intent) vs. *vääristymä* (distortion, possibly unintentional)
- eu: *gezurra* (lie, deliberate) vs. *oker* (wrong/mistaken, without implying intent); *faltsifikatu* (to forge, implying intent)
- ta: *poy* (lie, deliberate) vs. *tavaṟu* (mistake/error, without implying intent); *vañcaṉai* (deliberate deception)
- id: *bohong* (deliberate lie) vs. *keliru* (innocent error/misunderstanding); *salah* (wrong, neutral to intent)
- tr: *yalan* (deliberate lie) vs. *yanlış* (wrong/incorrect, neutral to intent); *aldatıcı* (deceptive, implying intent) vs. *yanıltıcı* (misleading, possibly unintentional)
- ko: *거짓말* (deliberate lie) vs. *실수* (mistake, innocent); *허위* (falsehood, formal) vs. *오류* (error/fallacy, neutral)

**Distribution:** Present in all eight languages. Explicitly documented in F3 grouping tables for at least six languages (ka, fi, eu, id, tr, ko). id shows the most explicit lexical differentiation, with *bohong* (deliberate lie) vs. *keliru* (innocent error) explicitly distinguished in the F3 grouping tables. tr shows elaboration through the *aldatıcı* (deceptive, implying intent) vs. *yanıltıcı* (misleading, possibly unintentional) distinction. fi shows elaboration through the *väärentää* (to forge, implying intent) vs. *vääristymä* (distortion, possibly unintentional) distinction.

## Evaluation of Cross-Linguistic Support

### Strongly Supported Dimensions

The following dimensions are clearly lexicalized in all eight languages, appear in the F3 semantic grouping tables of all eight languages, and are supported by explicit contrasts in the F5 opposition tables of multiple languages:

- **D1 (Propositional Correspondence)** — The most consistently attested dimension. Every language has dedicated nominals for truth and falsehood in the propositional sense, and these are the most productive derivational bases in all eight languages.
- **D2 (Personal Honesty and Integrity)** — Universally present. The evaluative target (person/character) consistently distinguishes this from D1 across all languages. The absence of a single-word agentive for "truth-teller" is consistent across all eight languages.
- **D3 (Source Trustworthiness vs. Content Credibility)** — Explicitly documented in all eight languages, with the source/content distinction noted in F3 boundary notes for multiple languages.
- **D5 (Legal/Procedural Validity vs. Moral/Substantive Legitimacy)** — Present in all eight languages. The operative validity vs. invalidity sub-distinction is documented in all eight languages.
- **D9 (Evidential Grounding and Proof)** — Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages. The act-of-proving vs. product-of-proof distinction is documented in at least five languages.
- **D10 (Truth Revelation and Concealment as Processes)** — Present in all eight languages. The intransitive/passive framing of truth-revelation and the proverbial assertion that truth ultimately prevails are both documented in all eight languages.
- **D12 (Deliberate Deception vs. Innocent Error)** — Present in all eight languages. Explicitly documented in F3 grouping tables for at least six languages.

### Moderately Supported Dimensions

The following dimensions are present in most languages but show variable degrees of lexical elaboration:

- **D4 (Genuineness of Objects vs. Fraudulent Imitation)** — Clearly lexicalized in all eight languages, but the neutral-copy vs. fraudulent-fake sub-distinction is documented in only six languages. yo shows the least elaboration.
- **D6 (Precision and Exactness of Correspondence)** — Clearly lexicalized in at least six languages. Less elaborated in yo and ta as a distinct dimension separate from D1.
- **D7 (Authenticity of Inner States and Expressed Feelings)** — Present in all eight languages, but degree of elaboration varies considerably. ko shows the most elaboration; ta and tr show less.
- **D8 (Appearance vs. Underlying Reality)** — Present in at least six languages with explicit documentation. eu shows the most elaboration. yo and ta show less elaboration as a distinct lexical dimension.
- **D11 (Correctness of Reasoning, Judgment, and Understanding)** — Present in all eight languages, but degree of differentiation from D1 varies. Some languages use the same root for both propositional correctness and correctness of reasoning.

### Dimensions That Split, Merge, or Vary Across Specific Languages

**D1 and D11 merge in yo and ta.** The *tọ́* root in yo covers both propositional correctness (*ó tọ́*, "it is correct") and procedural/moral correctness (*ó tọ́ pé*, "it is right that") without lexical differentiation. Similarly, ta *cari* covers both factual correctness and procedural correctness. ka, fi, and ko maintain more distinct vocabulary for these two functions.

**D2 and D7 partially merge in eu and id.** eu *benetakoa* covers both "genuine (not fake)" and "sincere (not performed)," merging D4 and D7 partially. id *tulus* and *ikhlas* cover both personal honesty (D2) and authenticity of inner states (D7) without a sharp lexical boundary.

**D4 and D7 partially merge in eu.** *Benetakoa* applies to both genuine objects (D4) and genuine feelings/intentions (D7), while fi and ko maintain more distinct vocabulary for these two functions.

**D5 splits into three sub-dimensions in tr and ko.** tr distinguishes *yasal* (legal), *meşru* (legitimate), and *geçerli* (valid/in force) as three distinct terms. ko similarly distinguishes *합법* (lawful), *정당* (legitimate/justified), and *유효* (valid/in force). Other languages show less lexical differentiation within D5.

**D6 is weakly attested in yo and ta.** The precision/exactness dimension is not elaborated as a distinct lexical category in these languages; the concept is expressed through the general correctness vocabulary of D1.

**D8 is weakly attested in yo and ta.** The appearance-vs.-reality dimension is not elaborated as a distinct lexical category in these languages; the concept is expressed through more general vocabulary and discourse markers.

**D9 shows unique elaboration in eu.** The three-way *egiaztagarria* (verifiable) / *egiaztagaitza* (difficult to verify) / *egiaztaezina* (impossible to verify) distinction within the verifiability sub-dimension has no parallel in any other language in the dataset.

**D9 shows unique morphological elaboration in tr.** The *doğrulamak*/*yanlışlamak* productive morphological pair encoding the verification/falsification distinction, with parallel *doğrulanabilirlik*/*yanlışlanabilirlik* nominalizations, is unique in the dataset.

**D10 shows unique institutionalization in ko.** The *진상 규명* (clarification of the true facts) and *진실화해위원회* (Truth and Reconciliation Commission) expressions represent an institutionalized elaboration of this dimension not paralleled in other languages.

**D7 shows unique elaboration in ko.** The *진정성* (authenticity of inner state) cluster is more elaborated as a public evaluative category in ko than in any other language in the dataset, with a rich collocation network (*진정성 있다/없다*, *진정성 논란*, *진정성을 의심받다*) that has no close parallel elsewhere.

# G5 — Cross-Language Construction Comparison

## 1. Recurring Constructional Functions

The F4 data across the eight languages reveals the following main constructional functions in the truth domain. These are identified inductively from the documented construction types; the labels below are descriptive rather than theoretical.

**Function A: Attributing a truth-domain property to a subject (predicative attribution)**
Every language has a primary construction for asserting that something is true, false, genuine, accurate, valid, honest, etc. The subject receives a truth-domain predicate.

**Function B: Denying a truth-domain property (negative attribution)**
Every language has a construction for asserting that something is *not* true, not genuine, not valid, etc. This may be the same construction as Function A with a negation element, or it may use a distinct form.

**Function C: Modifying a noun with a truth-domain adjective (adnominal modification)**
Every language has a construction for placing a truth-domain evaluative term as a modifier of a noun (e.g., "accurate information," "forged document," "reliable source").

**Function D: Expressing that something transitions into a truth-domain state (inchoative/change-of-state)**
Every language has constructions for expressing that something comes to be true, turns out to be false, becomes valid, is revealed as genuine, etc. The subject undergoes a change.

**Function E: Expressing that an agent causes a truth-domain state (causative)**
Every language has constructions for expressing that an agent makes something true/false/valid/verified, forges a document, reveals the truth, conceals the truth, etc.

**Function F: Naming a truth-domain quality as an abstract entity (abstract nominalization)**
Every language has a strategy for producing a nominal that names a truth-domain property (truthfulness, accuracy, credibility, validity) as an abstract entity that can serve as subject, object, or genitive modifier.

**Function G: Naming the agent of a truth-domain action (agentive nominalization)**
Every language has constructions for naming persons who habitually lie, forge, or deceive. No language has a parallel lexicalized form for habitual truth-tellers.

**Function H: Framing a statement as frank, corrective, or truth-asserting (discourse framing)**
Every language has constructions that function as sentence-level markers signaling that what follows is the speaker's honest assessment, a correction of a prior assumption, or a frank disclosure.

**Function I: Evaluating whether a truth-domain quality is present or absent (existential/scalar predication)**
Several languages have constructions that treat a truth-domain quality as something that can be possessed or lacked, or that can be measured on a scale.

**Function J: Expressing that truth is revealed or concealed (truth-revelation/concealment)**
Every language has constructions in which truth is the grammatical subject of an emergence or concealment verb, treating truth as an entity that moves between hidden and visible states.

## 3. Narrative Analysis

### Recurring Cross-Language Constructional Patterns

**Predicative attribution (Function A) is the most universal construction type in the dataset.** All eight languages use a subject + copula/predicate construction to assert that something is true, false, genuine, accurate, valid, or honest. The main variation is in the form of the copula: Georgian uses an enclitic *-a* as the default (with the full copula *aris* required under negation), Yoruba uses a zero copula for stative predicates but requires *jẹ́* for nominal predicates, Finnish requires the partitive *totta* in the specific *olla totta* construction, Basque uses the 3sg copula *da* throughout, Tamil uses a zero copula with optional emphatic particles, Indonesian uses a zero copula with *adalah/merupakan* available in formal registers, Turkish uses a null copula as default with the *-dır* suffix restricted to formal/assertive contexts, and Korean uses *-ida* as the standard copular suffix. Despite this surface variation, the underlying constructional function is identical across all eight languages.

**The intransitive truth-revelation construction (Function J1) is documented in all eight languages and shows a consistent structural pattern.** In every language, truth can be the grammatical subject of an intransitive verb expressing emergence or disclosure. The spatial metaphor of truth "coming to light" or "coming to the surface" is consistent across all eight languages and all language families represented. This is one of the most robust cross-linguistic constructional patterns in the dataset. The specific verb varies (Georgian *gamovida*, Yoruba *farahàn*, Finnish *tulee ilmi*, Basque *ateratzen da azalera*, Tamil *veḷippaṭṭatu*, Indonesian *terungkap*, Turkish *ortaya çıktı*, Korean *드러나다/밝혀지다*), but the constructional pattern — truth as subject, intransitive emergence verb as predicate — is consistent.

**The agentive asymmetry (Function G) is consistent across all eight languages.** Every language has lexicalized single-word agentives for habitual liars and forgers, but none has a parallel lexicalized agentive for habitual truth-tellers. This is explicitly documented in the F4 construction tables for all eight languages and is not a gap in documentation. The concept of "truth-teller" is expressed periphrastically in all eight languages: Georgian *simarṭlis madziebeliˈ* (seeker of truth), Yoruba *ẹni tó bá sọ òtítọ́* (whoever speaks the truth), Finnish (no documented form), Basque *egiazale* (marginal), Tamil *uṇmaiyāḷar* (marginal), Indonesian (no documented form), Turkish (no documented form), Korean *진실을 말하는 사람* (a person who tells the truth). This asymmetry is consistent across unrelated language families and appears to reflect a cross-linguistic pattern in how the truth domain is lexicalized.

**The discourse-framing construction (Function H) is present in all eight languages but shows the widest variation in degree of grammaticalization.** At one extreme, Indonesian *sebenarnya* and Turkish *aslında* are fully grammaticalized discourse markers whose compositional meanings are no longer active. At the other extreme, Yoruba uses a hortative construction (*jẹ́ kí a sọ òtítọ́*, let us speak the truth) for the same discourse function rather than a grammaticalized adverbial. Between these extremes, Georgian *simartle rom vtq̇vat* is a subjunctive construction that retains compositional transparency, Finnish *totta puhuen* is a participial phrase, Basque *egia esan behar* is a purposive construction, Tamil *uṇmaiyil* is a locative case form, and Korean *사실을 말하자면* is a conditional verbal phrase. The functional outcome is the same across all eight languages — signaling that what follows is the speaker's honest assessment or a correction of a prior assumption — but the constructional form varies from fully grammaticalized to fully compositional.

**The abstract nominalization strategy (Function F) is universal and productive in all eight languages.** Every language produces abstract nouns naming truth-domain qualities through a suffix or circumfix on an adjectival or verbal base. The specific morphological mechanism varies — Turkish *-luk*, Finnish *-uus*, Basque *-tasun*, Tamil *-mai*, Indonesian *ke-...-an* circumfix, Korean *-seong*, Georgian *-eba/-oba*, Yoruba *ì-* prefix — but the functional outcome is the same. In all languages, the resulting nominal names the property as an abstract entity and participates in evaluative constructions. This pattern is productive in all eight languages and shows no signs of being lexicalized or fossilized.

---

### Important Asymmetries, Substitutions, and Restrictions

**The most important asymmetry is the one-way blocked pathway for truth-teller agentives.** As documented above, the agentive derivation that produces liars and forgers does not produce truth-tellers in any of the eight languages. This is not a gap in documentation; it is explicitly noted in the F4 construction tables for all eight languages. The asymmetry is consistent across unrelated language families (South Caucasian, Niger-Congo, Finno-Ugric, isolate, Dravidian, Austronesian, Turkic, Koreanic) and appears to reflect a cross-linguistic pattern in how the truth domain is lexicalized.

**The *있다/없다* existential frame in Korean substitutes for the copular predication strategy used in other languages for abstract quality nominals.** In Korean, *-seong* quality nominals (*진정성*, *신빙성*, *타당성*) cannot take *-hada* as a predicative suffix; they require the existential *있다/없다* frame instead. This is a morphological restriction documented in the F4 construction tables for Korean and has no parallel in other languages. In all other languages, abstract quality nominals participate in the standard copular predication construction (Function A). The Korean restriction creates a constructional substitution: where other languages say "it is credible" (copular predication), Korean says "credibility exists" (existential predication).

**The *osoittautua* + translative construction in Finnish substitutes for the periphrastic *menjadi/di* constructions used in other languages for inchoative truth-evaluation.** Finnish uses the verb *osoittautua* (to turn out to be) with a translative case complement (*väite osoittautui epätodeksi*, the claim turned out to be false) as the primary inchoative construction for truth-domain adjectives. The translative case is obligatory and encodes the resultant state. Other languages use periphrastic constructions with general-purpose change-of-state verbs (Indonesian *menjadi*, Basque *bihurtu*, Turkish *çıkmak*, Korean *밝혀지다/드러나다*) without a dedicated case form for the resultant state. The Finnish construction is more morphologically compact but requires knowledge of the translative case.

**The *fi* instrumental serial verb construction in Yoruba substitutes for the morphological causative constructions used in other languages.** Yoruba uses the serial verb *fi* (use/take) as the primary causative strategy: *ó fi ẹ̀rí hàn lójú ìgbìmọ̀* (he presented evidence before the court), *wọ́n fi ìtànjẹ́ gbà owó rẹ̀* (they used deception to take his money). This construction encodes the instrument or means by which an outcome is brought about. Other languages use morphological causatives (Finnish *väärentää*, Turkish *doğrulamak*, Indonesian *memalsukan*) or transitive verbs (Georgian *gaq̇alba*, Korean *위조하다*) for the same function. The Yoruba serial verb construction is more periphrastic but more transparent in encoding the causal chain.

**The *değil* negation strategy in Turkish is more restricted than the negation strategies in other languages.** In Turkish, *değil* is the sole negation strategy for adjectival predicates; no alternate negation construction is attested in this domain. In other languages, multiple negation strategies are available: Georgian has both *ar aris* (syntactic) and *u-...-o* privative circumfix (morphological); Finnish has both *ei ole* (syntactic) and *epä-* prefix (morphological); Indonesian has both *tidak* (syntactic, for adjectival predicates) and *bukan* (syntactic, for nominal predicates); Korean has both *아니다* (for nominal predicates) and *-지 않다* (for adjectival predicates). The Turkish restriction to a single negation strategy is notable.

**The *bukan/tidak* distinction in Indonesian and the *아니다/-지 않다* distinction in Korean represent a cross-linguistically unusual split in negation strategy based on predicate type.** In both languages, nominal predicates and adjectival predicates require different negation forms: Indonesian *bukan* (nominal) vs. *tidak* (adjectival), Korean *아니다* (nominal) vs. *-지 않다* (adjectival). This split is not documented in the other six languages, where a single negation strategy applies across both predicate types (Georgian *ar aris*, Yoruba *kò*, Finnish *ei ole*, Basque *ez da*, Tamil *illai*, Turkish *değil*).

**The three-way inchoative verb distinction in Korean (*드러나다/밝혀지다/판명되다*) substitutes for the single inchoative verb used in most other languages.** Korean documents three distinct inchoative verbs for truth-revelation with slightly different nuances: *드러나다* (exposed/surfaced, stronger sense of unwanted revelation), *밝혀지다* (revealed through investigation, more neutral), *판명되다* (officially determined, most formal). Other languages typically use a single inchoative verb for this function (Georgian *gamovida*, Finnish *tulee ilmi*, Basque *ateratzen da*, Tamil *veḷippaṭṭatu*, Indonesian *terungkap*, Turkish *ortaya çıktı*). The Korean three-way distinction encodes nuances of agency, formality, and the nature of the revelation process that other languages express through context or additional modifiers.

---

### Cases Where a Function Is Weakly Expressed, Constructionally Indirect, or Absent

**The discourse-framing function (Function H) is most weakly expressed in Yoruba.** While all other languages have a grammaticalized or semi-grammaticalized adverbial form for introducing frank disclosures or corrections, Yoruba uses a hortative construction (*jẹ́ kí a sọ òtítọ́*, let us speak the truth) for this function. This construction is more compositionally transparent and less grammaticalized than the equivalents in other languages. The F4 data for Yoruba does not document a grammaticalized discourse marker parallel to Indonesian *sebenarnya*, Turkish *aslında*, or Tamil *uṇmaiyil*.

**The existential/scalar predication function (Function I) is most weakly expressed in Georgian, Finnish, and Turkish.** In these languages, abstract quality nominals participate in the standard copular predication construction (Function A) rather than in a dedicated existential or scalar frame. The *있다/없다* existential frame documented in Korean, and the *badago/ez dago* frame documented in Basque, have no parallel in Georgian, Finnish, or Turkish. In these languages, the evaluative question "does this source have credibility?" is expressed through the same copular construction as "is this statement true?" — there is no constructional differentiation between the two evaluative targets.

**The morphological causative-inchoative chain (Function E2) is absent or marginal in Yoruba, Tamil, and Korean.** While Turkish shows a productive *-laş-/-leş-tir-* chain and Basque shows a *-tu* causative on adjectival bases, Yoruba, Tamil, and Korean do not document this chain. In these languages, causative meaning is expressed through light-verb constructions (Yoruba *fi...hàn*, Tamil *col/pēcu*, Korean *하다*) rather than through morphological causative derivation.

**The morphological inchoative (Function D2) is restricted or absent in most languages.** Only Georgian (*-deba* suffix, restricted to the *mart-* root), Turkish (*-laş/-leş* suffix, restricted to some bases), and Basque (*-tu* intransitive, lexically restricted) show morphological inchoatives in the truth domain. In Finnish, the morphological inchoative (*aitoutua*, to become authentic) is explicitly marked as marginal. In Yoruba, Tamil, Indonesian, and Korean, the periphrastic inchoative (Function D1) is the only documented strategy. This means that the morphological inchoative is a minority strategy in the dataset, with the periphrastic inchoative being the universal default.

**The parallel morphological opposition for verification/falsification (documented in Turkish as *doğrulamak/yanlışlamak*) is absent in most languages.** While Turkish shows a productive morphological pair encoding the verification/falsification distinction with parallel derivational stacking (*doğrulanabilirlik/yanlışlanabilirlik*), no other language in the dataset shows this as a productive morphological pair. Finnish has *todistaa* (to prove) and *osoittaa epätodeksi* (to show to be false), but these are not morphologically parallel. Basque has *frogatu* (to prove) and *gezurtatu* (to give the lie to), but these are not a parallel pair encoding the same philosophical distinction. This is a single-language observation for Turkish.

**The three-way verifiability distinction (*egiaztagarria/egiaztagaitza/egiaztaezina*) documented in Basque is absent in all other languages.** No other language in the dataset documents a three-way morphological distinction within the verifiability sub-domain. Other languages show only a binary verifiable/unverifiable opposition (Finnish *todistettavissa/ei todistettavissa*, Korean *증명 가능한/불가능한*, Indonesian *dapat dibuktikan/tidak dapat dibuktikan*). The Basque three-way distinction — capable of being verified / difficult to verify / impossible to verify — is a single-language observation.

**The *-hada/-doeda* stative/agentive distinction documented in Korean is absent in all other languages.** Korean documents a systematic semantic distinction between *jinsil-hada* (to be truthful, active/performed quality) and *jinsil-doeda* (to be truthful, inherent/resultant quality). This morphological distinction between performed and inherent quality is not documented in any other language in the dataset. In all other languages, a single predicative form covers both the active/performed and the inherent/resultant readings of truth-domain predicates.

## 2. Narrative Analysis

### Patterns Recurring Across Unrelated Language Families

**Abstract property nominalization is universal in the dataset.** Every language produces abstract nouns naming truth-domain qualities through a suffix or circumfix on an adjectival or verbal base. The specific morphological mechanism varies — Turkish *-luk*, Finnish *-uus*, Basque *-tasun*, Tamil *-mai*, Indonesian *ke-...-an* circumfix, Korean *-seong*, Georgian *-eba*, Yoruba *ì-* prefix — but the functional outcome is the same: a nominal that names the property as an abstract entity and participates in evaluative constructions. This pattern is productive in all eight languages and shows no signs of fossilization; new forms can be created as needed.

**The agentive asymmetry (liar lexicalized, truth-teller not) is consistent across all eight languages and all language families represented.** Georgian (South Caucasian), Yoruba (Niger-Congo), Finnish (Finno-Ugric), Basque (language isolate), Tamil (Dravidian), Indonesian (Austronesian), Turkish (Turkic), and Korean (Koreanic) all have lexicalized single-word agentives for habitual liars and forgers, but none has a parallel lexicalized agentive for habitual truth-tellers. The derivational process that generates *yalancı* (liar), *aṣírọ́* (liar), *valehtelija* (liar), *gezurti* (liar), *poyyaṉ* (liar), *pembohong* (liar), *거짓말쟁이* (liar) does not generate a corresponding positive-role agentive in any of the eight languages. The concept of "truth-teller" is expressed periphrastically in all eight languages. This is not a gap in documentation; the F4 construction tables for all eight languages explicitly note the absence and describe the periphrastic alternatives. The asymmetry is consistent across unrelated language families.

**The spatial metaphor of straightness underlying truth and correctness is attested in all eight languages.** Georgian *marṭl-* (straight/right), Yoruba *tọ́* (straight/correct), Finnish *oikea* (right, also directional), Basque *zuzen* (straight/correct), Tamil *nēr* (straight/direct), Indonesian *benar* (correct), Turkish *doğru* (straight/correct/true), and Korean *olbareuda* (upright/correct) all show a root or base that combines spatial straightness with epistemic or moral correctness. The antonym in several languages is also spatial: Turkish *eğri* (crooked/dishonest), Basque *oker* (crooked/wrong). This convergence across unrelated language families is the most consistently attested morphological/semantic pattern in the dataset.

**The intransitive/passive framing of truth-revelation is documented in all eight languages.** In every language, truth can be the grammatical subject of an intransitive or passive verb expressing emergence or disclosure. This constructional pattern — treating truth as an entity that moves from concealment to visibility — is consistent across all eight languages and all language families. The specific verbs vary (Georgian *gamovida*, Yoruba *farahàn*, Finnish *tulee ilmi*, Basque *argitara atera*, Tamil *veḷippaṭṭatu*, Indonesian *terungkap*, Turkish *ortaya çıkmak*, Korean *드러나다*), but the structural pattern is the same.

**The discourse-framing adverbial derived from a truth base is attested in seven of eight languages.** Georgian *marṭla* (really/truly), Finnish *totta puhuen* (to tell the truth), Basque *egia esan behar* (truth be told), Tamil *uṇmaiyil* (in truth/actually), Indonesian *sebenarnya* (actually/in truth), Turkish *aslında* (actually/in fact), and Korean *사실을 말하자면* (to tell the truth) all function as sentence-level discourse markers introducing corrections, frank statements, or contrasts with appearance. The degree of grammaticalization varies — Indonesian *sebenarnya* and Turkish *aslında* are fully grammaticalized, while others are more compositional — but the functional pattern is consistent across unrelated language families.

---

### Striking Asymmetries

**The most striking asymmetry is the one-way blocked pathway for truth-teller agentives.** As documented above, all eight languages have lexicalized agentives for liars and forgers but none for truth-tellers. This is not a gap in documentation; it is consistently documented as an absence across the F4 construction tables and F7 agentive nominalization sections for all eight languages. **The degree of morphological productivity of the primary truth root varies enormously across languages.** Turkish *doğru* and Georgian *marṭl-* generate the largest documented derivational families, extending into technical domains (Turkish: *doğrusal*, linear; *doğrultu*, direction; *doğrulanabilirlik*, verifiability), religious domains (Georgian: *marṭlmadidebeli*, Orthodox Christian; *marṭlsaidumlo*, true sacrament), and institutional domains (Georgian: *marṭlmsajuleba*, justice system; *marṭlc̣era*, orthography). This asymmetry is not explained by language family or morphological type alone; it reflects the specific historical and cultural elaboration of the truth domain in each language.

**The negative agentive derivation is more productive than the positive agentive derivation in all eight languages.** Not only is the truth-teller agentive absent, but the forger/deceiver agentive is more elaborated than any positive-role agentive in the truth domain. Finnish has *väärentäjä* (forger), *valehtelija* (liar), and *pettäjä* (deceiver) but no parallel positive-role agentives. ### One-Way or Blocked Derivational Pathways

**The truth-teller agentive pathway is blocked in all eight languages.** The agentive derivation productive for negative roles does not generate truth-tellers. This is the most consistently documented blocked pathway in the dataset, attested across all eight languages and all language families represented.

**The *-hada* predicative suffix is blocked for *-seong* quality nominals in Korean.** Korean *-seong* nominals (*jinjeongseong*, *sinbyeongseong*, *tadangseong*) cannot take *-hada* as a predicative suffix; they require the existential *있다/없다* frame instead. This is a morphological restriction documented in the F4 construction tables for Korean and has no parallel in other languages.

**The *-garri* potential suffix in Basque does not extend to all truth-domain bases.** While *egiaztagarria* (verifiable), *fidagarria* (trustworthy), *sinesgarria* (believable), and *frogagarria* (provable) are all attested, the suffix does not apply freely to all truth-domain bases. **The *-itas* suffix in Indonesian applies only to loanword bases.** Indonesian *validitas*, *kredibilitas*, and *otentisitas* use the *-itas* suffix, but this suffix does not extend to native Indonesian roots (*\*benarittas*, *\*asliitas* are not attested). **The causative-inchoative chain (*-laş-/-leş-*) in Turkish is restricted to bases that have already undergone *-laş-* derivation.** *Meşrulaştırmak* (to legitimize) is attested because *meşrulaşmak* (to become legitimate) is attested, but the chain does not apply freely to all truth-domain adjectives. *\*Doğrulaştırmak* (to make more correct) is not documented as a standard form; *doğrulamak* (to verify) uses a different derivational path (*-la-* directly on the base).

# G5 — Cross-Language Construction Comparison

## 1. Main Recurring Constructional Functions

The F4 data across the eight languages reveals the following main constructional functions in the truth domain. These are identified inductively from the documented construction types; the labels are descriptive rather than theoretical.

**Function A: Attributing a truth-domain property to a subject (predicative attribution)**
Every language has a primary construction for asserting that something is true, false, genuine, accurate, valid, or honest. The subject receives a truth-domain predicate.

**Function B: Denying a truth-domain property (negative attribution)**
Every language has a construction for asserting that something is *not* true, not genuine, not valid, etc. This may be the same construction as Function A with a negation element, or it may use a distinct form.

**Function C: Modifying a noun with a truth-domain evaluative term (adnominal modification)**
Every language has a construction for placing a truth-domain evaluative term as a modifier of a noun (e.g., "accurate information," "forged document," "reliable source").

**Function D: Expressing that something transitions into a truth-domain state (inchoative/change-of-state)**
Every language has constructions for expressing that something comes to be true, turns out to be false, becomes valid, is revealed as genuine, etc. The subject undergoes a change.

**Function E: Expressing that an agent causes a truth-domain state (causative)**
Every language has constructions for expressing that an agent makes something true/false/valid/verified, forges a document, reveals the truth, conceals the truth, etc.

**Function F: Naming a truth-domain quality as an abstract entity (abstract nominalization)**
Every language has a strategy for producing a nominal that names a truth-domain property (truthfulness, accuracy, credibility, validity) as an abstract entity that can serve as subject, object, or genitive modifier.

**Function G: Naming the agent of a truth-domain action (agentive nominalization)**
Every language has constructions for naming persons who habitually lie, forge, or deceive. No language has a parallel lexicalized form for habitual truth-tellers.

**Function H: Framing a statement as frank, corrective, or truth-asserting (discourse framing)**
Every language has constructions that function as sentence-level markers signaling that what follows is the speaker's honest assessment, a correction of a prior assumption, or a frank disclosure.

**Function I: Evaluating whether a truth-domain quality is present, absent, or measurable (existential/scalar predication)**
Several languages have constructions that treat a truth-domain quality as something that can be possessed or lacked, or that can be measured on a scale, distinct from simple copular predication.

**Function J: Expressing that truth is revealed or concealed (truth-revelation/concealment)**
Every language has constructions in which truth is the grammatical subject of an emergence or concealment verb, treating truth as an entity that moves between hidden and visible states.
